Jlratorial  hearings. 

The  arms  of  Robert  Hovell  of  Ashfleld,  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664,  were  Sable,  a 
ci’oss  Or.  His  crest  was  a  greyhound  couchant  Or,  collared  and  lined  Sable.  Beneath  the 
tricking  in  Harl.  MS.  1085  are  the  words  “p  Wm  Flower,  Norroy.”  Flower  was  Voitov  King 
of  Arms  from  1580  to  1588. 

The  arms  allowed  at  the  same  Visitation  to  John  Hovell  als  Smith,  of  Ash  Booking, 
.  clerk,  who  married  the  daughter  and  coheir  of  Horsman,  of  Berge  Apton,  and  was  cousin  german 
to  Robert  Hovell  above  mentioned,  were : — Sable,  a  cross  Or  between  four  water  bougets  Argent, 
a  crescent  for  difference ;  on  a  shield  of  pretence,  for  Horsman,  Azure,  a  horse  barnacle  (an 
instrument  used  by  farriers  to  curb  horses)  Or  between  three  plates ;  on  a  chief  party  per  pale 
indented  Gules  and  Sable,  two  roses  Argent.  The  authority  for  these  insignia,  Harl.  MS.  1085, 
corresponds  to  a  similar  MS.  at  the  Gollege  of  Arms. 

Martin,  the  son  of  Adam  Hovell,  a  kinsman  of  the  Hovells  of  Wyverstone,  is  the  first 
member  of  the  family  who  is  known  to  have  owned  lands  in  Ashfield,  Bad  well,  and  Hunston. 
He  purchased  them  in  1258  by  Fine  dated  42  Henry  III.  In  “Guillim’s  Roll  of  Arms,” 
Harl.  MS.  6137,  written  about  the  year  1300,  Sir  Robert  Hovell,  of  Wyverstone,  bears  the  golden 
cross  on  the  black  shield  allowed  to  Robert  Hovell,  of  Ashfield,  in  1664.  According  to  the 
Roll  in  Cottonian  MS.  Caligula,  A.  16,  which  has  been  printed  in  “Parliamentary  Writs,  Vol.  I,” 
the  same  arms  were  used,  a  generation  later,  by  Sir  Hugh  Hovell  and  Sir  Stephen  Hovell, 
Sir  Robert’s  sons. 

The  inscriptions  in  Great  Ashfield  chancel  to  Lord  Thurlow’s  grandfather,  Smith  (als 
Hovell),  and  his  son  are  accompanied  by  shields  bearing  a  bend  between  six  billets,  the  crest 
being  a  talbot  collared  and  lined.  Lord  Thurlow’s  hatchment,  on  the  other  hand,  had  Thurlow 
quartering  the  rightful  arms  of  Hovell  of  Ashfield,  Sable,  a  cross  Or.

Mill  of  Hokrt  Unapp,  1565. 

Robert  Knappe  of  Wetheringsett  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolk,  yeoman,  7th  Sept.  1563.  I 

and  my  son  John  Knapp  the  elder  stand  bound  to  Nicholas  P’trich  of  Creting  and  Thomas 
Colby  of  Brockford  to  pay  yearly  to  Anne  my  wife,  late  the  wife  of  Robert  Horseman,  the 
suihe  of  tenne  powndes,  by  way  of  dower.  I  give  and  bequeath  to  the  said  John  lands  in 
Nedham  M’kett  and  Barkinge,  the  lease  of  Bosberowe  and  the  annuity  payable  to  me  out  of 
the  Manor  of  Bushoppeshall  in  Battisford.  Unto  John  Knapp  the  yonger  my  son  tenement  and 
lands  in  Barking,  Creating,  Battisford  and  Badley.  To  Robert  Knappe  my  son,  lands.  To 
Thomas  Knapp  my  son  lands  in  Coddenham.  Studds,  after  the  decease  of  my  wife,  to  pass  to 
John  Knapp  the  younger  my  son.  Lands  in  Battisford  and  Combs  to  George  Knapp  my  son 
at  his  age  of  one  and  twenty  years.  (Many  other  lands  described  in  detail.)  To  Myrable 
my  daughter.  To  Thomas  Horsman  and  Mary  Horsman,  children  of  Anne  my  wife,  when 

twenty  one.  My  four  youngest  children,  viz :  John  the  longer,  Robert,  Thomas  and  George. 
To  the  children  of  John  Knapp  the  elder  my  son  when  twenty  one.  He  and  John  Knapp 

the  younger  to  be  my  executors.  Last  will  of  Julyan  Aldame  my  late  mother.  Probat. 

2  May  1564.  Norwich  Consistory,  Book  “  Knightes,”  fo.  304b. 

The  first  wife  of  the  testator  and  the  mother  of  his  children,  was  Margaret,  daughter  of 

Edmond  Poley  Esq.,  of  Badley,  by  Mirabel,  daughter  of  John  Garneys,  of  Kenton.  Her  brother, 

John  Poley,  married  Anne,  daughter  of  Lord  Wentworth  of  Nettlestead,  a  near  kinswoman  to 
Queen  Elizabeth.  Mirabel  Knapp,  her  daughter,  who  became  the  wife  of  Robert  Hovell  ats  Smith, 
of  Ashfield,  was  thus  connected  with  some  of  the  best  families  of  Suffolk.  Her  will  follows  those 

of  her  husband  and  her  eldest  son,  who  predeceased  her. 

Many  yeomen  of  the  sixteenth  century  were  large  landed  proprietors,  and,  like  Robert 
Knapp,  married  the  daughters  of  the  gentry  around  them.  Like  him,  too,  they  founded  families 
whose  pedigrees  are  given  in  the  Heralds’  Visitations.

The  Reverend  Thomas  Thurlow,  testator’s  brother  in  law,  was  the  husband  of  Elizabeth 
Smith  ats  Hovell,  testator’s  sister,  and  the  father  of  Edward  Thurlow,  afterwards  Lord  Chancellor 
of  England.  Susan  Thurlow,  the  aunt,  was  widow  of  the  Rev.  Nicholas  Thurlow,  Vicar  of 
Brent  Eleigh,  whose  will  had  been  proved  at  Norwich  on  the  22‘*  of  January  1 73|,  and  sister 
of  Robert  Smith  ats  Hovell,  testator’s  father.  The  marble  stones  bequeathed  by  the  testator 
still  paved  the  sanctuary  in  Ashfield  church  when  Davy  visited  the  place  in  the  earlier  years 
of  the  nineteenth  century.

Mary  Torkington  of  Brettenham  in  the  County  of  Suffolk,  widow,  10th  May  1693.  To 
my  daughter  Elizabeth  Torkington  my  ffarme  called  Keeler’s  Rick-a-downe  in  Helmsted  and

The  testatrix  was  widow  and  executrix  of  Robert  Torkington  of  Brettenham,  gent.  Mary 
her  eldest  daughter  married  her  cousin  James  Torkington  of  Stewkeley,  co  Hunt.,  one  of  the 
representatives  of  the  fine  old  visitation  family  of  that  place.  Elizabetli  her  second  daughter 
married  the  Rev.  Benjamin  Brundish,  Rector  of  Bildeston  in  Suffolk.  Anne  the  youngest  daughter,, 
whose  will  is  given  above,  married  Robert  Smith  (ats  Hovell)  of  Ashfield. 

Mary  Torkington  the  testatrix  was  daughter  and  heir  of  William  Gilbert  Esq.  of  Colchester, 
whilst  her  husband’s  mother  was  daughter  of  Ambrose  Gilbert  of  that  town.  Through  their 
ancestress  Jane  Wingfield,  daughter  of  Robert  Wingfield  of  Brantham,  these  ladies  derived  from 
King  Edward  the  First  and  the  Fitz-Alan’s.  The  steps  of  this  descent  are  given  in  Burke’» 
Royal  Descents,  in  the  section  relating  to  Lord  Thurlow.

HOVELL  OF  ASH  FI  ELD. 


11 


This  pedigree,  of  which  variants  exist  at  the  College  of  Arms,  is  referred  to  by  Sir 
Edward  Bysshe  in  his  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1661 ;  but  it  is  full  of  mis-statements,  and  save 
when  corroborated  by  other  testimony,  doubtful  throughout.  William  Smyth,  otherwise  called 
Ilovell,  the  grandfather  of  Richard  Hovell  of  Stratford,  died,  an  old  man,  in  1510.  (See  Hovell 
ok  Haugitlev.)  The  Gawdy  wills  and  pedigrees  are  alike  silent  respecting  Anne  Gawdy,  his 
supposed  wife,  the  daughter  of  Anne  Bassingborne.  If  she  ever  existed  she  lived  a  generation 
later  than  her  husband,  for  her  brother,  Thomas  Gawdy,  and  sister,  Katherine  Everard,  were 

still  alive  in  1581.  There  was,  indeed,  an  Anne  Gawdy,  who  did  marry  ....  Hovell  ats 

Smyth.  But  she  was  grand-daugliter  to  Anne  Bassingborne  and  is  one  of  the  devisees  of  Honor 

Gawdy  her  mother,  in  her-  will,  dated  25  May  1601,  now  in  the  Probate  Registry  at  Ipswich. 

Robert  Hovell  ats  Smyth,  the  husband  of  Mirabel  Knapp,  so  far  from  being  the  heir  of 
William  Hovell  and  the  mythical  Anne  Gawdy,  was,  as  his  widow  and  children  testified  officially 
in  1612,  the  son  of  a  Thomas  Hovell  ats  Smyth,  and  the  grandson  of  John  Hovell  ats  Smyth. 
(Camden’s  Visitation  of  Suffolk,  College  of  Arms.)  Besides,  he  lived  two  generations  later  than  the 
parents  assigned  him  in  the  pedigree. 

We  read  again  of  Hugh  Hovell,  the  4th  son  of  Anne  Gawdy,  who  dwelt  at  Nayland, 

and  died  sine  prole.  The  wills  and  evidences  ignore  him.  Hugh  Hovell,  the  grandson  of 

William  Smyth,  otherwise  Hovell,  died  at  Haughley  in  1597,  leaving  a  wife  and  a  brood  of 

children  behind  him. 

There  are  other  slips ;  “  Christian,”  for  example,  “  Wife  to  Hobart  of  Waldingfield,” 
married  quite  another  man,  John  Sharpe  of  Norton.  It  was  her  sister,  Marian  Smyth,  who 
became  the  wife  of  William  Hubbard.  See  Hovell  of  Badwell. 

And  what  shall  we  say  respecting  the  mysterious  William  Hovell  who  is  said  to  have 
married  Elizabeth  Harsick  1  He  made  no  will,  paid  no  subsidies,  bought  or  sold  no  lands. 

His  very  existence  is  as  yet  unproven.  The  inscription  of  1535,  formerly  in  Lopharn  chancel, 
according  to  Blomefield, 1  who  had  never  seen  it,  but  quotes  from  Le  Neve’s  Collections,  is  to 
the  memory  of  a  William  Novell.  There  were  other  Novells  in  Norfolk  at  the  time.  But 

here  again  we  have  a  glimpse  of  that  ignis-fatuus  evidence,  which  the  compiler  of  the  pedigree 
seems  to  have  followed  throughout.  A  William  Smyth  of  Ashfield,  apparently  of  the  Smyth 
ats  Hovell  family,  made  his  will,  now  at  the  Bury  Registry,  in  1545,  leaving  house  and  lands  at 
Lopham  in  Norfolk.  It  would  seem  from  faded  indications  in  the  Register  Book  called  Longe 
to  have  been  copied  officially,  a  proof  that  it  had  attracted  the  attention,  years  ago,  of  some 
forgotten  lawyer  or  genealogist.  The  following  is  an  abstract : — 

“The  viij  daye  of  June,  1545,  I,  Wiltm  Smyth  of  Lyttle  Ashfeild,  otherwise  called  Badwell 
ashe,  in  the  Countie  of  Suffie  yeoman  make  my  laste  will.  I  bequeathe  to  Robarde  my  sonne  & 
his  lieyres  my  house  A  lande  in  little  Ashfeild  &  greate  Ashfeild  at  his  age  of  xxiiij  yeares,  he 
then  to  have  yt  peaceably.  If  he  fortune  to  dye  wthowte  yssue  said  landes  to  remayne  to  my 
daughters  equally.  I  give  my  house  &  lande,  free  &  coppie,  in  Loppam  in  the  Countie  of  Norfolke 
to  Margarett  my  doughter  at  her  age  of  xxtie  jTeares.  Robarte  my  sonne  to  go  to  schole  tyll  he 
can  both  wryte  &  reade.  To  my  daughters  Alice  &  Marion  twentye  markes  a  pece  «kc.  To  the 
mendynge  of  the  Slowe  at  Porland  gate.  To  Robarte  Smyth,  Arthure  my  neve’s  child.  To  Richearde 
my  nevewe  a  cowe.  Executors  Robarte  Smyth  A  John  Gayford.  Probat  vij°  die  Julij  1545.”

Will  of  Ht'llen  Herrington,  1664. 

The  fourteenth  day  of  March  1664  I  Hellen  Kerrington  of  Great  Waldingfeild  in  the 
Countie  of  Suffolke  late  the  wife  of  Robert  Kerrington  of  Newton  neare  Sudbury  in  the  Countie 
aforesaid,  Gentleman,  doe  make  this  my  last  will  in  manner  following.  I  bequeath  my  soule  into 
the  hands  of  Almightie  God  trusting  through  the  meritts  of  Jesus  Christ  to  be  made  pertaker 

of  life  everlasting.  My  said  husband  did  make  me  sole  executrix  of  his  last  will  and  did 

thereby  giue  vnto  his  and  my  five  daughters,  Elizabeth,  Hellen,  Mary,  Judith  and  Lettice  to 
every  of  them  three  hundred  pounds  at  theire  dayes  of  marriage  or  ages  of  twenty  one  yeares, 
and  vnto  me  Boyton  Hall  in  Monkes  Eliegh  that  I  should  dispose  of  it  to  augment  the  portions 
of  my  said  daughters  and  of  my  sonne  also.  The  personall  estate  of  my  late  husband  is  nothing 
neare  sufficient  to  pay  his  debts  and  satisfie  his  daughters  portions  (that  is  to  say)  Mary  the 
wife  of  Master  Samuell  Newson  to  whom  I  haue  already  given  her  three  hundred  pounds  with 
one  hundred  more  as  an  increase,  Elizabeth,  Hellen,  Judith  and  Lettice.  I  doe  hereby  giue  my 
other  fower  daughters  more  over  and  above  the  money  giuen  vnto  them  by  theire  fathers  will, 
To  my  grandchild  Mary  Newson  tenn  pounds.  At  the  request  of  my  sonne  Robert  Kerrington- 
by  my  Indenture  bearing  date  13th  August  in  the  fifteenth  yeare  of  his  Majesties  Raigne  that 
now  is  I  have  conveyed  to  him  the  aforesaid  messuage  and  farme  called  Boyton  Hall,  in  Monkes 
Eleigh  and  other  messuages  and  closes  in  Glemsford,  Monkes  Eleigh  and  Milding,  as  alsoe  that 
messuage  called  Fennes  in  Monkes  Eleigh  which  John  Howell  ats  Smith  Gentleman  late  father 
of  mee  the  said  Hellen  Kerrington  late  purchased  of  one  Tho :  Cutler  Esquire  and- Alice  Cutler, 
widdowe,  his  mother.  I  will  that  the  farme  called  the  Tyled  place  and  the  said  Messuage  called 
Fenns  shall  be  sold  to  discharge  the  sevarall  legacies  of  my  said  daughters.  I  doe  nominate  Hellen 
Kerrington  my  daughter  and  Thomas  Plampyn  of  Bredstreete,  London,  silkman,  my  louing  freind 

and  kinsman  Executors  of  this  will.  To  this  my  last  will  containing  tenn  sheetes  of  paper  to 

everie  of  them  I  have  subscribed  my  name  as  alsoe  to  the  Head  and  last  sheete  thereof  I  have 
put  my  Seale.  Probatum  tricesimo  die  Junij  1669  Juramento  Thomie  Plampyn  vnius  Executorum, 
Hellena  Kerrington  filia  et  alter  Execu?  renunciante. 

P.C.C.  73  Coke.

This  is  the  earliest  known  will  of  any  Hovell  alias  Smyth.  The  Hovells  of  Wyverstone 
had  formerly  held  the  manor  of  Horpole  in  Wickham  Market  which  adjoins  Dallinghoo,  and 
there  was,  in  1512,  a  way  in  the  latter  parish  called  Hoi’pole  Street,  and  a  messuage  named 
Hewals  which  had  belonged  to  one  Margaret  Hewale.  In  1557  Henry  Hovell  ais  Smyth,  the 

youngest  son  and  next  heir  of  Robert  Smith  and  Alice  his  wife,  was  in  possession  of  the  lands 

which  had  belonged  to  his  father.  Dallinghoo  Court  Dolls,  Public  Record  Office,  Portfolio  203,  77.

Will  of  Joint  Jfobdl,  1568. 

The  first  daie  of  September,  1568,  I  John  Hovell,  clex-ke,  vicker  of  the  Churche  of 
Parham  in  the  countie  of  Suff :  in  the  dioces  of  Norwch,  al  thoughe  sicke  in  bodye  yet  of  hole 
and  gfighte  Remembrance,  lauded  be  God,  make  this  my  laste  will  &  Testament.  I  bequeathe 
my  soule  to  allmightie  god  my  savior  and  Redemer,  suerlie  beleveinge  and  trustinge  thorowe 

his  mercie  to  be  saved.  And  my  bodie  I  will  shalbe  buried  at  the  discretion  of  my  executor

The  Arms  allowed  to  Richard  Ho  veil  of  Hillington  at  the  Norfolk  Visitation  of  1613 
were  Sable,  a  crescent  Or  with  a  crescent  for  difference.  Upon  the  monument  in  Hillington 

church  to  the  memory  of  Richard  Hovell,  who  married  Margery  Ford  and  died  in  1611,  is  a 

shield  in  which  Hovell  as  above  impales  Ford  of  Essex.  Upon  a  later  monument,  evidently  for 
Richard  Hovell,  his  son,  who  married  Frances  Ferneley  and  died  in  1653,  Hovell  quarters  Ford 
and  impales  Ferneley,  Or,  on  a  bend  Vert  three  bucks’  heads  caboshed  Argent  attired  of  the 
field.  At  the  Norfolk  Visitation  of  1664  (Harl.  M.S.,  1085),  the  arms  assigned  to  Sir  William 
Hovell  of  Hillington,  who  married  the  daughter  and  heir  of  Thomas  Lilly,  of  South  Lynn,  were  : — 
Quarterly,  1  and  4,  Hovell  ;  2,  Harsick,  Or,  a  chief  indented  Sable  ;  and  3,  Ford,  Argent,  a 
wolf  salient  Sable  ;  on  a  shield  of  pretence,  Lilly,  Argent,  a  fess  Ermine  between  three  roses 

Gules.  A  pedigree  by  Sir  Richard  St.  George  is  referred  to  in  support  of  this  achievement,  but 

the  quartering  of  Harsick  rests  upon  doubtful  authority,  as  we  have  shown  on  page  11  when 
treating  of  the  Hovell  pedigree  in  Harl.  MS.,  1103.

In  the  will  of  John  Ford,  1557,  Richard  Hovell,  his  son-in-law,  is  called  Richard  Smyth. 
In  the  Visitation  pedigree  of  Foord  of  Essex  (Harl.  MS.,  1541)  he  is  styled  Richard  Hovell, 
alias  Smyth.  In  the  parish  registers  of  Stratford,  in  Suffolk,  where  he  resided  for  some  years, 
his  children  are  baptised  as  Smyths  from  1567  to  1571,  as  Hovells  alias  Smyth  in  1573  and 
1574,  and  as  Hovell  only  in  1576.  In  their  several  wills  his  father  writes  himself  “William 
Hovell  alias  Smyth”  in  1582,  and  his  grandfather,  “William  Smyth,”  in  1540.  All  three,  father, 
son,  and  grandson,  are  frequently  entered  in  the  earlier  Suffolk  Subsidies  or  Tax  Rolls  as  Smyth 
only. 

The  earliest  known  mention  of  Hovell,  alias  Smyth,  occurs  in  a  survey  of  Ashfield  with 
Badwell  Ash  in  1512.  (Rentals  Surveys,  Public  Record  Office,  Portfolio  if).  In  this 
manuscript  the  lands  of  “  Wiffrn  Smyth  otherwise  called  Willm  Hovell  ”  are  described  in  detail. 
In  December,  1524,  Robert  Hovell  ats  Smyth,  a  substantial  Suffolk  landowner,  made  his  will 
(Arch.  Suff.)  desiring  to  be  buried  in  the  church  of  Dallinghoo.  In  1541  William  Hovell  alias 
Smyth  purchased  lands  in  Ashfield  by  a  Fine  recorded  in  Easter  Term  in  the  thirty-third  year 
of  King  Henry  the  Eighth. 

Why  William  Smyth  of  Ashfield  in  1512  was  otherwise  called  William  Hovell  we  do  not 
know.  Conjecture  has  been  rife  as  to  the  origin  of  this  and  similar  alternative  surnames.  A 
small  treatise  could  be  written  upon  the  subject.  So  far  from  necessarily  indicating  illegitimacy 
they  were  not  infrequently  assumed  as  a  mark  of  distinction,  and  by  people  of  means  and 


HOVE LL  OF  HAUGHLFA. 


25 


standing.  They  were  rather  numerous  in  the  sixteenth  century.  Amongst  the  Visitation  families 
of  Suffolk  were  Chapman  alias  Barker,  Chapman  alias  Felton,  Herberd  alias  Yaxley,  and  Reeve 
alias  Wright.  What  we  do  know  is  that  about  the  middle  of  the  sixteenth  century  a  number 
of  well-to-do  Smyths  in  Suffolk,  Essex  and  London,  began  to  call  themselves  Hovell  alias  Smyth 
indicating  that  they  considered  the  latter  form  of  appellation  the  more  honourable  of  the  two.

Norfolk.  By  another  deed,  dated  6th  June,  5th  James  I,  he  enfeoffed  to  Thomas  Hovell,  gent., 
her  son,  his  Manors  of  Pontes  and  Bunnetts,  Ac.,  in  Bulmer,  Henney,  Gestingthorpe,  Middleton 
and  Twynstede,  co  Essex.  He  held  also  the  Manors  of  Borowall,  Hillington,  Albyons  in 
Hillington,  Ac.,  co.  Norfolk,  together  with  lands  in  Flitcham,  Ac.  He  died  on  the  first  of

On  the  north  wall  of  the  Chancel  is  a  mural  monument,  with  the  effigies  of  a  gentleman 
in  his  gown,  and  his  wife,  on  their  knees,  thus  inscribed : 

“  The  monument  of  Richard  Hovell  of  Hillington,  in  the  countie  of  Norfolk,  Esq.  ;  being 
of  the  age  of  77  years  and  upwards,  finished  his  course  the  30th  of  November  1611,  in  peace  with 
God,  in  charity  with  all  men,  and  now  resteth  here  with  expectation  of  the  Resurrection,  in 
assurance  of  eternal  glorification.  Margery  Hovell,  wife  of  the  aforesaid  Richard  Hovell  Esq  : 
deceased,  and  one  of  the  daughters  and  heyres  of  John  Ford,  of  Frating,  in  the  Countie  of 
Essex,  Esq. ;  who  having  lyved  vertuously  and  comfortably  with  her  said  husband,  44  years,  did 
beare  unto  him  4  sonnes  and  9  daughters,  whereof  there  are  yet  twelve  alive  to  her  great 
comfort,  being  all  growne  to  the  perfect  state  of  men  and  women.” 

On  the  summit  is  the  shield  of  Hovell ,  sable ,  a  crescent  or  impaling  Ford,  argent,  a  wolf 
salient  sable.” 

Blomefield’s  “  Norfolk,”  vol.  viii,  466.

In  the  seventeenth  century  siege  of  Lynn,  1642,  the  burgesses  and  their  adherents,  about 
five  thousand  in  number,  headed  by  Sir  Hamon  L’Estrange,  Sir  Richard  Hovell  (who  had  been 
knighted  the  previous  year)  and  other  Royalist  gentlemen,  bravely  defended  the  place  for  three 
weeks  against  the  Earl  of  Manchester  with  his  army  of  eighteen  thousand  soldiers ;  but  the  Earl 
of  Newcastle,  who  la)’  at  Lincoln  with  the  King’s  troops,  refusing  to  assist  them  they  were 
compelled  to  surrender.  Sir  Richard  was  one  of  the  hostages  taken  by  the  enemy.  There  is  a 
fine  portrait  of  him  at  Hillington  Hall,  which  was  originally  erected  by  Richard  Hovell,  Esq., 
his  father,  in  1627.  See  “  History  of  Lynn,”  1812,  by  William  Richards,  whose  sympathies, 
however,  were  with  the  Puritans;  “A  Norfolk  Tour,”  2  vols.,  Norwich,  1829  ;  and  “The  Civil 
War  in  the  East  of  England,”  recently  published,  for  brief  details  respecting  this  event.

Founder’s  kin  of  Henry  Chichele,  Archbishop  of  Canterbury,  their  collateral  ancestor,  at  All  Souls’  College,  Oxford.  Their 
pedigrees,  Hovell’s,  ffolkes’s,  Stuart’s,  Wake’s,  etc.,  are  given  in  “  Stemmata  Chicheleana”  and  other  works  bearing  upon  this

The  Will  of  Humphrey  Style,  Esq.,  of  Langley,  in  Beckenham,  co.  Kent  (P.C.C.  152  Tenison)  is  dated  27th  March  1718. 
and  contains  the  following  passages : — “  To  be  buried  in  my  vault  in  the  South  Isle  of  Beckenham  church  amongst  my 
ancestors.  Upon  the  marriage  of  my  daughter  Elizabeth,  wife  of  Sir  John  Elwill,  I  settled  Manors  &c.  in  Kent  to  uses 
as  are  mentioned  in  the  settlements  for  the  benefit  of  said  daughter,  her  husband  and  their  children.  I  brought  Frances 
Shippe  out  of  Norfolk  from  her  parents.  She  thus  became  destitute  of  the  comfort  and  assistance  she  would  have  had 
from  them.  I  give  her  £500  if  living  with  me  at  the  time  of  my  death,  and  also  all  the  household  ffunuture  which  shall 
then  be  in  my  now  dwelling  house  or  appartment  at  Kenninghall  Place  in  the  County  of  Norfolk.  Unto  my  son  Humfrey 
Style  (whom  I  make  with  Mr.  Edward  Gilbert  of  Breadstreet,  London,  my  Executors)  the  rest  of  my  messuages,  lands, 
goods,  &c.”  This  will  was  proved  4th  July  1718,  by  the  oath  of  Humphrey  Style,  one  of  the  Executors.

William  Hovell  went  to  Ireland  in  1641  and  served  under  Lords  Broghill  and  Inchequin. 
He  became  a  merchant  at  Kinsale,  co.  Cork,  and  was  “Sovereign”  or  Mayor  of  that  place  in 
1656.  He  was  forty-four  years  old  when  Prince  Rupert  occupied  Kinsale,  as  appears  from  a 
deposition  which  Dr.  Caulfield  has  printed  in  the  Appendix  to  his  edition  of  the  Kinsale 

Council  Book.  This  would  give  1610  as  the  approximate  date  of  his  birth.  His  descendants 

believe  that  he  was  a  scion  of  the  Hillington  Hovells,  one  of  whom,  Francis  Hovell,  the 
brother  of  Sir  William,  was  living  at  Portsmouth  when  he  was  Surveyor  of  the  Custom  House 
there.  Now  Hugh  Hovell,  of  Kenninghall,  in  Norfolk,  Francis  Hovell’s  cousin,  had  a  brother 
William  Hovell,  who  exactly  corresponds  with  his  Irish  namesake.  He  is  last  mentioned  in  1637 
in  Chancery  Proceedings  connected  with  his  mother’s  will.  He  was  then  about  six  and  twenty 
years  of  age,  and  able  to  make  a  start  in  life  with  the  legacy  which  she  bequeathed  him. 
(See  Pedigrees,  Hovell  of  Hillington.)  And  there  was  another  contemporary  William  Hovell, 
brother  of  Sir  Richard,  who  married  Anne,  daughter  of  Richard  Bulwer,  by  Grissel  his  wife, 
concerning  whose  later  life  we  seem  to  be  equally  in  the  dark.

The  information  upon  which  this  Pedigree  is  based  was  derived  mainly  from  Lieut.  Colonel  E.  F.  Jemmett  Browne, 
late  35th  Regiment,  of  the  family  of  Browne  of  Riverston,  descendants  of  the  Archbishop.  There  is  a  pedigree  at  the  Heralds 
College,  London,  of  Hovell  of  Mount  Hovell,  connected  with  Farmar. 


The  traditional  account  of  the  Irish  Hovells,  as  handed  down  in  the  Farmar  family,  is  this.  Robert  Farmar,  second 
son  of  Richard  Farmar  of  Thurles  Beg,  co.  Tipperary,  and  his  wife,  Elizabeth  Phaire,  married,  in  1700,  Grace,  daughter  of 
William  Hovell,  who  had  been  Mayor  of  Cork  in  1693.  The  latter  was  of  an  old  Norfolk  family,  and  Hugh  Hovell,  his 
uncle,  resided  on  part  of  his  estate  named  Kenninghall  Park.  His  father,  William  Hovell,  was  a  major  in  the  Army,  and 
served  under  Lords  Broghill  and  Inchiquin  during  the  Irish  rebellion  of  1641.  His  name  (usually  spelt  Howell)  is  frequently 

mentioned  in  the  records  of  the  time.  William  Hovell,  the  younger,  his  son,  escaped  with  difficulty  from  Cork  when  James 

the  Second  invaded  Ireland  in  1689,  the  city  being  closely  '  guarded  by  James’s  troops,  aud  suffered  heavy  losses,  but 
returned  when  tranquility  was  restored.  He  was  a  man  of  literary  ability  and  political  foresight.  His  work  (anonymous) 

on  the  consequences  of  prohibiting  the  export  of  woollen  materials  manufactured  in  Ireland,  printed  in  Dublin  in  1690,  lias 

been  disastrously  confirmed  by  subsequent  events.  He  died  6th  June  1697,  Grace,  his  wife,  predeceasing  him  in  1694. 
They  were  interred  in  St.  Peter’s  church,  Cork,  the  burial  place  of  so  many  of  their  kindred.  Hovell  Farmer,  their 
grandson,  the  husband  of  Katherine  Dorothea  Russell,  was  a  popular  and  successful  physician  in  that  city. 


1  Jemmett  Browne  (grandson  of  Thomas  Browne  of  Cork,  who  married  Helena  Hovell  in  1666)  was  son  of  Edward 
Browne,  Mayor  of  Cork,  by  Judith,  daughter  of  Warliam  Jemmett  of  Derry,  whose  wife,  Judith  Richmond  alias  Webb,  was 
granddaughter  of  Nicholas  St.  John,  the  brother  of  Oliver  St.  John,  Lord  Deputy  of  Ireland. 

He  entered  Trinity  College,  Dublin,  in  1718,  and  was  ordained  priest  in  1723  by  Peter  Browne  his  kinsman,  then  Bishop 
of  Cork.  From  1733  to  1743  he  was  Dean  of  Ross ;  from  1743  to  1745,  Bishop  of  Killaloe ;  from  1745  to  1772,  Bishop  of 
Cork;  from  1772  to  1775,  Bishop  of  Elphin;  and  from  1775  to  1782  Archbishop  of  Tuam. 

He  married,  first,  Alice  Waterhouse,  in  1723,  and  had  issue.  His  second  wife  was  Jane  Barry,  widow,  of  St.  Anne’s 
parish,  Dublin.  He  died  in  June,  1782,  and  was  buried  at  Ballinaspic,  county  Cork.  Dr.  Maziere  Brady’s  Clerical  Records  of 
Cork,  Cloyne  and  Ross,  vol.  ii,  428.

brother  in  law  of  Robert  Hovell,  was  buried  at  Fransham  Magna  in  1594,  he  is  probably 

identical  with  the  younger  of  these  men.  Davy  says,  on  what  authority  we  know  not,  that 

Mary  Sexton  married  as  her  second  husband  John  Smith,  a  suggestive  name  in  this  connection.

to  Defendant  as  cozen  and  next  heire  to  deceased.  Conscience  followeth  the  law  in  such  cases.

Barnes  is  yet  living,  and  may  over  live  Cheslyn.  Confesseth  he  doth  refuse  to  join  in  sale  with

The  Arms  in  Harl.  MS.  1476,  and  in  the  original  Visitation  of  London  at  the  Herald’s  College,  are  Sable,  a  crescent 
Or,  charged  with  a  crescent  for  difference,  Hogan  Ilovell  having  been  the  younger  brother  of  Nicholas  Hovell,  and  the  second 
son  of  his  father.  The  Crest,  a  sea  lion  Ermine,  is  also  charged  with  a  crescent. 

It  will  be  noticed  that  these  are  the  Armorial  bearings  of  Hovell  als.  Smith  of  Haughley,  and  their  descendants  the 
Hovells  of  Hillington. 

The  spelling  “  Howell  ”  crops  up  with  remarkable  frequency  in  Hovell  evidences,  and  is  occasionally  used,  even  now, 
by  strangers  in  addressing  members  of  the  latter  family.  In  ignorance  of  this,  Hovell  documents  of  great  interest  have 
been  overlooked  by  antiquaries  and  genealogists.  In  the  thirteenth  and  fourteenth  century  the  name  was  mostly  written  Houell.

Jtrntorial  Searings. 

The  arms  allowed  to  William  Hovell  at  the  Northampton  Visitations  were  those  of  Hovell 

of  W  y  verstone  in  Suffolk,  Sable,  a  cross  Or.  A  crest,  too  suggestive  perhaps  of  a  legend  to 

please  exact  heralds,  was  added,  viz.,  A  griffin  sejant  Argent,  beaked,  legged,  and  winged  Azure, 
plucking  a  broken  spear  Or  from  his  breast  (vulned  Gules)  with  his  dexter  claw,  and  holding 
the  handle  thereof  with  his  sinister  claw.  Marl.  MS.  1553,  fol.  7J+. 

The  Houell  pedigree  which  follows,  taken  from  the  Visitations  of  Northamptonshire,  1566 
and  1619  (Marl.  MS.  1553),  is  collated  with  those  entered  in  the  Visitation  of  Oxfordshire  and 
Dorset  in  1574  (Marl.  MSS.  1556  and  1539).  In  the  two  latter  the  name  is  written  “  Hovell.” 
There  is  a  mass  of  evidence  to  show  that  the  names  Howell  and  Hovell  were  interchangeable, 
the  alternative  spellings  sometimes  occurring  in  the  same  document.  The  Hovells  appear  to  have 
been  Oxfordshire  landowners  as  early  as  the  thirteenth  century.  Hugh  de  Hawille  held  lands 
in  Garsington,  near  Oxford,  of  Sir  William  de  Valence  by  the  service  of  half  a  knight’s  fee  in 

the  7th  year  of  King  Edward  the  First,  1279.  Rotuli  Hundredorum,  vol.  ii,  721.

[which]  I  haue  assigned  to  Anthonye  Winkefelde  Esquior,  one  of  the  gent,  vsshers  to  her  Majestie,

1  “  According  to  the  Norman  authorities  the  cradle  of  the  great  Baronial  House  of  Doyley  was  Ouilly-le-Basset,  in  the 
arrondisement  of  Falaise.  They  were  a  branch  of  the  Bassets,  and  undoubtedly  continued  in  Normandy  till  the  close  of  the 
last  century,  as  they  were  represented  at  the  Assembly  of  the  Nobles  in  1789.  Their  coat  of  arms,  Argent  a  bend  Gules, 
became  in  England  Or,  two  bendlets  Azure,  sometimes  varied  with  a  counterchange. 

“  Cil  d’Oillie,”  entered  in  the  Roman  de  Rou  among  the  combatants  at  Hastings,  was  the  Robert  D’Oily  who  became, 

through  the  Conqueror’s  favour,  one  of  the  most  potent  nobles  of  the  realm.  He  received  the  two  baronies  of  Oxford  and 

St.  Valery,  acquired  the  honour  and  Castle  of  Wallingford  through  his  Saxon  wife  Algitha,  and  was  appointed  the  King’s 

Constable.  Within  six  years  of  the  Conquest  he  had  built  at  Oxford  a  strong  castle,  a  bridge  over  the  Isis,  and  a  collegiate 
church  dedicated  to  St.  George,  besides  either  repairing  or  re-erecting  the  walls  of  the  town.  This  fortress  gave  him  “  the 
sway  of  the  whole  County,  and  he  was  so  powerful  a  Man  in  his  time,”  says  Dugdale,  “  that  no  one  durst  oppose  him.” 

“  In  1084  William  the  Conqueror  kept  his  Easter  at  Abingdon,  and  was  most  splendidly  entertained  by  Robert  D’Oilly  ” — 

Lysons.  “Dugdale  does  not  furnish  us  with  the  date  of  Robert’s  death.  He  left  an  only  daughter  Maud,  married  first  to 
Milo  Crispni,  and  then  to  Brien  Fitz  Count,  but  she  had  no  children  and  died  a  nun.  She  had  inherited  her  mother’s 
barony  of  Wallingford.  That  of  St.  Valery  -was,  it  is  believed,  given  by  her  father  to  “his  very  familiar  frieiyl  John  de 

Ivery,  who  had  accompanied  him  in  the  wars,  as  his  sworn  brother  ” ;  and  the  honour  of  Oxford  (or  Hocknorton,  as  it  is 


48 


SUFFOLK  MANORIAL  FAMILIES. 


called  in  the  pedigree),  with  the  office  of  Constable  of  England  passed  to  her  uncle  Nigel.  The  son  of  the  last  mentioned, 
Robert  II,  was  a  great  benefactor  to  the  Church.  He  founded  a  Priory  for  Black  Canons  at  Ossney,  near  Oxford,  “  among 
the  Isles  that  Isis  Ryver  there  maketh,”  in  1129.  Besides  this  he  founded  and  richly  endowed  Missenden  Abbey  in  Oxfordshire 
His  eldest  son  Henry  was  the  father  of  two  brothers,  with  whom  the  line  ended  in  the  time  of  Henry  III,  and  of  three, 

sisters  who  became  their  heirs.  The  eldest,  Marjory,  was  the  wife  of  Henry  de  Newburgh,  Earl  of  Warwick,  to  whom  she 

brought  the  Barony  of  Hocknorton;  Maud  married  Maurice  de  Gant:  and  Joan,  Simon  Fitz  Walter.” 

“  There  remained,  as  next  in  blood,  Henry  D'Oiley,  a  son  of  Robert’s  (II)  second  son  Gilbert.  His  family  remained 
in  Oxfordshire.  One  of  them,  Thomas  D’Oyley,  first  bought  Chiselhampton,  for  many  generations  the  principal  residence  of 
his  descendants.  His  grandson,  Sir  Robert  D’Oyley,  “  a  great  courtier  in  the  reign  of  Queen  Elizabeth,”  met  his  death  at 
the  so-called  Black  Assizes  of  Oxford  in  1577.”  His  wife  was  Elizabeth,  daughter  of  Lord  Keeper  Nicholas  Bacon. 

“  The  family  had  their  share  of  trouble  in  the  Civil  War.”  “  Greenland  House,  the  property  of  Sir  John  Doyley,  was 
in  the  month  of  May,  1644,  garrisoned  for  the  King,  with  a  view  of  commanding  the  passage  of  the  Thames  from  Henley 
and  Reading  to  London.  After  sustaining  a  long  and  severe  siege  from  the  Parliamentary  forces  under  Major-General 
Browne,  the  house  having  been  almost  reduced  to  ashes,  it  surrendered  on  the  11th  of  July. — Lyson’s  Bucks.  “  Sir  John 
Doyley,  impoverished  by  his  loyalty  and  unable  to  undertake  the  cost  of  the  restoration  of  Greenland  House,  sold  the  ruins 
and  retired  to  Chiselhampton,  in  which  estate  he  was  succeeded  by  his  son  Sir  John  Doyley.  Of  the  old  home  of  the 
Doyleys  at  Greenlands  nothing  remains,  but  in  the  grounds  of  the  present  house  may  still  be  seen  piles  of  cannon-balls 
which  have  been  gathered  *  from  the  site  of  the  former  mansion.” — Memorials  of  the  Danver’s  Family.  “Sir  John  D’Oyley  was 
created  a  baronet  in  1666,  whose  last  descendant,  Sir  William,  died  in  the  early  part  of  the  present  century.  With  him  the 

title  is  supposed  to  have  expired;  though  Sir  Bernard  Burke  declares  “that  fact  to  be  very  doubtful.”  But  he  makes  no 

further  allusion  to  any  existing  representative  or  possible  claimant.  Another  baronetcy  was  given  in  1821  to  Sir  John 
D’Oyley,  British  Resident  at  Kandy,  but  speedily  became  extinct.  A  third  was  granted  (1663)  to  Sir  William  D’Oyley  of 
Shottisham,  in  Norfolk,  who  had  served  with  great  gallantry  under  Gustavus  Adolphus.”  Duchess  of  Cleveland,  R.B.A. 

For  a  full  account  of  this  family,  based  upon  authorities  which  have  been  carefully  verified,  see  Bavley’s  Account  of 
the  House  of  D’Oyley.  London :  Bowyer,  Nichols  and  Son,  1845. 

The  following  particulars  concerning  the  Danvers  Family,  more  immediately  connected  with  William  Hovell  of  Sulgrave, 
are  taken  from  chapter  x  of  the  Memorials  of  the  Danvers  Family,  by  Dr.  Macnamara,  who  spells  the  name  “Howell” 
throughout: — John  Danvers  came  of  age  in  1545,  and  amongst  the  Additional  Charters  in  the  British  Museum,  Culworth 
Series,  No.  38,886,  is  the  deed  of  livery  from  the  Crown  to  John  Danvers,  son  and  heir  of  William  Danvers,  of  his  father’s 
lands.  The  deed  has  attached  to  it  a  fine  impression  of  the  groat  seal,  and  is  dated  at  Westminster,  6th  December, 
37  Henry  VIII.  John  Danvers  married  his  third  cousin,  Dorothy  Ravnesford,  daughter  of  Sir  William  Raynesford,  of  Great 
Tew.  His  life  was  short,  for  he  died  in  August,  1556,  aged  32,  leaving  his  children  in  the  charge  of  their  mother  and  Sir 
William  Raynesford.  John  Danver’s  will  (P.C.C.  11,  Kitchen),  1556,  provides  for  the  burial  of  his  body  in  the  chancel  of 
Culworth  Church.  He  leaves  legacies  to  his  four  daughters,  Temperance,  Justice,  Prudence,  and  Fortitude,  mentions  his  wife, 
Dorothy,  and  his  sons,  Samuel  and  Daniel.  As  overseers  to  his  will  he  appoints  Sir  William  Raynsford,  his  father-in-law, 
his  cousin,  Sir  William  Hungerford  (the  son  of  his  aunt,  Susan  Danvers,  and  Lord  Walter  Hungerford),  and  Sir  Richard 
Fenys,  who  was  also  his  first  cousin.  The  will  was  proved,  7th  August,  1556,  by  Sir  William  Raynsford,  acting  for  his 
daughter  Dorothy,  and  Additional  Charter  38,889,  dated  12th  November,  2  Elizabeth,  with  impressions  of  the  great  seal 
attached,  allows  Dorothy  to  comply  with  the  provisions  of  her  husband’s  will.  John  Danvers’  Inquisition  Post  Mirtem  (No. 
71,  3  and  4  Philip  and  Mary,  part  i).  was  taken  at  Daventre,  in  Northampton,  18th  January,  1556-57.  His  widow,  Dorothy, 
married  again;  her  second  husband  was  Sir  Thomas  Benger  ( vide  Berry’s  Kent  Genealogies,  228).  Her  daughter  Temperance 
married  Anthony  Dillon  ( vide  Betham’s  Baronetage),  of  Farthinghoe,  Northampton.  The  next  daughter,  Justice,  married  Richard 
Andrewes  {vide  Harleian  MSS.,  1553,  pp.  210-214,  and  1094,  pp.  78-89).  The  third  daughter,  Prudence,  married  William 
Hovell,  son  of  John  Hovell  of  Eynsham. 

Amongst  the  proceedings  in  Chancery  of  the  time  of  Elizabeth  (D.  d.  7,  No.  34,  7th  May  1585),  which  have  been 
preserved,  and  one  now  in  the  Record  Office,  is  a  petition  from  members  of  the  family  of  Danvers  of  Culworth  to  the  Lord 
Chancellor,  setting  forth  that  they  were  all,  through  John  Danvers,  of  the  blood  and  kindred  of  the  late  father  in'  God, 
William  Wickham,  and  asking  that  their  children  might  be  admitted  to  the  privilege  of  Founder’s  kin  at  Winchester  College 
and  at  New  College,  Oxford.  The  petition  was  refused  on  the  score  of  certain  technical  objections  which  the  wardens  of 
the  two  Colleges  raised,  one  of  them  being  that  the  petitioners  had  not  named  their  children,  or  shewn  that  they  had  any 
who  were  admissible  as  scholars ;  but  the  descent  was  not  denied,  and  the  document  is  valuable  as  a  confirmation  of  the 
descent  of  those  members  of  the  family  who  signed  it.  The  following  is  a  part  of  the  petition: — “Samuel  Danvers  of 
Culworth,  in  co.  Northampton,  Esq.,  and  Daniel  Danvers,  Gent.,  Anthony  Dalande,  Gent.,  and  Temperance  his  wife,  Richard 
Andrewes,  Gent.,  and  Justice  his  wife,  William  Hovell,  Gent.,  and  Prudence  his  wife,  Robert  Barker  Gent.,  on  behalf  of  his 
sons  being  infants  by  Mary  his  late  wife,  Henry  Sacheverell,  Gent.,  and  Dorothy  his  wife,  and  George  Blunte,  Gent.,  and 
Anne  his  wife,  complain  that  whereas  William  of  Wickham  sometime  Bishop  of  Winchester  founded  2  Colleges  and  the  same 
endowed  with  large  possessions,  and  ordained  among  other  things  that  his  kinsmen  should  enjoy  the  special  privilege  of 
being  admitted  fellows  and  scholars  of  the  said  Colleges  before  all  others :  And  whereas  the  said  Samuel  Danvers,  Daniel 
Danvers,  Temperance,  Justice,  Prudence,  Mary,  Dorothy  and  Anne  are  lineally  descended  of  the  ‘  bloude  and  kynred’  of  the 
said  Bishop,  to  wit,  the  said  Samuel,  Daniel,  Temperance,  Justice  and  Prudence  being  the  lawful  sons  and  daughters  of  John 
Danvers  of  Culworthe,  Esq.,  deceased,  son  of  William  Danvers  of  Culworthe,  Esq.,  deceased  and  Elizabeth  his  wife  also 
deceased,  and  the  said  Mary  late  wife  of  the  said  Robert  Barker,  Dorothy  late  wife  of  the  said  Henry  Sacheverell,  and  the 
said  Anne  now  wife  of  the  said  George  Blunte,  sisters  of  the  said  John  Danvers  son  of  the  said  William  and  Elizabeth, 
which  Elizabeth  was  daughter  of  one  Richard  Fenys,  of  Broughton  in  co.  Oxford,  Esq.,  son  of  Henry  Fern’s  Lord  Saye  and 
Setele  and  Margaret  his  wife,  which  Margaret  was  the  daughter  and  heir  of  William  Mickham,  Esq.,  son  of  Sir  Thomas 
Wickham  alias  Perrott,  Knight,  son  of  William  Perrott,  Gent.,  and  Alice  his  wife  which  Alice  was  the  daughter  of  one 

C  hampneys  and  Agnes  his  wife  which  Agnes  was  the  daughter  of  Wickham . of  the  said  Reverend  Bishop.”  The 

lower  part  of  this  document  is  torn  away.

The  26th  day  of  December  in  the  first  yeare  of  King  James,  I,  Thomas  Smith  of  Ashfield 
Magna  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolk,  do  pronounce  this  to  be  my  last  will  and  testament.  I 
bequeath  my  soul  to  Almighty  God  my  maker,  and  to  Jesus  Christ  his  deare  sonne  my 
Redeemer,  with  full  hope  and  assurance  of  pardon  and  forgiveness  of  my  sinnes.  I  give  to 

Elizabeth  my  wife  the  house  I  dwell  in  and  the  lands  thereto  belonging  in  Ashfield  and  Badwell 

Ashe,  to  hold  for  her  life,  except  a  close  called  Hargins,  bought  of  John  Whitehead  of  Hunston 
gent.,  which  I  give  to  Arthur  Smith  my  brother,  together  with  the  reversion  of  my  other  lands 

on  my  wife’s  decease.  To  the  poore  of  Ashfield  five  pounds.  My  wife  to  pay  John  Smith  and 

William  Smith  my  brothers  xx3  a  piece  yearly  during  their  lives.  To  Margaret  Noble,  wife  of 

Thomas  Noble,  and  to  Luce  Smith,  wife  of  John  Smith  my  brother,  and  to  Charity  Smith,  wife  of 

William  Smith  my  brother,  ten  shillings  each.  To  Elizabeth,  Dorothie  and  Thomasin,  the  daughters 

of  John  Smith  my  brother,  vi1  xiij8  iiijd  a  piece.  To  Ann,  Marie  and  Elizabeth  Smith,  the 
daughters  of  my  brother  William  Smith,  vi1  xiijs  iiijd  a  piece.  To  Thomas  Smith,  son  of  John 
Smith  my  brother,  and  to  John,  son  of  Richard  Smith  my  brother,  to  each  ten  pounds.  To 
Robert  Smith  my  brother  xxs :  and  to  Elizabeth,  the  wife  of  Francis  Morris,  xx*.  John  Baker 
and  George  Carter,  witnesses.  Proved  on  the  second  day  of  April,  1604,  by  the  executrix. 

Arch.  Sudb.  Book  “  Copping,”  fo.  304. 

The  bequest  to  Elizabeth,  the  wife  of  Francis  Morris,  connects  the  testator  with  the 
llovells  of  Surrey;  and  in  spite  of  discrepancies  one  seems  to  identify  him  with  Thomas  Smyth 
of  Ashfield,  the  uncle  of  that  lady,  who  died  sine  prole.

The  nyn tenth  daie  of  Julie  1617  I  Robert  Smith,  Cittizen  of  London,  doe  make  this  my 
last  will.  My  psonall  estate  shalbe  accordinge  to  the  Lawdable  custome  of  the  Cittie  of  London 
devided  into  three  equal  partes.  One  thirde  parte  I  give  vnto  my  deare  and  lovinge  wife, 
Elizabeth  Smith.  One  other  third  parte  I  give  vnto  my  sonne  Robert  Smith.  Out  of  the  other 
third  parte  I  give  theise  legacies  heare  after  specified,  viz.  : — Vnto  my  deare  and  lovinge  mother, 
Elizabeth  Smith,  one  Annuytie  of  tenne  poundes  duringe  her  life.  Vnto  my  brother  Thomas 
Smith  two  hundreth  poundes.  Vnto  my  brother  John  Smith  two  hundreth  poundes,  and  to  the 
use  of  his  children  one  hundreth  poundes,  be  they  more  or  lesse,  to  be  equallie  devided  betweene

Andrea  Bassano  of  London,  1633,  who  married  Anne,  daughter  of  Francis  Morris  of 
Wanstead,  in  co.  Essex,  Esq.,  was  the  second  son  of  Arthur  Bassano,  musician  to  Queen 
Elizabeth,  and  grandson  of  Anthony  Bassano,  an  Italian,  musician  to  Henry  the  Eighth,  Edward 
the  Sixth  and  Queen  Mary.  He  and  other  members  of  his  family  entered  pedigrees,  since 
printed  by  the  Harleian  Society,  in  the  Visitations  of  London,  Essex,  Hertfordshire,  etc.,  and 
have  had  numerous  descendants.

The  following  account  of  John  Smith  als  Hovell,  Vice  Provost  of  King’s  College,  Cambridge 
who  seems  to  have  been  a  near  kinsman  of  the  Smiths  of  Badwell  and  of  Surrey,  is  taken 
from  the  manuscript  Catalogue  by  Anthony  Allen  relating  to  the  Provosts  and  Fellows  of  that 
house. 


“John  Smith,  the  younger.  John  Smith,  alias  Hovell,  was  born  at  Eton,  Bucks,  about 
the  Feast  of  the  Nativity  [1627];  he  was  son  of  John  Smith,  a  member  of  this  College,  who 
was  admitted  in  1603;  a  separate  account  of  whom  I  give  below. 


“The  first  named  John  Smith  was  admitted  Scholar,  August  25,  1646,  being  17  years  of 
age,  and  Fellow,  August  25,  1649.  In  1668  he  was  Senior  Proctor  of  the  University;  Vice 
Provost  of  this  College  from  1694 — 1706.  I  do  not  know  the  year  he  took  his  B.A.  degree. 
He  was  M.A.  1653.  He  died  August  23,  1706,  and  was  buried  two  days  later  in  the  Vestry  of  the 
College  Chapel  near  the  Clock-house.  He  was  blind,  through  age,  some  years  before  his  death. 
The  inscription  (see  below)  on  his  body-stone  was  written  by  Provost  Roderick.  He  was  a 
little,  merry,  inoffensive  old  man,  and  had  in  some  measure  applied  himself  to  the  study  of 
physic  and  not  unseen  in  cookery.” 

So  much  from  Anthony  Allen.  He  does  not  appear  to  have  left  any  will,  as  administi’a- 
tion  of  his  estate  was  granted  by  the  Provost  of  this  College  to  “  Marie  Symcots,  spinster,  of 
the  parish  of  S*  Botolph,  Aldersgate,  London,”  on  August  27,  1706.  He  held  no  Benefice,  as 
he  was  always  a  Fellow  of  the  College  and  therefore  not  eligible. 

The  following  inscription  on  his  Body-stone  is  in  the  ninth  side  Chapel  from  West  on 
North  side : —

“John  Smith,  the  Elder.  This  John  Smith  or  Smithe  was  born  at  Huntstone  or  Hunston 
(near  Stowmarket)  in  Suffolk  about  the  Feast  of  Saint  Michael.  He  was  admitted  Scholar, 

August  25,  1G03,  at  the  age  of  17.  He  was  admitted  Fellow,  August  26,  1606.  On  January  9, 
1624,  he  was  presented  by  this  College  to  the  Vicarage  of  Broadchalke,  Wilts,  which  he  resigned 
about  July  following  on  being  chosen  Fellow  of  Eton.  In  1630  he  was  presented  by  Eton 
College  to  the  Vicarage  of  Mapledurham,  Oxon.  He  died  the  latter  end  of  the  year  1635  at 
Eton  College,  and  was  buried  in  Eton  College  Chapel.  He  was  an  excellent  Scholar,  and  a  very 
good  and  pious  man,  answerable  to  which  character  his  death  became  universally  lamented.” 

In  an  early  catalogue  relating  to  the  Fellowes  and  Provosts  of  King’s  College,  Cambridge, 
written  about  the  middle  of  the  seventeenth  century,  the  Coat  of  Arms  is  the  same  for  both 
Smiths,  viz.,  Sable,  a  cross  Or.  We  are  indebted  to  Mr.  F.  L.  Clarke,  of  King’s  College, 

Cambridge,  for  the  above  particulars. 

Eut  who  was  the  father  of  John  Smith  als  Hovell,  the  Fellow  of  Eton  1  In  November 
1607  Thomas  How  of  Langham,  whose  will  was  proved  at  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  bequeathed  a 
pasture  to  Julian,  wife  of  John  Smith  of  Hunston,  whom  he  named  as  his  executor.  John 
Smith,  the  eldest  son  of  this  John  and  Julian,  who  are  usually  described  as  of  Langham,  an 
adjoining  village,  was  born  in  or  about  the  year  1585,  and  would  have  been  seventeen  years 
old  in  August  16t3.  It  may,  after  all,  have  been  this  eldest  son  who  put  together  the  Langham 
section,  otherwise  unaccounted  for,  of  the  Smith  als  Hovell  pedigree  which  found  its  way  into 
the  Harleian  MSS.  (See  Suffolk  Manorial  Families,  vol.  ii,  20,  21).  On  the  other  hand,  John 
Smith,  the  brother  of  Arthur  Smith  of  Hunston,  had  a  son  who  is  named  in  the  pedigree  of 
Smith  als  Hovell  of  Surrey  (see  p.  53),  and  who  seems  equally  to  correspond  with  the  John 

Smith  who  was  chosen  Fellow  of  Eton  in  1622.  There  is  no  entry  of  his  baptism  in  the 

parish  registers  of  Hunston,  Langham  or  Badwell  to  decidq  the  question.

It  will  be  noticed  that  the  sons  of  the  testator  are  referred  to  in  the  same  order,  and 
have  the  same  names,  and  must  have  lived  at  the  same  time  as  those  of  Robert  Smith  als 
Hovell  in  the  pedigree  on  the  opposite  page.  So  striking  a  coincidence  suggests  the  question 
whether  “  Robert  ”  was  not  inadvertently  substituted  for  “  Arthur  ”  by  the  Herald  or  the 
copyist  who  transcribed  the  Visitation.  For  he  made  other  blunders,  describing  Badwell  Ash  as 
in  Norfolk,  and  Robert  the  son  of  Robert  Smyth  of  London  as  two  years  old  in  1623,  when 
he  must  have  been  eleven  at  the  least.  We  have  no  evidence  of  a  Robert  Smyth  of  Badwell 
at  the  period  indicated,  whilst  there  is  abundant  testimony,  besides  his  will,  respecting  the 
Arthur  Smyth,  who  seems  so  exactly  to  fill  his  place.

There  is  abundant  evidence  as  to  the  arms  of  the  knightly  family  of  Hovell  of  Wyverstone 
in  the  thirteenth  and  fourteenth  centuries.  Some  authorities,  indeed,  allude  to  their  adoption  in 
the  time  of  King  Henry  III,  but  all  are  agreed  as  to  the  shields  of  Sir  Hugh  Hovell  and 
Sir  Stephen  Hovell  in  the  wars  of  Edward  I.  Amongst  the  many  MSS.,  some  contemporary 
with  the  men  they  treat  of,  which  describe  these  insignia,  is  that  known  as  “  Guillim’s  Roll,” 
Harl.  MS.  6,137,  which  has  been  printed  in  the  first  volume  of  The  Genealogist ,  with  an 
introduction  by  the  late  Mr.  Greenstreet.  He  estimated  its  date  as  about  the  year  1300.  Under 
the  heading  “  Names  of  all  that  were  with  King  Edward  I.  in  Scotland  and  France,”  we  find 
“  Sr  IIeweh  Hovell,”  Sable,  a  cross  Or,  and  “Sr  Esteven  Hovell,”  Sable,  a  cross  Or  with  a 
label  of  three  points  Argent.  Amongst  the  Knights,  possibly  of  a  later  reign,  were  “  Robert 

Hovell”  (fo.  46b.)  and  “Sire  Roberd  Houell  ”  (fo.  59),  with  Sable,  a  cross  Or.  .  There  are  also 

names  akin  to  Hovell,  as  “  Sr  Geffery  de  Hautevile,”  who  bore  Argent,  semee  of  crosses  croslet 
a  lion  rampant  Sable ;  Sir  John  Hovile,  Per  cross  Or  and  Sable,  in  the  first  quarter  a  martlet 
Gules ;  and  Hugo  de  Houile,  Argent  a  bend  Azure  with  a  label  of  five  points  Gules.  But  these 
seem  to  have  belonged  to  counties  other  than  Suffolk. 

In  the  first  volume  of  “Parliamentary  Writs,”  a  folio  work  published  by  the  Record 
Commissioners,  are  given  “  Les  Nohs  e  les  Armes  a  Baneres  de  Engletere,”  from  Cotton  MS. 

Caligula,  A.  16.  Amongst  the  Knights  of  “  Suthfolk  ”  are  “Sire  Huge  Houel  :  de  sable  a  une 

crois  de  or,”  and  “  Sire  Estevene  Houel :  meisme  les  armes,  a  un  label  de  argent.” 

Under  the  heading  “  Milites  Comitatus  Suffolk  ”  there  are  drawings  of  the  arms  of  Sir  Hugh 

and  Sir  Stephen  Hovell  in  Harl.  MS.  1,386,  a  volume  of  Heraldic  Collections.  A  memorandum 
on  the  title  page  tells  us  it  had  been  “  Bought  of  Mr.  John  Gwillim,  pursuivant  of  Armes, 

14°  May  1612.”  This  was  the  editor  of  “  Gwillim’s  Display  of  Heraldry,”  printed  in  1610.  He 

was  appointed  Portsmouth  Herald,  and  died  in  1621. 

In  Harl.  MS.  1086,  amongst  the  “  Knightes  that  were  in  the  tyme  of  Kinge  E.  ye  4,” 
is  “  Sr  Hugh  Hovell,  S.,  a  plaine  cros  Or.”  We  have  no  other  evidences  of  a  Sir  Hugh  Hovell 
at  this  date,  and  the  name  was  probably  so  inserted  by  an  error. 

“  bes  Nomes  de  Chevaliers  en  le  champ  de  Henry  3”  are  given  in  Lansdown  MS.  855, 

which  has  been  printed  in  the  “Antiquarian  Repertory,”  vol.  i,  93.  It  agrees  with  a  MS., 

formerly  belonging  to  Tom  Martin,  quoted  by  Davy  in  his  “Suffolk  Armoury,”  which,  under 

“  SouthfolU,”  enumerates  “Sir  Hugo  Houel  and  Sir  Estevene  Houel.”  These  names  occur,  too,  in 
Harl.  MS.  6,589  in  “  The  Copy  of  a  very  ancient  Role  wrought  in  Colours  in  Parchment  in  the

tyme  of  King  Edward  y°  first,  remayning  in  the  custody  of  Mr.  John  Guilement,  Portesmouth,

Papworth  states,  in  his  “  Ordinary  of  British  Armorials,”  that  Sable,  a  cross  Or  was  borne 
at  various  periods  by  Bellesly,  Braham,  Faunell,  Havell,  Havenell,  Hovell,  Howell  of  Soulgrave, 
and  Smith  of  Chertsey  in  Surrey,  and  gives  us  his  authorities  for  each  name.  Whatever  its 
origin,  the  golden  cross  on  a  black  shield  is  at  once  one  of  the  simplest  and  most  sightly 
coats  accorded  by  the  heralds. 

The  evidences  respecting  the  Hovells  of  Wyverstone  are  numerous,  and  the  twenty-eighth 
volume  of  the  Harrison  MSS.  in  the  Public  Record  Office  abounds  in  references  to  early  Fines, 
Close  Rolls,  Judicial  Proceedings,  Charters  and  Feudal  Aids  bearing  upon  the  history  of  the 
family.  Some  of  these,  mostly  in  abstract,  are  given  below.

Domesday  of  all  the  Manors  of  St.  Edmund . At  Wiverston  nine  pounds  and  a 

half  (rental)  from  one  hundred  and  ten  acres  of  land  :  of  these  Richard  Hoverel  holds  five  and 
a  half  of  St.  Edmund  and  Baldwin  the  abbot. 

In  another  Bury  MS.,  also  in  the  University  Library  at  Cambridge,  called  “  Liber  Niger,” 
this  entry  occurs  again,  but  the  name,  contracted  in  Liber  Pinchebeck  into  “  Houel,”  is  extended 
into  “  Houerel.” 

It  is  probable  that  the  name  “Hovel”  was  converted  into  “Hoverel”  by  a  thoughtless 
flourish  of  the  original  writer.  For  the  Hovells  were  connected  with  Wyverstone  for  centuries 
following  the  Conquest.  Within  an  hundred  years  of  the  time  when  Baldwin  was  Abbot  of  Bury,  as 
will  be  seen  below,  Adam  Hovell  is  known  to  have  held  lands  in  that  parish.  Baldwin  died  in 
1098,  and  Adam  Hovell  acquired  these  lands  before  1189.  As  Richard  “Hovell,”  the  so-called 
“  Hoverill  ”  gave  certain  tithes  to  the  Priory  of  Eye,  a  gift  which  was  confirmed  by  Henry  I 
(1100—1135),  and  afterwards  by  King  Stephen: — 

“  Robtus  Malet  p  cartam  suam  fundationis  Ecclie  conv  de  Eya  confirmavit  Monachis  ibm 
donationem  quam  Ricus  Hovel  dedit  eis  de  duabj  ptbij  decime  sue  in  Wiuerdeston.  (Peg.  Prior 
de  Eya  fo.  17).  Henr  Rex  confirmavit  eisd  decimam  Ric  Houel  Wyuerdeston.  (lb.  fol.  19). 
Stephus  Rex  confirmavit  similr.”  (Ib.  fo.  21.)  See  Davy’s  Suffolk  Collections,  under  “Wyverstone.” 

Robert  Malet  by  his  charter  of  the  foundation  of  the  Conventual  Church  of  Eye  confirms 
to  the  monks  there  the  gift  which  Richard  Hovel  gave  to  them  of  two  parts  of  his  tythes  in 
Wyverstone.  King  Henry  confirmed  to  them  the  tythe  of  Richard  Hovell  at  Wyverstone.  King 
Stephen  made  a  similar  confirmation. 

Baldwin,  King  Edward  the  Confessor’s  physician,  became  Abbot  of  Bury  in  1065,  on  the 
death  of  Leofstan  his  predecessor.  He  died  in  1098.  There  is  an  excellent  memoir  of  him  in 
the  Dictionary  of  National  Biography.

Domesday ,  vol.  ii,  371. 

“  Registrum  W.  Pinchebeck,”  one  of  the  most  valuable  of  the  old  Bury  records,  now  in 

the  University  Library  at  Cambridge  (EE.,  iii,  60),  is  a  parchment  quarto  of  329  leaves,  relating 

to  the  property  of  the  Abbey  of  St.  Edmund.  It  was  compiled  from  many  sources  by  the  monk 
whose  name  it  bears  The  general  heading  to  the  MS.  is  “  De  itiner  Salamonis  de  Roff  T; 

socioi^,  Anno  rf  E.  fit  R.  H.  xiiii0,  Incipiente  xv°  ”  (1287). 

Amongst  the  companions  of  William  the  Conqueror  ennumerated  in  some  extant  copies  of 
the  Roll  of  Battle  Abbey  occur  the  names  of  Hovell  and  Hautville.  The  Roll  itself  is  no 
longer  in  existence,  and  the  transcripts  are  notoriously  untrustworthy.  There  is  every  reason 

to  think  that  Hovell  who  witnessed  the  charter  of  Leofstan  in  the  reign  of  Edward  the 

Confessor,  and  was  perhaps  identical  with  the  Richard  Hovell  of  Liber  Pinchebeck,  was,  as  his 
name  implies,  a  Saxon.  The  Hautvilles,  on  the  other  hand,  were  indubitably  of  continental 
descent,  and,  adopting  other  Arms,  retained  the  Norman  spelling  of  their  name  for  many 
generations.

Curia  Regis,  4  John,  No.  28,  m.  2,  dorso  (103). 

Rob1  de  Giselingham  demands  against  Adam  Hovell  xl  acres  of  land  with  appurtenances  in 
Wiverdeston  as  his  right ;  which  land  Hubert  fitz  Walter,  his  kinsman,  whose  heir  the  said 
Robert  is,  mortgaged  to  the  said  Adam  Hovell  for  a  term  which  is  past,  in  the  time 
of  Henry,  the  King’s  father.  Adam  comes  and  defends  the  mortgage  and  says  the  said  land 
is  his  right  and  inheritance,  and  he  puts  himself  on  the  great  assize  of  the  Lord  King 
to  know  which  of  them  hath  the  greater  right  in  the  said  land  :  and  Robert  de  Giselingham 

does  the  same.  A  day  was  given  them  in  the  octave  of  St.  Martin,  and  then  come  iiij  to 

choose  xij.  Adam  puts  in  his  place  Adam  his  son,  etc. 

Amongst  the  Suffolk  Pleas  in  the  thirteenth  year  of  Henry  III  (1229)  is  one  in  which 
the  Jury  decided  that  Gilbert  Fitz  Ralph  had  defrauded  Adam  Hovell  of  common  pasture  in 
Hunston  belonging  to  his  freehold  there  ( Coram  Rege  Roll  13  II.  3,  m.  18).  In  the  same 
year  he  was  found  to  have  owed  rent  for  a  mill  in  Hunston  or  Hunterston  which  had  been 
pulled  down  ( lb .  m.  37  dorso).  He  was  also  a  juryman  in  a  plea  relating  to  the  presentation 
to  the  church  of  Barningham  in  that  county.  In  one  of  the  Suffolk  Fines  of  the  twelfth  year 
of  King  John  (1211)  he  acted  as  attorney  for  Hubert  de  Monte  Kamiso  in  the  purchase  of 

lands  of  John  Fitz  Roland  (Fine,  Suff.  12  John,  No.  55).  The  mill  in  Hunston  seems  to  have 

been  sold  in  1291  by  William  Hovell,  his  grandson.  (De  Banco  Roll,  Mich.  18  and  19  Edw.  I ,. 
Harrison  MSS.  XXVIII,  233).

Pleas  at  Westminster  in  Hillary  Term,  19  Henry  III,  Suffolk.  Thomas  de  Hay  seeks 
versus  Robert  de  Hovell  and  Margery  his  wife  his  Manor  of  Weston  as  his  right,  etc.  And 
Robert  and  Margery  came  and  said  that  they  held  that  manor  of  the  King,  and  the  King  took 
it  into  his  hands  and  now  holds  it.  And  Thomas  Hay  acknowledged  this ;  and  therefore  it  will 
be  returned  to  them  upon  some  day  not  as  yet  determined. 

Robert  Hovell  and  Margery  his  wife  are  mentioned  in  legal  documents  in  1225  and 
again  in  1253.  (Close  Boll,  37  II.  S,  m.  3  dorso).  He  held  the  manors  of  Weston,  Wiverstone, 
and  Horpole  in  Wickhambrook,  and  lands  in  Cheston  and  Westhorpe.  (Suffolk  Fines,  2J/.  II.  3, 
No.  39).  In  1231  he  had  the  King’s  licence  to  hunt  foxes  and  hares  in  the  forest  of  Essex, 
and  a  grant  of  free  warren  at  Wiverstone,  with  a  fair  there  yearly.  (Close  Boll,  15  II.  3,  m.  3). 
He  is  called  Robert  Hovell,  senior,  and  was  perhaps  an  old  man  in  1258,  when  Ada,  the  widow 
of  Hubert  Hovell,  his  son,  claimed  her  dower  of  his  Horpole  lands  He  seems  to  have  (Jied 
before  1268,  for  Weston  and  Horpole  had  then  passed  to  Robert  Hovell,  Hubert’s  brother,  the 
husband  of  Alianora.  (Coram  Bege  Boll,  52  II.  3,  m.  2).

the  following  Easter,  which  would  be  just  one  year  later.

Whereas  it  was  brought  to  the  notice  of  the  King  that  he  had  pardoned  Hubert  Ho  veil 
the  transgression  he  had  committed  in  taking  out  of  the  King’s  custody  one  of  the  daughters 
of  Henry  de  Hasting,  and  in  marrying  her  without  the  King’s  licence :  and  that  the  same 
Hubert  was  outlawed  (the  word  “unjustly”  is  here  struck  out)  the  King  pardoned  him  the 
outlawry  promulgated  against  him,  and  granted  him  his  firm  peace.  And  it  is  commanded 
the  Sheriff  of  Bedfordshire  who  arrested  the  said  Hubert  in  his  outlawry  that  he  permit  him 
to  go  freely  and  to  remain  in  peace  where  he  would. 

Hubert  Hovell  seems  to  have  died  in  1258.  As  will  be  seen  below,  his  widow  claimed 
dower  out  of  the  Manor  of  Horpole,  of  Robert  Hovell  senior,  probably  her  husband’s  father.  In 
1268  this  manor  was  held  by  Robert  Hovell  (apparently  Hubert’s  brother)  and  Alianora  his  wife.

This  is  the  final  agreement  made  in  the  King’s  Court  at  Ipswich  in  the  octave  of 
St.  Hillary  in  the  42d  year  of  the  reign  of  King  Henry,  son  of  King  John,  before  Gilbert  de 
Preston  and  others,  Justices  Itinerant  Ac.  then  present.  Between  Ada,  who  was  (late)  the  wife 
of  Hubert  Hovel,  plaintiff,  and  Robert  Hovell,  senior,  deforcent,  of  the  third  part  of  the  Manor 

of  Horpol,  which  the  same  Ada  claims  as  her  reasonable  dower  in  the  free  holding  of  Hubert 

Hovell,  formerly  her  husband.  A  plea  was  entered  upon  between  them  in  the  same  Court.  Ada 
to  remit  all  her  right  and  claim,  and  Robert  Hovell  to  render  her  each  year  two  marks  of 
silver.  And  after  the  decease  of  Ada,  Robert  Hovell  and  his  heirs  to  be  quit  of  this  payment. 
And  if  it  so  happens  that  Robert  or  his  heir  fails  to  pay  the  two  marks,  Ada  has  licence  to 
distrain  upon  all  his  cattle,  lands  and  tenements  found  in  the  Manor  of  Wyverstone.  And 
besides  the  said  Robert  gives  the  said  Ada  ten  marks  of  silver.

Roger  and  Hawisia  twenty  marks  of  silver.

SUFFOLK  MANORIAL  FAMILIES. 


This  is  the  final  agreement  made  in  the  King’s  Court  at  York  in  Michaelmas  term  in 
the  twelfth  year  of  King  Edward  the  Third,  between  Robert  Hovell  and  Alianora  his  wife, 
plaintiffs,  and  Matthew  de  Cambridge,  deforciant,  of  fifteen  tofts,  three  hundred  acres  of  arable 
land,  fifteen  acres  of  meadow,  thirty  acres  of  pasture,  thirty  acres  of  woods,  and  . 
shillings  rent  charge  in  Westhorpe,  Cotton,  Finningham,  Gislingham  and  Nether  Rickinghall,  and 
of  the  Manor  of  Westhope  and  the  advowson  of  the  church  of  that  manor.  A  covenant 

was  made  between  them  in  the  same  Court.  Namely  that  Robert  Hovell  acknowledges  the  said 
manor,  lands  and  advowson  to  be  the  right  of  Matthew  de  Cambridge,  as  those  which  he  had 
by  the  gift  of  the  said  Robert.  And  by  this  recognizance,  fine  and  covenant,  Matthew  de 

Cambridge  grants  the  said  manor,  etc.,  to  Robert  Hovell  and  Alianora  his  wife,  to  have  and 
to  hold  to  them  and  to  their  heirs  for  ever  in  capite  of  the  lord  of  that  fee,  by  the  services  which 
pertain  to  the  said  manor  and  advowson,  for  ever. 

This  fine  connects  the  Hovells,  as  early  as  1349,  with  Rickinghall,  Cotton,  Gislingham,  etc., 
so  long  associated  with  their  name.  In  the  semi-apocryphal  pedigree  of  Harl.  MS.  1103  (see 
pp.  10-11),  Richard  Hovell,  Esquire  of  the  Body  to  King  Henry  the  Fifth,  circa  1420,  is 
described  as  of  Rickinghall.  Whilst  in  1584  Thomas  Hovell  ais  Smyth  of  Thelvetham  bequeathed 
lands  in  Rickinghall,  Hinderclay,  Weston,  etc.  (See  his  will,  Arch.  Sudb.  Liber  “  Frende,”  fol.  317).

“This  is  the  final  agreement  made  in  the  King’s  Court  at  Westminster,  in  Trinity  term 
in  the  thirtieth  year  of  King  Edward  the  Third,  between  John  Hovell  and  Matilda  his  wife,

Robert  for  ever.”

daughters  by  the  Fine  of  1343.

In  the  name  of  God,  Amen.  I  Sir  William  de  Hemphale,  Knight,  sane  in  mind  and  ‘of 
good  memory,  on  the  Monday  before  the  feast  of  St.  Bartholomew,  1379,  make  my  will  at 

Gislingham.  First,  I  commend  my  soul  to  God  and  the  Blessed  Virgin  Mary  and  my  body 
to  be  buried  according  to  my  instructions.  I  leave  to  Amy  de  Bordesawe  xx1 ;  to  Agnes  de 
Grymmesby  liij1  xis  viiid  ;  to  Robert  Hovell  and  his  wife  xx11;  and  to  Ralph  de  Hemphale  my 
nephew  (or  grandson)  xx11.  I  leave  to  Joan  Hovell  one  bed  with  red  hangings,  (embroidered 
with  my  arms)  ;  to  Agnes  de  Grymmesby  one  bed  of  Gawne  powdered  with  red  leaves. 
I  will  that  all  my  other  beds  be  sold  and  (the  proceeds)  be  expended  for  my  soul.  I  leave 
twenty  marks  to  William  Kynge.  I  appoint  Sir  William  Goldsmith,  parson  of  the  church  of 
Rickinghall,  Sir  Ralph  Gothelarde,  parson  of  the  church  of  Chelton,  Sir  Stephen  Harvy,  parson 
of  the  church  of  St.  Margaret  of  Brunham  and  William  Kynge  to  be  the  executors  of  this 
will,  that  they  may  dispose  and  order  for  my  soul  as  seems  best  to  them.  Given  at  the  day 
and  place  abovenamed.  In  testimony  whereof  I  affix  my  seal.  Proved  at  Norwich  23  Octr 
1379.  Register  “Haydone”  in  the  archives  of  the  Registrar  of  Norwich:  fol.  108a. 

From  the  transcript  of  Sir  Symond  D’Ewes,  Harl.  MS.  10,  fo.  27b. 

Sir  William  de  Hemphale,  or  Hemenhale,  was  of  Gislingham,  one  of  the  villages  named 

in  the  endless  deeds  relating  to  the  Hovells.  The  chief  legatees  in  his  will  were  presumably 
relations.  Robert  Hovell  of  Wyverstone  (afterwards  Sir  Robert)  and  Joan  his  wife  were 
neighbours.  It  is  probable  that  parts  of  this  document,  which  is  confessedly  an  abstz’act,  have 
been  omitted  by  the  transcriber.

This  Fine  establishes  the  title  of  Sir  John  de  Tuddenham  and  Margery  his  wife  to  the 
Manors  of  Bealings,  Grundisburgh,  Sutton  and  Newton  near  Ipswich.  By  a  legal  fiction  the 
Tuddenhams  acknowledge  them  to  be  the  right  of  their  kinsman,  Hugh  Hovell.  And  in 
consideration  of  this  acknowledgment  Hugh  Hovell  grants  them  to  the  Tuddenhams  and  to  their 
heirs  for  ever.

They  gave  names  to  the  Manors  in  Wiverston ,  Weybread  and  Cheston.  Sir  Hugo  Hovel  tempe  E.  1 ,  Dnus.

The  manuscript  “quondam  penes  Sir  Jno  Blois,”  so  frequently  quoted  by  Jermyn  and  Davy  (Add.  MS. 
8210,  etc.)  was  evidently  that  bequeathed  by  William  Blois,  Esqr.,  of  Grundisburgh  (Will,  Cur.  Ep.  Norw.)  to 
Sir  William  Blois,  his  son,  in  1672.  Its  genealogical  value  is  very  great,  and  its  very  mistakes,  as  a  rule, 
are  but  misplaced  facts,  and  serve  as  guides  to  future  research.  There  is  reason  to  believe  that  the  pedigree 
above  given  represents  in  a  great  measure  the  true  ancestry  of  the  early  Hovells  of  Wyverstone. 

The  pedigree  on  the  next  page  from  the  Harrison  MSS.  in  the  Public  Record  Office,  like  most  com¬ 
pilations  of  the  kind  relating  to  persons  who  were  living  in  the  twelfth,  thirteenth,  and  fourteenth  centuries, 
is  founded  upon  imperfect  evidence,  and  many  of  its  statements  are  doubtful.  It  has  the  merit,  however,  qf 
arranging  a  number  of  facts,  tentatively,  in  a  tabular  form,  and  of  preparing  the  way  for  one  more  reliable 
and  exact.  It  forms  the  basis  of  the  “  Reconstructed  Pedigree  of  the  Hovells  of  Wyverstone,”  which  follows 
it,  in  which  the  descents  are  connected  by  dotted  lines  only,  and  unproven  marriages,  even  if  probable,  are 
omitted ;  whilst  the  identity  of  contemporary  Hovells  of  the  same  name  in  Norfolk  and  Suffolk,  insufficiently 
established,  is  no  longer  assumed. 

There  is  no  known  evidence  as  to  the  William  Hovell  of  Wyverstone  in  the  time  of  William  the 
Conqueror,  named  in  the  Pedigree  from  the  Harrison  MSS.  Robert  Hovell,  the  supposed  son  of  Adam  Hovell 
Hovell  of  Wyverstone,  erroneously  described  therein  as  of  Attleborough  in  Norfolk,  was  of  Attlebridge  in  that 
country.  Harrison  MS.  xxviii,  303.

Fine,  2  E.  3.  ( See  p.  82.)  Probable  ancestor  of  the 

Hovells  of  Cowling,  1473,  1563.  (See  p.  83.) 


We  give  below,  in  brief  summary,  some  of  the  many  contemporary  evidences  which  bear  upon  the 
above  pedigrees. 

In  1240  Roger  de  Westhorpe  claimed  two  parts  of  a  Knight’s  Fee  in  Westhorpe  of  William  de  Haudleye, 
whom  Robert  Hovell  called  to  warranty.  A  plea  of  dead  ancestors  was  summoned  between  them.  Haudleye 
acknowledged  the  two  parts  to  be  the  right  of  Westhorpe,  who  gave  them  to  Hovell,  with  the  advowson  of 

Westhorpe,  etc.,  to  hold  for  sixteen  years,  etc.  Fines,  Suffolk,  24  H.  3,  No.  39. 

In  1260  Robert  Hovell  acknowledged  that  he  owed  Richard  de  Clare,  Earl  of  Gloucester,  200  marks. 

He  would  pay  20  marks  on  the  feast  of  St.  Michael  each  year,  to  be  a  lien  in  the  Manors  of  Weston  and 

Cheston.  The  Earl  could  distrain  in  default.  Coram  Rege  Roll,  44  H.  3,  m.  32  dorso. 

In  the  Suffolk  Assizes  of  1286  Adam,  the  son  of  William  Hovell,  sued  Assellina,  who  had  been  the 
wife  of  Robert  Parson  of  Wyverston,  concerning  a  plea  of  dowry.  He  was  plaintiff  in  a  suit  against 
John  Hovell  and  Henry  de  Chamberlyn  and  Matilda  his  wife  in  a  plea  of  land;  and  in  another  suit  against 
William  the  son  of  Martin  Hovell  of  Hunterston.  Assize  Roll,  14  E.  1,  memb.  53,  53  dorso,  and  57. 

Hugh  Hovell  and  Johanna  his  wife,  in  1301,  bought  of  Hugh  Pecche  and  the  heirs  of  the  said  Hugh 
six  messuages,  170  acres  of  arable  land,  etc.,  in  Cheston  and  South  Elmham.  Fine,  Suffolk,  29  E.  1,  No.  80. 

Sir  Hugh  Howell,  1316,  returned  as  lord  of  Wyverstone  and  Weston,  and  joint  lord  of  Cheston  and 

Blithford,  co.  Suffolk,  9  E.  2 ;  summoned,  1324,  as  knight  for  Suffolk  to  attend  the  Great  Council  at  West¬ 
minster  17  E.  2.  Parliamentary  Writs,  vol.  ii,  1025. 

Robert  Hovell,  senior,  son  of  Hugh  Hovell,  Chevalier,  and  Joan  his  wife,  in  1332  and  1333,  buys  lands 
in  Wickham  Market  of  Vincent  Morwan  of  Pettistree  and  of  Robert  Loveday  and  Agnes  his  wife.  Suffolk 
Fines,  5  and  6  E.  3. 

In  1340  Robert  Hovell  bought  of  Robert  of  Wyllasham  [and  Scientia  his  wife,  two  messuages,  forty  acres 

of  land,  etc.,  in  Combes,  Battisford,  Hecham,  Finborough  Magna  and  Finborough  Parva.  Suffolk  Fines, 

13  E.  3,  No.  16.

Just  two  hundred  and  thirty  six  years  later,  viz.  in  1524,  Robert  Hovell  alias  Smyth — 
the  first  of  that  name  to  make  any  will — directed  that  he  should  be  buried  in  the  church  of 
Our  Lady  in  Dallinghoo.  ( See  page  22).  It  is  interesting  to  note  how  many  Smiths  of 
Ashfield,  Badwell,  Dallinghoo,  Huiiston  and  Rickinghall— places  where  the  Hovells  had  once 
owned  lands — began  to  style  themselves  Hovell  alias  Smith,  in  the  sixteenth  century.  In  Cowling 
alone,  as  we  shall  presently  show,  and  the  adjoining  village  of  Kirtling,  is  there  any  trace 
of  an  unbroken  line  of  Hovells  from  the  days  of  Edward  the  First  to  those  of  Queen  Elizabeth  : 
and  there  the  name,  whenever  met  with,  is  Hovell  or  Howell  only. 

It  will  be  noticed  that  Morston  occurs  as  the  name  of  a  Suffolk  township,  in  connection 
with  Hugh  Hovell  and  Agnes  his  wife,  in  1326.  ( See  Fine,  p.  81.)

Tliis  is  one  of  the  first  of  a  small  series  of  documents  relating  to  the  Hovells  of 

Cowling,  Bradley,  Wratting  and  Kirtling,  a  group  of  adjacent  villages,  in  the  fourteenth, 

fifteenth  and  sixteenth  centuries.  Their  exact  connection  with  the  Hovells  of  Westhorpe  and 
Wyverstone  has  not  as  yet  been  fully  ascertained,  but  they  were  probably  descendants  of  Martin 
Ho  veil  and  Sarah  his  wife,  who  (see  page  61)  owned  lands  in  Great  and  Little  Wratting  in 
1269.  Blomefield  states  (Hist,  of  Norfolk ,  viii,  465),  on  what  authority  we  know  not,  that  a 
Sir  John  Hovell  of  Wratting  Parva  was  living  in  1370.

To  establish  her  title  to  messuage  and  lands  in  Cowling,  Lydgate,  Bradley,  <tc.,  Margaret, 
widow  of  Edmund  de  Shardelow  acknowledges,  in  the  King’s  Court  at  York,  that  she  had  given 
them  to  William  Payn,  Chaplain,  and  William  the  son  of  Richard  de  Hauvyle,  and  that  they 


HOVELL  OF  WYVERSTONE. 


83 


were  the  right  owners.  Whereupon  they  render  them  again  to  her  and  her  heirs,  specifying 

the  future  line  of  entail  in  the  Shardelow  family.  From  1269  downwards  there  are  scattered 
indications  of  a  line  of  Hovells  of  Cowling  and  its  neighbourhood  until  the  middle  of  the 

sixteenth  century,  when  John  Hovell  of  that  place  devised  his  lands  to  female  relatives. 

[Will,  P.C.C.  27  Chayre,  1568).  Amongst  the  wealthier  inhabitants  of  Suffolk  in  1436  was  a 
Thomas  Hovyle  ( Subsidies ,  Divers  Counties,  14  H.  6,  Iff) ;  but  the  family  had  evidently  suffered 
from  the  unsettled  state  of  the  country  when  Thomas  Hovell  of  Hovell’s  in  Cowling  made  his 

will  in  1473,  of  which  we  give  an  abstract.  William,  his  son,  was  very  young,  and  may  have 

been  identical  with  the  William  Howell  of  Cowling,  who  made  his  will  [Arch.  Sudb.)  in  1538, 
but  this  is  very  doubtful. 

Camden  in  his  Magna  Brittania  ( Gough's  Edition ,  vol.  ii,  82)  tells  us  of  a  house  in 

Cowling  “  which  commands  a  fine  view  of  the  venerable  remains  of  Kirtling  in  Cambridgeshire, 
the  antient  seat  of  the  North  family.”  There  were  several  Hovells  in  Kirtling  in  1522  ( Subsidy , 
Cambridgeshire,  14  H.  8,  -jV,),  of  whom  a  certain  William  Hovell  was  the  chief.  In  1543  he 

was  replaced  by  Stephen  Hovell  ( Subsidy ,  Carnb.,  34  &  85  II.  8,  TyT),  who  afterwards  removed 

to  Horningsea,  where  he  made  his  will  ( Ely  Consistory)  13  July  1552.

This  is  the  last  will  of  me  Thomas  Hovell,  made  on  the  16th  day  of  March,  1473.  I 
will  that  Alice  my  wife  shall  have  the  tenement  called  Hovells  with  all  the  lands,  feedings 
and  pastures,  Ac.,  together  with  Farwelles  Crofte,  Ac.,  until  William  my  son  attain  his  age  of 
eighteen  years.  And  if  it  happen  to  the  said  William  to  die  before  he  attain  that  age  I  will 
that  my  wife  have  the  said  tenement  and  premises  for  the  term  of  her  life,  and  that  after

her  decease  they  be  sold,  and  the  money  be  disposed  at  the  discretion  of  my  executors  in  the 
church  of  Cowling  and  in  other  works  of  charity  for  the  health  of  my  soul.  And  when  the 
said  William  may  be  eighteen  years  old  I  will  that  his  mother  and  he  divide  all  goods,  ifec.,

Stephen  Howell,  the  testator,  was  of  Kirtling  in  1543,  but  in  1545  had  already  settled 
at  Horningsea.  Lay  Subsidies,  Cambridge,  vrV  He  was  probably  the  son  of  William 

Hovell  of  Kirtling,  who  was  assessed  at  a  substantial  sum  in  1522.  Lay  Subsidy,  Cambridge, 

In  these  documents  the  name  is  sometimes  written  Hovell,  and  sometimes  Howell.  Joan, 
his  widow,  became  the  wife  of  Thomas  Willowes  or  Willys,  also  of  High  or  Ey  Hall,  by  whom 
she  had  further  issue,  her  great  grandson,  Sir  Richard  Willys,  being  created  a  baronet  by 
Charles  I  in  1646.  Burke’s  Extinct  Baronetage.  From  her  father,  Martin  ffooxe  or  ffolkes 

of  Westley,  in  Cambridgeshire,  descended  Martin  ffolkes,  Attorney  General  to  Katherine  of 

Braganza,  Queen  of  Charles  II,  who  married  Dorothy,  daughter  and  coheir  of  Sir  William 
Hovell  of  Hillington  in  Norfolk,  and  became  the  ancestor  of  a  line  of  Baronets  now  represented 
by  Sir  William  Hovell  ffolkes,  of  Hillington  Hall. 

As  has  been  pointed  out,  on  page  83,  Kirtling  adjoins  Cowling,  where  a  line  of  Hovells, 
kinsmen  of  the  knightly  family  of  Hovell  of  Wyverstone,  can  be  traced  from  1344  to  1563. 
See  Pedigree,  p.  77.  It  is  almost  certain  that  the  Cowling  and  Kirtling  Hovells  were  of 

the  same  stock.

This  document  being  much  damaged  its  date  is  supplied  from  the  Visus  Compoti  in  the 
Court  of  Wards.  Book  No.  7,  fo.  S8b.  The  will  of  Thomas  Willowes  was  proved  in  the 
Prerogative  Court  of  Canterbury  Octr  3d  1568.  P.C.C.  20  Babington. 

The  testator  married  the  widow  of  Stephen  Hovell  of  High  Hall,  Horningsea,  and  became 
by  her  the  ancestor  of  the  fine  old  Cavalier  family  of  Willis,  Baronets.  His  will  is  full  of 
suggestive  genealogy,  naming  as  it  does  Thomas  ffookes  or  ffolkes,  doubtless  his  wife’s  brother ; 
Edward  Hovell  his  wife’s  son ;  William  Morden,  whose  daughter  Edward  Hovell  married  ;  and 
Edward  Willowes,  probably  the  husband  of  Agnes  Hovell,  his  wife’s  daughter.

others,  descend  from  the  Hovells  of  Bury  and  Wyverstone : — The  Heighams  of  Hunston,
