The  wife  of  the  testator  was  Elizabeth,  daughter  of  the  Rev.  Alexander  Burrell,  M.A., 
Rector  of  Adstock,  Bucks,  and  Prebendary  of  Lincoln,  who  was  of  the  ancient  Visitation  family 
of  Burrell  of  Cuckfield  in  Sussex,  now  represented  by  Lord  Gwydyr  and  Sir  Merrick  Raymond 
Burrell,  Baronet.  Her  cousin  and  namesake,  Elizabeth  Burrell,  daughter  of  Peter  Burrell,  of 
Beckenham,  in  Kent,  and  sister  of  Sir  Peter  Burrell,  Bart.,  of  a  younger  branch  of  the  family, 
married  (first)  the  Duke  of  Hamilton,  and  (secondly)  the  Marquess  of  Exeter,  whose  previous 
marriage  to  Sarah  Hoggins,  one  of  the  most  delightful  romances  of  the  peerage,  has  been 
immortalized  by  Tennyson  in  his  “  Lord  of  Burleigh.”

Arms  and  Crest  of  Hovell. 

It  is  greatly  to  be  regretted  that  the  fine  Armorial  gravestone  which  formerly  lay  above 
the  remains  of  William  Hovell  and  other  members  of  his  family,  in  Badwell  chancel,  was 
removed  during  the  restoration  of  the  church.  What  was  done  with  it  is  unknown.  Davy 
and  other  antiquarians  had,  fortunately,  copied  it,  or  all  local  record  of  those  whom  it 
commemorated  would  have  been  utterly  lost. 


Inscription  on  Altar  ®omb  at  Mnbcrstonc. 

Sacred  to  the  Memory  of  Mary  wife  of  William  Hovell,  formerly  of  this  Parish,  who 
departed  this  life  5th  of  March  1806,  aged  47  years. 

Also  of  Hannah  Maria  their  daughter.  She  died  the  27th  of  July  1807,  aged  24  years. 

Also  of  five  of  their  children  who  died  in  their  infancy. 

Also  of  Ann,  wife  of  Thomas  Hovell  of  Bacton  in  this  County,  Attorney  at  Law,  mother 
of  the  above  William  Hovell.  Her  remains  are  interred  in  the  Chancel  of  this  Church.  She 
died  the  7th  of  February,  1777,  aged  61  years.

jffolfets  of  Ruslibrook 


Armorial  ©tarings* 

The  Arms  claimed  by  Folkes  of  Cheveley,  co.  Cambridge,  and  Mildenhall,  co.  Suffolk,  at  the 
Visitation  of  the  former  County  in  1684,  were  a  fleur  de-lys,  and  the  Crest,  a  goat’s  head  erased. 
Cole,  the  Cambridgeshire  antiquary,  who  copied  them  from  the  original  tricking  at  the  Heralds’ 

College,  has  omitted  the  tinctures.  Cole’s  MSS.,  vol.  xxi,  fol.  37.  In  an  earlier  Visitation  of 

Shropshire  ( Earl .  MS.  12J/.1,  fo.  lJ/.Sb )  Foulkes  of  that  county  and  of  Staffordshire  bore,  Vert  a 
fleur-de-lys  Argent.  The  present  Ax-ms  of  Ffolkes  of  Hillington  are,  Per  pale,  Vex-t  and  Gules,  a 

fleur-de  lys  Ermine ;  and  the  Crest  is  A  dexter  arm  embowed,  vested  per  pale  Vert  and  Gules, 

holding  in  the  hand  a  spear  pi-oper. 

Like  their  Rushbrook  cousins  the  Folkeses  of  Cheveley  and  Mildenhall  were  lineal  descendants 
of  Martin  Folkes  of  Westley,  who  made  his  will  in  1571.  A  too  brief  account  of  the  family  is 
given  in  that  delightful  book  “  Rushbi-ook  Parish  Registers,  with  Jerrnyn  and  Davers  Annals,” 
edited  by  the  Rev.  Sydenham  H.  A.  Hervey,  M.A.

the  Image  of  saint  xpofur  dui-yng  all  dyuyne  suyce.  To  the  sayd  church  to  the  Rodeloftyng

The  Resydew  of  all  my  goodis  I  bequeith  to  Symond  folkys  my  brother,  Wyftm  folkys  and

my  soule.  Probatum  apud  lamehith  iiijt0  die  Julij  [1494].  P.C.C.  13  Vox.

SUFFOLK  MANORIAL  FAMILIES. 


Thomas  Goodwin,  L.L.B.,  the  first  husband  of  the  testatrix,  was  Commissary  for  the 
Archdeacons  of  Norfolk  and  Norwich,  1556  and  1563.  Being  in  priest’s  orders  his  marriage  was 
disallowed  in  the  time  of  Queen  Mary,  and  his  son,  for  a  time,  took  the  name  of  Theodore 
Goodwin  als  Rickes.  Anne  Goodwin  als  Rickes  was  the  second  wife  of  Thomas  Folkes,  having 
married  him  at  Burwell,  14th  October  1570  Theodore  Goodwin,  her  son,  who  was  Feodary  of 
Norfolk  and  owned  manors  in  Norfolk,  Suffolk,  Yorkshire  and  Cambridgeshire,  married  Anne 
Ffolkes,  the  daughter  of  his  stepfather,  and  their  descendants  entered  a  pedigree  in  the 
Cambridge  Visitation  of  1619.  See  “Goodwin  of  Stonham  Parva,”  vol.  i,  p.  235.

daughters  (to  each)  £200.  Vnto  Symon  ffolkes  my  youngest  sonne  my  tenement  bought  of

clarke,  and  Martin  ffolkes  my  sonne  to  be  executors.  Theodoret  ffolkes  a  witness.  Probatum 
secundo  die  Septembris  1637  juramentis  executorum.  P.C.C.  126  Goare.

1  Soame,  1618)  Sir  Stephen  Soame  mentions  his  sister  Morden,  widow;  Stephen  Morden,  his 

godson,  son  of  J ohn  Morden,  deceased ;  and  the  children  of  Oliver  Morden.  Another  brother, 
Thomas  Soame,  of  Little  Bradley  in  Suffolk,  also  names  his  sister  Morden  in  his  will,  P.C.C., 
made  in  1606.

ffiljanrm)  Depositions,  JJtor&en  t.  JKortien,  1585. 

The  interrogatories  on  the  part  of  Nicholas  Mordon,  plaintiff,  and  of  Robert  Morden  and 
Barbara  his  wife,  defendants,  elicited  the  following  statements 

John  Morden,  of  Exning,  grandfather  to  Robert  Morden  the  defendant,  and  great  grand¬ 
father  to  Nicholas  Morden  the  plaintiff,  died  circa  1558  ( see  his  will  on  page  1 14).  He  had 
previously  settled  a  messuage  in  Weston  and  West  Wratting,  in  Cambridgeshire,  upon  John 
Morden  the  younger,  also  of  Exning,  his  second  son. 

This  John  Morden  the  younger  was  father  of  Robert.  He  died  early,  and  Johan  his 
widow,  Robert’s  mother,  remarried  one  Oliver  Thorneton. 

The  tenants  of  the  Wratting  messuage  acknowledged  John  Morden  the  younger  as  their 
landlord.  After  his  death  it  was  held  by  Johan,  his  widow  :  and  when  she  died  it  passed  to 
Robert  Morden,  her  son.  There  was  another  house  in  Wratting  which  William  Morden,  brother 
of  John  the  younger,  inherited  from  their  father.  One  William  Morden  (so  it  is  deposed)  still 
has  the  lease  of  the  land  at  variance. 

Nicholas  Morden,  the  plaintiff,  claims  to  be  “cousin”  (that  is,  blood  relation)  and  next 
heir  to  John  Morden,  of  Exning,  his  great  grandfather. 

Mitford  Depositions,  680,  Moredon  c  Moredon,  and  681,  Mordan  c.  Mordan. 

The  will  of  Robert  Morden,  of  Soham,  was  proved  at  Bury  in  1591.  He  bequeaths  the 
house  he  lives  in,  with  its  lands,  to  Barbara  his  wife,  with  remainder  to  Henry  his  son ; 
his  houses,  etc.,  in  West  Wratting  to  Roger  his  son;  pastures,  etc.,  in  Soham  to  John  his 
son ;  and  monies  to  Anne,  his  daughter,  when  she  marries,  or  comes  of  age. 


® battery  Will,  JHorta  r.  JHorbnt,  jFrb.  1674-5. 

Mary  Morden,  the  plaintiff,  was  widow  of  Oliver  Morden,  of  Exning,  co.  Suffolk,  gentle¬ 
man,  son  of  John  Morden,  who  had  held  the  Rectory  there,  with  the  Parsonage  house,  tythes 
and  glebe  lands,  of  the  yearly  value  of  £500  or  £600,  of  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of  Canterbury. 
About  May  1663  (15th  Chas.  I)  the  said  Oliver,  with  John  Morden  his  brother  and  Mary  his 
sister,  wife  of  William  Raymond,  of  Newton,  co.  Cambridge,  were  seized  for  their  three  lives 
of  this  Rectory,  etc.  By  Indenture,  dated  the  19th  of  that  month,  in  consideration  of  her 
considerable  portion,  he  settled  said  Rectory  upon  trustees  for  plaintiff’s  use.  In  1668,  being 
straitened  for  money,  they  mortgaged  it  to  Oliver  Morden,  of  Wicken,  co.  Cambridge,  gent. 
In  May  1674  John  Morden  the  brother  died,  and  Oliver,  of  Wicken,  put  in  a  life  in  his 
room.  He  has  now  gotten  all  the  deeds,  etc.,  into  his  possession,  and  refuses  to  pay  the  £30 
per  annum  which  he  covenanted  to  allow  her.  Morden  c  Morden,  Whittington,  480. 

In  the  pedigre  of  Ho  veil  of  Bury  (see  page  103),  it  is  inexactly  stated  that  Oliver 
Morden,  of  Exning,  brother  to  Margaret  Hovell,  was  ancestor  to  Lord  Suffield.  Subsequent 
researches  have  shown  that  the  lineage  of  that  peer,  as  hitherto  accepted,  was  based  upon 
imperfect  information.  He  derives  from  John  Morden,  Margaret  Hovell’s  uncle.  Her  brother, 
therefore,  was  his  collateral  ancestor  only.  See  the  Morden  pedigree  on  the  next  page.

The  Arms  allowed  to  Sir  John  Morden  at  the  London  Visitation  of  1664 — Argent,  a  fleur-de-lis  Gules — were  those 
borne  by  Mordon,  Lord  Mayor  of  London,  in  1368.  Lord  Suffield  bears : — Quarterly  1  and  4,  quarterly  Azure  and 
Gules,  four  lions  rampant  Argent,  and  in  the  centre  an  imperial  crown  Or,  for  Harbord ;  2  and  3  Morden,  as  above.

Armorial  Hearings. 

The  arms  which  accompany  the  Whiting  pedigree  in  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664  are 
three  chevrons  on  a  shield  (Harl.  MS.  1085).  They  are  more  fully  described  in  the  contemporary 
manuscript  formerly  in  the  possession  of  Sir  John  Blois,  so  frequently  quoted  by  Jermyn  and 
Davy,  as  Sable,  three  chevrons  Argent. 

Thomas  Whiting  of  Boxford,  who  heads  the  pedigree  in  the  Candler  MSS.,  was  probably 
descended  from  the  clothmakers  of  the  name,  who  had  lived  there  for  some  generations.  He 
may  even  have  been  the  “  Thomas  Whiting,  son  of  Thomas  Whiting  of  Boxford,”  who  entered 
Caius  College  in  1573  ;  but  this  is  doubtful.  Sir  Edward  Bysshe  has,  perhaps  mistakenly, 
described  him  as  of  Norfolk. 

The  Hadleigh  Whitings  are  especially  remarkable  for  their  near  relationship  to  a  very 
unusual  number  of  the  early  emigrants  to  New  England.  Besides  their  pedigree  entered  at  the 
Heralds’  College  in  1664,  they  and  their  connections  are  very  fully  dealt  with  by  Matthias 
Candler,  their  neighbour  and  contemporary,  in  his  Manuscripts,  now  in  the  Bodleian  Library  and 
the  British  Museum. 


Mill  of  foljn  Minting,  1057.

Armorial  Hearings. 

“  Sable,  a  fess  Argent,  between  three  escallops  Or,  is  born  by  the  name  of  Bright,  and 
was  at  first  granted  to  Thomas  Bright  of  St.  Edmondsbury  in  Suffolk,  son  of  Thomas  and  Mary 
his  wife,  daughter  of  ...  .  Peiton,  by  William  Camden,  Clarencieux,  in  the  14th  year  of  the 
Reign  of  King  James  the  First  (1616).” 

“  Afterwards  the  same  coat  was  confirmed  to  one  Thomas  Bright  of  Netherhall  in  Suffolk, 
eldest  son  of  Robert  Bright,  who  was  second  brother  to  Thomas  Bright  of  Sfc  Edmondsbury 

abovesaid,  by  Sir  John  Borough,  the  29th  of  July  1641,  and  17th  year  of  the  reign  of  King 

Charles  the  First.”  Guillim’s  Heraldry ,  Sixth  Edition,  pp.  244,  245. 

At  the  Visitation  of  Suffolk  in  1664,  William  Bright,  Esq.,  of  Talmach  Hall,  the  grandson 

of  Thomas  of  St.  Edmundsbury,  bore  the  arms  above  described  together  with  a  crest,  viz.  : — 

A  dragon’s  head  Gules,  collared  and  lined  Or,  vomiting  flames  of  fire.  And  Thomas  Bright  of 
Net  her  hall,  son  of  the  Thomas  Bright  to  whom  these  insignia  had  been  confirmed  “p.  Boroughe 
Garter”  in  1641,  was  allowed  the  same  properly  differentiated  by  a  crescent.  Ilarl.  MS.  1085. 

“  The  Brights  of  Suffolk,  England,”  a  model  work  of  its  kind,  printed  at  Boston,  Massachusetts, 
in  1858,  gives  an  almost  exhaustive  history  of  the  family,  together  with  the  wills,  pedigrees, 
monumental  inscriptions  and  other  records  upon  which  it  is  based.  The  documents  which  we 
now  subjoin  are,  for  the  most  part,  the  outcome  of  more  recent  research,  and  some  of  them  are 
new  to  genealogists. 


Mill  of  Shorn  as  iSright,  1587. 

The  twentith  daie  of  Auguste,  1587,  and  in  the  nine  and  twentith  yeare  of  the  raigne 
of  our  most  noble  and  soueraigne  ladie  Queene  Elizabeth,  I  Thomas  Brighte  the  elder  of  Burye 
saincte  Edmondes,  draper,  do  herebie  declare  this  my  laste  will  and  testamente.  And  herein  first 
and  especiallie  I  commende  my  sowle  into  the  mercifull  handes  of  allmightie  god,  trustinge  in 
the  merites  and  passion  of  Jesus  Christe  to  haue  pardon  of  my  sinnes.  I  giue  vnto  Margarett 
my  wife  my  mannor  known  by  the  name  of  Botters  in  Tompson  in  the  countie  of  Norff.  and  the 
stocke  of  foure  hundred  sheepe  vnto  the  said  mannor  belonginge,  and  also  my  tenementes  called 
Bees  and  Brightemears  in  Tompson  aforesaid :  also  my  porcon  of  tithyes  dewe  oute  of  the  mannor 
of  Broocke  halle  in  Foxeyearthe  in  Essex,  and  other  my  meisuages  Ac.  in  Burie,  Barton  next 
Burye,  Nowton  and  Fornham  sainct  Martin,  to  houlde  duringe  the  whole  tearme  of  (her)  life,  yf 
she  shall  keape  her  vnmarried.  And  yf  the  said  Margarette  shall  happen  to  marrie  again  all

This  will  is  in  part  recited  in  the  Inquisition  post  mortem  of  Thomas  Bright  taken  at 
Thetford  in  the  43rd  year  of  Queen  Elizabeth.  He  was  found  to  have  been  seized  of  the 
Manor  of  Butters  als  Buttalls  als  Tompson  Hall  in  Tompson  co.  Norfolk,  together  with  a  capital 
messuage  called  Brightmeres.  He  had  died  on  the  30th  of  August  in  the  29th  year  of  the  said 
queen  (1587);  and  Thomas  Bright  his  son  and  heir  was  aged  thirty  years  and  upwards. 
Escheats,  Eliz.,  1.  57.  Similar  Inquisitions  were  taken  at  Bury  St.  Edmunds  in  the  29th 
year  of  Q.  Elizabeth,  and  at  Stratford  Langthorne  in  the  43d  year  of  Q.  Elizabeth  in  connection

Katherine  Whiter,  widow,  the  first  wife  of  Stephen  Woodgate,  is  doubtless  identical  with 
Katherine  Woodgate,  daughter  and  devisee  of  William  Hovell  a  Is  Smyth  of  Haughley,  1582,  who 
refers  to  her  children  and  names  Stephen  Woodgate  of  Eastbergholt  in  his  will  (Suffolk  Manorial 

Families,  vol.  ii,  26).  She  was  sister  therefore  to  William  Hovell,  Esq.,  of  Hillington.  Mary 

Derehaugh,  Stephen  Woodgate’s  second  wife,  was  equally  well  connected.  She  was  daughter  of 
Thomas  Derehaugh  of  Badingham,  and  sister  of  John  Derehaugh  and  of  Julian  the  wife  of  John 
Barker  ais  Chapman  of  Sibton ;  and  Robert  Derehaugh  of  Gray’s  Inn  and  Edmond  Barker  of 
Sibton,  gentleman,  named  in  her  husband’s  will,  were  her  near  kinsmen.

Margaret  Bright  was  daughter  of  William  Payton  of  Risby  in  Suffolk.  Her  sister  Rose 
Payton  married  Simon  Langham  of  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  and  their  descendants  entered  pedigrees 
in  the  Visitations  of  London,  1634,  and  of  Sussex,  1662.  (S’ uffolk  Manorial  Families,  vol.  i, 

262,  375).  Her  sister  Margerie  Payton  married  Richard  Wilson,  Rector  of  Rattlesden.  Olorenshaw’s 
Notes  on'  Rattlesden,  p.  30).  Anne  Payton,  sole  daughter  and  heiress  of  her  brother  Thomas 
Payton,  became  the  wife  of  John  Hammond  of  Hawkedon,  whose  great  grandson,  John  Hammond 
of  Cresseners,  entered  his  pedigree  in  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664.  [Suffolk  Manorial  Families, 
vol.  i,  261).  See  Pedigree  of  Payton,  Hamond  and  Langham  in  Suffolk  Manorial  Families, 
vol.  i,  262.

In  1613  Joan  Bright  of  London,  widow  of  Jasper  Bright  late  of  London,  Salter,  sued 
John  Langham,  citizen  and  Leatherseller  of  London,  evidently  his  cousin  of  that  name  (see 
Pedigrees  of  Langham,  vol.  i,  pp  262,  376),  and  Edmund  Houghton,  citizen  and  draper  of 
London,  probably  her  brother  in  law  (see  Pedigree,  Bright  of  Talmach  Hall),  whom  she  had 
appointed  her  attorneys  to  assist  her  in  the  administration  of  the  estate.  She  charges  them  with 
misappropriating  monies.  This  seems  to  settle  the  question  as  to  whether  Jasper  Bright  the 
salter  and  his  namesake,  Margaret  Bright’s  son,  were  one  and  the  same.  Chancery  Bills  and 
Answers,  James  I,  38,  J+S-  Bright  contra  Ilo'ngliton. 

Thomas  Bright,  the  son  of  Jasper  Bright,  was  a  devisee  in  the  will  of  his  uncle  Robert 
Bright,  Esq.,  of  Pakenham,  in  1630,  an  abstract  of  which  is  given  on  the  next  page.

Mill  of  Kotef  bright,  1650 

I  Robert  Bright  at  this  fisent  time  in  bodely  health  and  in  sound  and  jifect  memory 
doe  ordaine  and  declare  this  to  be  my  last  will.  I  comitt  my  soule  into  the  hands  of  god  my 
mersifull  father,  trusting  to  the  merits  of  Jesus  Christ  for  the  pardon  of  my  sinnes.  I  hope  to 
be  an  inheritor  of  glory  after  this  life  ended.  Amen. 

I  give  to  my  sonne  Thomas  the  reversion  of  that  measuage  called  Battelies.  When  I

pond  bond  to  give  (it  him)  by  will.  Vnto  my  sonne  William  the  fearme  called  Barton  place

mesuages  and  houses  that  was  latelie  in  the  tenure  of  John  Manister :  all  which  lands  and 
tenements  I  have  conveyed  unto  Edmond  Millesone  and  Bennet  Barker  for  the  uses  of  my  two 
sonnes  William  and  Henry  by  a  Tripertite  Indenture  bearing  date  the  first  day  of  March,  1621  :

Pakenham.  Richard  Freston  the  son  made  his  will  in  1648,  and  died  without  issue.  Elizabeth 
Freston,  who  thus  became  sole  heiress  to  her  mother  and  her  brother,  married  first  Sir  Nicholas 
Bacon  of  Gillingham,  co.  Norfolk,  Baronet,  and  secondly  Sir  William  Godbold  of  Mendham, 
Knight,  and  the  estates,  conditionally  bequeathed  to  Borrowdale  Bright,  Elizabeth  Bright  and 
Agatha  Bright,  passed  to  her  legal  heirs.

The  Remembrance  of  the  shortness,  fraylety  and  corruptible  estate  of  man’s  lyfe,  not 
knowing  how  long  it  may  please  God  to  continew  the  same,  and  considering  allso  what  troubles, 
suits  and  chardges  in  law,  and  what  great  vnkindnes  doth  daylie  happen,  even  amongst  the 
neerest  in  blood,  for  the  not  making  of  men’s  wills,  Theise  and  suchlyke  considerations  have 
moved  me  S'  Nicholas  Carew  allias  Throckmorton  of  Bedington  in  the  countie  of  Surry,  Knight, 
to  make  my  humble  and  heartie  prayers  unto  allmightie  God,  that  it  may  please  him  to  grant 
me  the  assistance  of  his  gratious  directions,  that  I  may  advisedly  sett  in  order  those  worldly 
goods  which  it  hath  pleased  (him)  to  bestowe  vpon  me.  Vnto  Sr  Francys  Carew,  Knight  of 
the  bathe  and  to  his  heires  malles  lawfully  begotten  (I  give]  the  Mannor  of  Walton,  with  the 
windemill  and  howse  to  it,  and  the  howse  called  Newbarnes,  with  all  the  tithe  of  the  parishe 
of  Mitcham :  And  for  wante  of  such  issue,  Then  to  my  seconde  sonne  Nicholas  Carew  and  the 
heirres  malles  of  his  bodie :  And  for  want  of  such,  to  my  thirde  sonne  Geordge  Carew  and  the 
heirres  males  of  his  bodie :  And  for  want  of  such,  Then  to  my  fourthe  sonne  Edmund  Carew 
and  to  the  heirres  males  of  his  bodie :  And  for  wante  of  such  issue  male,  then  to  my  fifte 
sonne  Oliphe  Carew :  And  for  wante  of  such,  Then  to  my  heirres  for  ever.  By  severall  fines 
and  Indentures  I  have  levied  vnto  Sr  Thomas  Grymes,  Knight  and  Robert  Wolrich,  Esqr,  of  the 
Mannors  of  Biggin  and  Tamworth  in  Mitcham,  Tooting,  and  Martin  in  the  County  of  Surry, 
the  Rectorie  of  Cowdham  in  the  Countie  of  Kent,  and  fortie  acres  of  pasture  in  East  Barnet

in  the  Countie  of  Hertford.  I  doe  hereby  declare  that  I  haue  not  not  changed  or  made  void 
anie  of  the  vses  or  estates  appointed  by  the  Indentures  aforesaid.  And  my  will  is  that  all 
manner  of  writings  concerning  these  mannors  (fee.  be  deliuered  to  those  my  sonnes  to  whom  the 
said  premises  are  conveyed.  And  for  that  my  eldest  sonne  Sr  francys  Carew,  Knight  of  the 
bathe,  hath  runne  him  selfe  farre  in  debte  and  fearing  if  I  shoulde  make  him  my  executor  my 
hole  estate  would  be  dissipated,  I  make  and  ordaine  my  welbeloued  brothor  in  law  Sr  Thomas 
Grymes  of  Peckham  my  sole  executor  And  I  bequeath  (him)  forty  poundes.  I  geiue  the 
remainder  of  my  goods  to  my  grandchild  Nicholas  Carew,  sonne  of  Sr  francys  Carew,  at  the 
age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares. 

And  concerning  my  onely  daughter  Susanna  Carew  which  I  had  by  my  last  wife. 
According  to  a  covenant  in  an  Indenture  tripartite  made  the  13th  day  of  August,  1616, 
Betweene  my  selfe  of  the  first  part,  Susanna  Butler,  widdow,  of  the  second  parte,  and  Thomas 
Trevor  of  the  Inner  Temple  London  esquire  with  others  on  the  third  part,  That  I  should  pay 
vnto  my  said  daughter  at  the  day  of  her  maryage  or  her  age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares,  which 
of  them  shall  first  happen,  the  sume  of  three  thousand  pounds  for  her  portion :  Now  my  will 
is  that  it  be  accordingly  payed  vnto  her.  And  (I)  do  admonish  her  in  a  fatherly  care  that 
she  be  advised  and  guided  by  my  executor  and  overseers,  both  concerning  the  disposing  of  her 
said  portion  and  her  marriage.  And  my  will  is  that  vntill  the  day  of  her  marriage  or  her 
age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares  there  be  allowed  vnto  her  yearely  for  her  maintenance  the 
summe  of  sixe  score  poundes.  And  further  my  will  is  that  my  said  daughter  and  Elizabeth 
Butler  her  sister  shall  have  and  enioy  the  lodging  chamber  where  they  vsually  lye,  and  the 
lodging  and  diett  of  their  servants,  during  the  space  of  sixe  months  next  after  my  decease,  if 
my  said  daughter  shall  so  longe  like  to  liue  there. 

Allso  I  geiue  vnto  my  youngest  sonne  Oliphe  Carew  fiue  hundred  pounds  for  him  to 
imploye  in  his  trading.  Allso  I  geiue  vnto  my  grandchilde  Rebecca  Carew,  eldest  daughter  of 
my  eldest  sonne  Sr  francys  Carew  one  hundred  pounds  at  her  age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares 
or  the  day  of  her  mariadge.  Allso  I  geiue  vnto  Susanna  Carew,  Elizabeth  Carew  and  Phillip 
Carew,  the  second,  third  and  fourth  daughters  of  my  saide  eldest  sonne,  to  (every)  of  them 
one  hundred  pounds  Allso  I  geiue  to  the  parishe  Church  of  Bedington  to  be  vsed  one  the 
communion  table  one  siluer  flagon  with  my  armes  graven  vpon  it.  And  I  geiue  to  the  poore 
of  Bedington  fiue  pounds :  and  to  all  my  menseruants  &  maydseruants  which  are  with  me  at 
the  tyme  of  my  death  one  hole  yeares  wages  over  and  aboue  what  is  dew  vnto  them.  And  I 
doe  desyre  my  louinge  frendes  Sr  Thomas  Trevor,  Knight,  one  of  the  Barons  of  the  Exchequer 
and  Robert  Wolrich  of  Greies  I :  in  the  Countie  of  Middlesex  esquire  and  Edward  Harris  of 
the  Inner  Temple,  London,  esquire  to  be  the  supervisors. 

The  last  sheet  of  this  imperfect  transcript  (which  is  taken  from  the  Carew  Papers,  Add. 
MS.  29,605,  fol.  29b — 39b)  is  endorsed  “Copy  of  part  of  the  Will  of  Sr  N8  Carew  als 
Throckmorton.”  There  is  no  indication  of  date  or  witnesses. 

By  her  marriage  with  Sir  Nicholas  Carew,  Susan  Bright,  the  aunt  of  Henry  Bright,  the 
New  England  emigrant,  became  sister  in  law  to  Sir  Walter  Raleigh.  The  monument  which 
Susanna  Carew,  described  in  the  will  as  her  only  daughter,  placed  to  her  memory  in  Bedington 
church,  has  the  following  inscription : — 

“To  the  memory  of  my  deare  mother,  the  Lady  Carew,  late  wife  of  Sir  Nicholas  Carew 
of  Bedington,  Whose  vertuous  Life  doth  memory  deserue :  who  taught  her  children  Heauen’s 
great  God  to  serue.  She  departed  this  life  the  xith  day  of  December  in  the  yeare  1633.”

his  wife  widow  of  John  Whiter,  and  Richard,  Mary,  and  Anne  Whiter,  infants,  children  of  said  John,  complainants.  Whiter

Whyter’s  decease  she  came  to  the  Court  of  the  Manor  and  prayed  that  her  children  might  be  admitted  to  these  copyholds. 
William  Shelley  Esq.,  the  Lord  of  the  Manor,  answered  that  yf  she  woulde  marye  wl  one  William  Washyngton  she  and  her 
children  should  be  admitted  tennants ;  but  should  she  marye  Steven  Woodgate  they  must  give  Washyngton  20'  for  his  good 
will.  Complaynants  pray  that  a  subpena  be  granted  against  Shelley  and  Wasshington;  who  reply  that  the  charge  is  false 
and  slanderous.  Rejoinders  and  replications  follow  and  the  proceedings  are  voluminous.

The  will,  of  which  the  above  is  a  much  abbreviated  abstract,  is  given  verbatim  in  Bury  Wills 
and  Inventories ,  edited  for  the  Camden  Society  by  the  late  Samuel  Tymms.  In  that  work  it 
occupies  nearly  thirty  pages,  and  there  are  fourteen  more  of  descriptive  notes  and  illustrations.  It 
abounds  with  allusions  to  the  usages,  social  and  ecclesiological,  of  the  times  of  Henry  the  Sixth, 
and  is  most  interesting  reading.  John  Barrett,  who  is  supposed  to  have  been  Chamberlayn  or 
Treasurer  of  the  Abbey,  was  the  son  of  a  certain  Geoffrey  Barrett  of  Ci’atfield,  whose  will  was 
proved  in  1416  (Liber  “Osberne,”  fo.  142).  His  striking  altar  tomb  still  remains  in  St.  Mary’s

church  at  Bury.  Thomas  Barrett,  of  the  Westhall  family,  claimed  him  as  a  collateral  ancestor  in 
his  letter  to  Sir  Edward  Bysshe,  Clarencieux,  in  1671,  and  there  is  reason  to  believe  that  the 
statement,  although  yet  unproven,  is  correct.  It  is  to  be  regretted  that  the  extreme  length  of  the 
will  precluded  its  insertion,  in  a  complete  form,  in  Suffolk  Manorial  Families.

followinge.  I  commende  my  sowle  to  allmightie  god,  and  my  bodye  to  the  earthe.  I  gyve  to 
my  brother  Anthonye  Wingfeild  of  London  goldsmyth,  all  my  Landes,  Tenements,  Rentes  Ac. 
within  the  Realme  of  England  or  in  Ireland.  To  Owen  Barrett  and  Xpofer  Barrett  fyve  poundes 
a  peece,  and  to  my  sister  Prudence  Barrett  Tenne  poundes  to  be  paide  to  hir  at  hir  mariage 
or  age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares.  The  rest  of  all  my  gooddes  &c.  I  bequeath  to  my  saide  lovinge 
brother  Anthony  Wingfeild.  And  I  make  the  same  Anthonye  the  sole  Executor  of  this  will.  In 
witnes  whereof  I  the  same  Thomas  to  this  my  present  wrytinge  have  sett  my  hande  and  seale 
the  daye  and  yere  abovesaide,  1575.

The  chief  interest  in  Christopher  Barrett,  who  was  Mayor  of  Norwich  in  1634,  centres  in 
the  fact  that  Margaret,  his  daughter,  and  Simon  Huntington,  her  husband,  emigrated  with  their 
children  to  New  England  and  became  the  ancestors  of'  a  distinguished  American  family,  which 
numbers  amongst  its  scions,  Governors,  Judges,  Generals  and  Colonels,  Doctors  of  Divinity, 
Professors  and  Members  of  Congress,  particulars  of  whom  will  be  found  in  the  Genealogical 
Memoir  of  the  Huntington  Family ,  by  the  Rev.  E.  B.  Huntington,  A.M.,  Stamford,  Connecticut, 
1863.  In  the  State  Library  at  Hartford,  Connecticut,  is  a  letter  of  Peter  Barrett  of  Norwich, 
dated  20th  April  1650,  to  his  nephew  Christopher  Huntington,  referring  to  moneys  of  his 
brother  Stoughton  (Margaret  Barrett’s  second  husband)  and  to  the  death  of  her  father  in  the 
previous  August.

The  Barrett  Pedigree  in  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1561  is  here  given  in  italics.  Descents  are  added  from  the  Norfolk 
Visitation  of  1664,  and  from  the  written  statement  sent  to  Sir  Edward  Bysshe  by  Thomas  Barrett  of  Norwich  in  1671. 

The  Arms  of  Barrett  of  Westhall  at  the  Visitation  of  Suffolk  in  1561  were  Argent,  a  bend  Azure  between  three 
buckles  lozengy  Gules  (Harl.  MS.  1560).  At  the  Vistation  of  Norfolk  in  1664  these  were  borne  by  Thomas  Barrett  of  Norwich, 
the  then  representative  of  the  family,  with  the  addition  of  a  Crest,  on  a  helmet  two  ostrich  feathers,  the  one  Or,  the  other 
Argent  (Harl.  MS.  1085).  A  similar  shield  appears  upon  the  tomb,  in  the  church  of  St.  Mary,  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  of  John 
Baret,  the  pious  and  munificent  churchman,  who  died  in  1467,  but  the  bend  is  super-posed  over  one  of  the  buckles.  There 
is  no  reasonable  doubt  of  the  near  relationship  of  the  Bury  and  the  Westhall  Barretts,  although  the  exact  lines  of  descent 
have  not,  as  yet,  been  clearly  worked  out.

JUmoral  Hearings. 

The  arms  of  Partridge  of  Finborough,  as  recorded  in  the  original  manuscript  of  Cooke’s 
Suffolk  Visitation  of  1577  at  the  Heralds’  College,  were  Chequy  Argent  and  Sable,  on  a  bend 
Or  three  escallops  of  the  second.  Edmondson,  however,  usually  an  excellent  guide,  describes  the 
bend  as  Gules  ( Complete  Body  of  Heraldry ,  1780,  vol.  ii).  Harl.  MS.  1560  has  it  Sable. 
Harl.  MS.  1820  omits  the  escallops.  "We  need  scarcely  add  that  the  only  correct  authority  is 
the  Original  Visitation,  and  that  all  the  others  are  wrong.  The  Crest  was  a  horse’s  head  erased, 
per  fesse  Sable  and  Gules,  crined  (or  maned)  Or. 

Partridge  of  Finborough  was  one  of  the  “  cheife  gentry  ”  of  the  county  whose  arms 
Ryece,  the  author  of  the  Breviary  of  Suffolk  (1618),  caused  to  be  painted  on  the  windows  of 
Preston  church  early  in  the  seventeenth  century.  Partridge  impaling  Tymperley  was  formerly  in 
Hintlesham  church,  where  so  many  of  the  latter  family  were  buried.  (Add.  MS.  5,829,  fo.  202a.) 

Mr.  Charles  Partridge,  M.A.,  of  Stowmarhet,  Suffolk,  political  officer  in  Southern  Nigeria, 
W.  Africa,  writes : — “  Partridge  has  always  been  a  prolific  name  in  Suffolk.  As  far  as  I  know, 
the  only  branch  ever  entitled  to  use  armorial  bearings  was  that  of  the  ‘  Visitation  ’  family  of 
Partridge  of  Great  Finborough,  which  seems  to  have  resided  in  the  county  during  the  reigns 
of  Mary  and  Elizabeth  only.  The  other  branches  established  in  Suffolk  before  1600  may  be 
tabulated  as  follow  : — 

(1)  Of  Wood  bridge  •  Rob.  Pteriche  of  Woodbridge  made  his  will  16  May  1459,  proved 

Archd.  Suff. 

(2)  Of  Shotley ;  John  Pertryche  of  Shotley’s  will  is  dated  7  Aug.  1463,  proved  Archd.  Suff. 

(3)  Of  Acton,  Sudbury,  and  Lavenham  ;  see  Proceedings  of  the  Suff.  Institute  of  Archceology, 

vol.  x,  part  ii,  150-163. 

(4)  Of  the  Greetings  and  Stonhams ;  will  of  George  Partryche  of  Creeting  All  Saints 

proved  1536,  Archd.  Suff. 

(5)  Of  Ipswich. 

(6)  Of  Bradfield  S.  Clare  and  Great  Welnetham ;  see  The  Bast  Anglian,  or  Notes  and 

Queries,  on  subjects  connected  with  the  counties  of  Suffolk,  etc.,  third  ser.,  vol. 

viii,  190-191. 

(7)  Of  Higham  and  Capel  S.  Mary,  afterwards  of  Holton  S.  Mary  and  Shelley  Hall.” 

At  the  Visitation  of  Gloucestershire  in  1583  {Harl.  MS.  lOjl,  fo.  4b)  the  arms  allowed 

to  Partrich  of  that  county  were  Chequy,  Argent  and  Sable,  on  a  bend  Gules  three  escallops 

Or ;  the  Crest  being  out  of  a  ducal  coronet  Or,  a  horse’s  head  Sable.  These  insignia  had  been 

confirmed  by  Lawrence  Dalton,  Norx-oy,  in  1561,  and  afterwards  by  William  Hervey,  Clarencieux, 

in  1566.

No  ancient  pedigree  of  the  Ives  of  Suffolk  has  been  recorded  in  the  Harleian  MSS. ;  but  they  inter¬ 
married  with  the  families  of  Wade,  Partridge  and  Colby.  Metcalfe’s  Visitation  of  Suffolk,  pp.  17,  99,  173.  In 
the  twentieth  year  of  Edward  IV  (1480-81)  John  Tymperly,  sen.,  “purchased  by  Fine,  the  Manor  of  Boyton 
in  Finborougii  Magna,  Combes,  Stowmarket,  Hecham,  Buxhall  and  Felsham,  of  John  Ive  and  Alice  his  wife 
and  John  Colby  and  Isabella  his  wife,  daughter  of  said  John  and  Alice.  Now  John  Colby  of  Banham  in 
Norfolk  who  married  Isabel,  dau.  and  one  of  the  heirs  of  .  .  .  Ive  of  Finborough,  had  issue  John  Colby  of 
Brundish,  whose  children  were  living  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1561.  Marl.  MS.  1103.  Dorothy  Tymperley, 
a  descendant  of  John  Tymperley,  married  Thomas  Partridge,  the  son  of  Robert  Partridge  and  Ursula  Ive 
in  1578.  Thomas  Tymperley,  her  father,  was  the  then  lord  of  Boyton  Hall.

The  tenth  daie  of  Aprill,  1594.  I  Robert  Partridge  the  elder  of  greate  Fynborowe  in 
the  countie  of  Suff.,  gentleman,  doe  make  this  my  last  will  and  Testament.  I  bequeath  my

to  my  wife  Urcelie  Partridge  one  yeerelie  annuitie  of  twentie  poundes  payable  by  Richard  Howe 
of  Stowmarket,  gentleman,  as  is  specified  in  a  paire  of  Indentures  betweene  vs ;  provided  that 
{she)  shall  quite  release  to  my  sonne  Thomas  Partridge  all  that  right  which  she  maie  haue  in 
anie  of  my  landes  in  Beeston,  Sprowston,  Spixworth  and  Crostwicke  in  Norff  and  Dinington

naturall  life  with  condition  for  the  true  repaiement  thereof  to  my  sonne  Robert  after  her 
decease.  To  Dorothie  Richar,  the  wife  of  Henrie  Richer  of  Buxhall,  the  somme  of  tenne 
poundes ;  (they  to)  release  all  benefits  as  maie  befall  to  the  saide  Dorothie  by  the  death  of 
John  Rooke  her  father.  I  bequeath  to  Alice  Games,  the  wife  of  Adlord  Games  of  greate 
Fynbarowe  the  somme  of  five  poundes.  Also  to  the  saide  Alice  Games  a  dun  ambling  nagge 
which  her  husband  hath  nowe  in  his  occupation.  Adlord  Games  doth  owe  me  twentie  fouer 
poundes.  Yf  (he)  and  Alice  his  wife  shall  make  a  release  of  all  guiftes  and  benefittes  as  maie 
befall  to  her  by  the  death  of  John  Rooke,  her  father,  the  saide  Adlord  shall  be  acquitted  of 
the  debt.  I  giue  to  Anne  Devoros  the  wife  of  William  Devoros  tenne  shillinges.  Also  to 

Robert  Devoros  the  sonne  of  the  saide  William  the  somme  of  three  shillinges  fouer  pence.  The 
saide  William  Devoros  standeth  bounde  for  the  paiement  of  twentie  poundes.  Yf  (he)  and

father  then  the  saide  bonde  to  stand  voide  and  to  be  redeliuered  into  the  handes  of  the  saide 
William.  I  giue  to  Annis  Salter  my  daughter,  the  wife  of  John  Salter  of  Buxall,  a  syluer

Executo”.  The  rest  of  my  goodes  shalbe  equallie  deuided  betweene  my  saide  two  Executora 
Prouided  that  my  sonne  Thomas,  in  consideration  of  the  legacies  to  him  bequeathed,  shall 
deliuer  to  my  sonne  Robert  Partridge,  at  the  now  mansion  house  of  John  Scarlett  in  Stow¬ 
market  the  aforesaide  bond  wherein  I  stand  bounden  to  Thomas  Tymperlie  Esquier,  or  one 

sufficient  discharge  from  the  Executors  of  the  saide  Thomas  Tymperlie  for  the  saide  bonde. 
And  I  make  John  Scarlett  of  Stowmarket,  clothier,  Suprauiso1  of  this  my  last  will,  and  for  his 
paines  I  bequeath  (him)  the  somme  of  twentie  shillinges.  Theise  beinge  witnesses,  Richard 
Scarlette,  Richard  Smithe  et  mei  Johannes  Godard.

Some  seventeenth  century  pedigrees  describe  the  Partridges  as  of  Finborough  Hall.  In  his  will,  dated  10  Ap.  1594,  Robert 
P.  is  styled  of  G’-  Finborough,  and  the  last  entry  of  the  name  in  that  parish  register  is  the  burial  of  his  brother  Thomas  P. 
on  28  Oct.  1594.  Robert  P.’s  will  was  proved  3  Dec.  1597.  The  Partridges  seem  to  have  left  Finborough  between  1594  and 
1597,  and  were  succeeded  there  by  the  Gilberts.  The  lordship  was  granted  by  Q.  Eliz.  to  Hen.  G.  of  London,  goldsmith, 
whose  son  Sir  John  G.  of  Finb.  Hall  was  “bur  at  Finborough  by  his  father”  (Metcalfe,  202).  It  is  more  probable, 
however,  that  the  Partridges  lived  at  Boy  ton  Hall  in  Finborough,  a  manor  which  their  kinsmen,  the  Tymperleys,  purchased 
of  tho  Ives  and  Colbys  in  1481.  See  footnote  to  the  Partridge  pedigree,  p.  162. 

Tho  following  is  taken  from  the  pedigree  of  Devereux  of  Bacton  in  the  Candler  MSS.  (Harl.  MS.  6071,  pp.  376-377’ 
collated  with  Tanner  MS.  180,  pp.  52-53),  “  Wm.  Devereux  of  Bacton  (married)  Anne  Rooke  daughter  and  one  of  the  coheirs 
of  ...  .  Rooke  of  Badingham.  Dorothie  her  sister,  the  eldest,  (married)  ....  Richer.  Her  younger  sister  married  .... 
Games.  A  sister  of  the  liaulfe  blood,  daughter  of  their  mother  and  of  her  2d  husband,  Robt.  Pattrick,  married  .... 
Salter  of  Long  Stratton  in  Norff.  whose  3  sonnes  live  in  Long  Stratton.  Penelope,  one  of  his  (Salter’s)  daughters,  married 
.  .  .  .  Whiting  of  Ipswich.  Another  married  ....  Smith,  a  younger  brother  of  Brian  Smith  of  Cavendish.”  Some  of  the 
sons  of  William  Devereux  and  Anne  Rooke  fought  in  the  “  low  cuntry  warres,”  and  died  there.  And  one,  as  stated  above, 
Peter  Devereux,  Rector  of  Rattlesden,  became  “  Chaplain  in  Ordinary  to  George  Villiers  ye  1st  Duke  of  Buckingham.”  He 
married  and  had  sons  who  took  orders,  and  daughters  who  married  clergymen,  one  of  whom  was  Matthias  Candler,  the 
genealogical  Vicar  of  Coddenham.

poore  of  Capill  20/-.  The  moueables  wthin  the  house  shalbe  equallye  devyded  Amonge  Richard 
Partridge,  Thomas  Partridge  and  Robert  Partridge  my  sonnes  and  Susan  Partridge  my  daughter. 
The  residue  unbequeathed  I  giue  to  Richard  Partridge  my  sonne,  Prouided  that  he  allowe  his 
brother  Thomas  Partridge  sufficient  mayntenance  till  he  haue  commenced  mr  of  Arts.  Son  Richard 
to  be  executor.  This,  the  second  will  of  Thomas  Partridge,  was  proved  17  July  1627  by  Richard 
Pattridge.  Archd.  Suff,  year  1627-28,  fo.  100. 

Robert  Partridge,  youngest  son  of  the  testator,  lived  at  Roodings  in  Stoke,  then  at  Higham, 
and  finally  at  Holton  S.  Mary  Hall.  In  a  deed  dated  14  Jan.  163£,  now  in  the  possession  of 
Charles  Partridge  of  Stowmarket,  he  is  styled  “  Robarte  Partridge  of  Stoake  by  Nayland  yeoman.” 
Thomas  Rolfe’s  will,  dated  3  Nov.  1653  (original  probate,  endorsed  “  Rolfes  will  for  Goodman 
Pattridge,”  also  penes  C.P.),  devises  “to  Thomas  Partridge  my  Godsonn  the  sonne  of  Ro  :  Patteridge 
of  Holton  Hall  my  Little  Roane  mare  Colt  with  the  ball  face,  And  I  give  to  my  Ex :  and 
Super :  hereafter  named  my  bay  Colt  in  the  meadowe  I  make  Ro :  Patteridge  my 

Executor”  .  .  .  Richard  Patteridge  of  Capell  to  be  a  supervisor.  In  another  deed  penes  C.P., 
dated  12  Nov.  1672,  he  is  styled  Robert  Pattridge  the  elder  of  Holton,  gent.,  and  his  burial-entry 
in  Holton  register  describes  him  as  “Gen:”  in  1676.  He  bequeathed  his  “Deske  in  my  Chamber 
called  the  best  Chamber”  to  his  son  Robert.  It  now  belongs  to  Miss  Partridge  of  Hadleigh.

[In  167a  Daniel,  fourth  son  of  Rob.  Partridge  of  Holton  S.  Mary  Hall,  m.  Mary,  dau. 

of  the  late  Edward  Mann  of  Ipswich,  esq.  Edward  Mann  seems  to  have  been  married  no  fewer 

than  five  times  : 

(1)  His  first  wife  was  Eliz.,  dau.  of  Barthw  Brooke  of  Worlingworth  and  Southolt,  by 

Eliz.,  dau.  of  Sir  Rafe  Wiseman  ( see  Metcalfe,  118).  By  her  he  had  two  childQ 

bapt.  at  S.  Mary-at-the-Quay  church — Edward  in  1 6 1 S,  and  Eliz.  in  1620.  Edward 

(the  son)  was  a  Counsellor-at-law,  and  was  probably  the  “  Mr.  Mann,”  Recorder  of 
Ipswich,  who  entertained  the  diarist  Evelyn,  perhaps  at  Ashbocking,  on  10  Sept. 

1677.  He  d.  in  1681,  and  is  commemorated  by  an  heraldic  slab  in  S.  Nicholas’ 

church,  Ipswich,  displaying  Mann  impaling  Nicolson  and  Withe. 

(2)  His  second  wife  was  Dorothy,  dau.  of  Anth.  Mannock  of  Stoke-by-Nayland,  who, 

thro  his  mother  Dionisia  Roberts,  was  descended  thro’  the  FitzAlans  from  the 
Plantagenet  kings  of  England.  By  her  he  had  two  child11  bapt.  at  S.  Mary-Quay — 
Thomas  in  1627,  and  Jane  on  26  June  1628.  Their  mother  d.  16  Nov.  1629  ( see 
slab  in  S.  Mary-at-Stoke  church).  Jane,  whose  will  is  printed  above,  d.  unm.,  and 
was  bur.  at  S.  Mary-Quay  in  1679.  Thomas  Mann  was  of  the  Inner  Temple, 

Usher  of  the  Rolls,  and  of  Yoxford,  Suff.  He  d.  in  1669,  his  sisters  Jane  Mann 

and  Mary  Mann  being  among  his  devisees.  A  hatchment  displaying  Mann  impaling 
Alston  hangs  in  Yoxford  church.  His  grandson,  Rob.  Mann  of  Linton,  Kent,  was 
father  of  Sir  Horatio  Mann,  K.C.B.,  who  was  created  a  baronet  in  1775.  His 


PARTRIDGE  OF  SHELLEY  HALL.

nephew  Sir  Horatio  Mann,  M.P.,  was  succeeded  at  Linton  Place  in  1814  by  his 
nephew  James  Cornwallis,  fifth  Earl  of  Cornwallis,  who  assumed  the  surname  of 
Mann.  ( See  Burke’s  Extinct  Baronetcies.) 

(3)  On  27  July  1634,  “Katherine,  the  dau.  of  Edward  Man”  was  bapt.  at  S.  Mary-Quay. 

Her  mother  (name  unknown)  was  probably  Edward  Mann’s  third  wife. 

(4)  In  1644,  Arthur  Hopton  of  London,  gent.,  mentioned  in  his  will  his  cousin  Eliz.  Mann, 

wife  of  Edward  M.  of  Ipswich.  She  was  probably  his  fourth  wife,  and  mother  of 
his  dau.  Mary,  wife  of  Ban.  Partridge  of  Holton  (bapt.  1642). 

(5)  On  7  Sept.  1664,  a  licence  was  granted  (Archd.  Suff.)  for  a  marriage  at  Raydon 

between  Edw.  Mann  sen.  of  Ipswich,  gent,  and  widower,  and  Susanna  Day  of 
Holton ,  wid.  She  was  probably  his  fifth  wife. 

On  24  Feb.  167^  this  much  married  man  (Edward  Mann  of  Ipswich,  the  elder,  esq.) 
made  his  will,  desiring  to  be  buried  in  S.  Mary-Quay  church.  He  mentioned  his  three 
surviving  child11  (Tho.  had  d.  in  1669) — Jane  Mann,  Mary  Mann,  and  Edward  Mann.  On 
28  Feb.  167^,  “Mr.  Edward  Man  the  elder”  was  bur.  at  S.  Mary-Quay.  A  fortnight  later, 
15  March,  a  licence  was  granted  (Archd.  Suff.)  for  a  marriage  at  S.  Clement’s  church  between 
Dan.  Pattridge  of  Holton,  “  generosus,”  and  “  Mrs.  ”  Mary  Man  of  Ipswich,  and  they  wero 
married  there  on  23  March,  but  the  bride’s  name  was  incorrectly  entered  as  “Ann.”  In  1679, 
they  and  their  child3,  Daniel  and  Mary,  were  devisees  in  Jane  Mann’s  will  ( see  above).  Daniel, 
the  son,  was  progenitor  of  the  Partridges  of  Shelley  Hall. 


The  ten  asterisks  in  following  pedigree  of  Partridge  of  Shelley  Hall  indicate  that  the 
original  probates  are  in  possession  of  Charles  Partridge  of  Stow  market,  who  has  many  other 
family  deeds,  etc.,  dating  from  163f. 

The  pedigree  begins  with  Tho.  P.  of  Higham,  b.  circa  1560.  The  earliest  Partridge  entry 
in  the  Higham  register  is  1585,  when  his  eldest  s.  was  bapt.  He  (the  father)  was  perhaps 
brother  of  the  John  P.  who  m.  Gresell  Manhoode  at  Higham  6  June  1585.  They  had  s.  Rob. 
bapt.  Stratford  S.  Mary  1589,  and  child3  bapt.  Higham  1591-1 60| — Tho.,  Wm,  Eliz.,  Martha, 
Anth.  (bur.  there  1610).  Tho.  Browning  and  Gysell  Partrich  were  m.  Higham  159f,  Nich.  P. 
and  Marg1  Balls  1600,  and  Nich.  P.  and  Mary  Welles  1 6  First  mention  of  Partridge  under 
Higham  in  Suff.  Subsidy  Rolls  1  Ed.  VI  to  45  Eliz.  is  in  1597.

Garrad  there  1668,  and  was  bur.  there  fm  Shelley  11  May  1681.  His  wid.  prov.  his  will 
Arch  Suff.  1  Ap.  1682,  probate  penes  Mrs.  Hester  Payn,  da.  of  late  Hen.  Partridge  of  Shelley 
Dairy.  They  had  3  sons:  (1)  Rob.,  bur.  (s.  of  Tho.  P.  of  Whatfield)  at  Holton  4  Aug.  1674;.

Rob.  Partryche’s  will,  1525,  in  which  an  Edmund  Croehen  was  also  dev.,  and  to 
wh.  both  John  C.  and  Edm.  C.  were  witnesses.

Jlrntorial  Hearings. 

The  arms  of  Hamon  Le  Strange,  Esq.,  of  Pakenham,  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664 
were  Quarterly  of  9  (with  a  crescent  for  difference)  : — 

1,  Strange — Gules,  two  lions  passant  in  pale  Argent. 

2,  Vernon — Or,  on  a  fess  Azure,  three  garbs  of  the  field. 

3,  Camoys — Argent,  on  a  chief  Gules,  three  plates. 

4,  Walkfare — Argent,  a  lion  rampant  Sable,  charged  on  the  shoulder  with  a  mullet  of 

the  field. 

5,  Morieux — Gules,  a  bend  Argent,  billetee  Sable. 

6,  Beaman — Or,  a  cinquefoil  pierced  Gules. 

7,  Pyke — Argent,  three  piles  wavy  in  point  Gules. 

8,  Rushbrook — Sable,  a  fess  between  three  roses  Or. 

9,  Hastings— Or,  a  maunch  Gules. 

The  crest,  a  lion  passant  guardant  Or,  is  also  charged  with  a  crescent  for  difference. 

Hamon  L’Estrange  of  Pakenham  was  nephew  to  Sir  Nicholas  L’Estrange,  the  first  Baronet 
of  Hunstanton,  in  Norfolk.  Pedigrees  of  this  ancient  and  knightly  family  will  be  found  in 
the  Visitation  of  Norfolk  156S ,  edited  by  the  Rev.  G.  H.  Dashwood,  F.S.A.,  pp.  61-67  and  443,  and 
in  Carthew’s  History  of  Launditch,  vol.  i,  p.  142-145. 

The  L’Estranges  acquired  their  Pakenham  estate,  which  is  still  known  as  Beaumont  Hall, 
by  the  marriage  of  John  L’Estrange  with  Alice,  daughter  and  heir  of  Nicholas  Beaman  or 
Beaumont,  before  1436.

Dame  Elizabeth  Spring,  my  daughter,  Dorothy  Spring,  my  grandchilde,  Sr  William  Spring  Bar*

Mill  of  Hamon  ICe  Strange,  1660. 

Hamon  Le  Strange  of  Pakenam  co.  Sufff  Esquire.  As  for  my  body  I  desire  it  may  be 
layd  in  Holme  Chancell.  To  J udith  my  most  Beloved  wife  the  Bedd  she  wrought,  two  silver 
Plates  given  her  by  my  father,  with  the  silver  Bason  and  silver  Salte,  and  all  the  lynnen  and 
plate  bequeathed  her  by  my  deare  mother.  I  give  vnto  her  soe  long  as  she  shall  remayne  a 
widdowe  Eighty  pounds  per  annum.  I  give  flue  hundred  pounds  towards  the  advancements  of 
my  two  daughters,  Elizabeth  and  Judith,  which  I  had  by  Judith  my  deare  consort.  Vnto 
Dorothy  my  daughter  the  bed  which  her  mother,  [sic]  and  seaven  hundred  pounds  for  her 
portion.  I  giue  my  daughter  Elizabeth,  which  I  had  by  my  first  wife,  twentie  pounds  per 
annum.  Vnto  my  sonne  William  one  hundred  pounds  at  the  Expiracon  of  his  apprentiship.  I 
will  that  onely  forty  pounds  of  the  Annuity  of  eighty  pounds  bequeathed  to  my  wife  shalbe 
extinguished  notwithstanding  shee  shall  happen  to  marry  againe.  I  constitute  Hamon  Le  Strange, 
my  sonne,  sole  executor  of  this  will,  dated  the  fifteenth  of  June  1660.  Sealed  and  declared  in 
the  presence  of  Elizabeth  Spring.  William  Spring.  Probatum  vicesimo  sexto  die  Septembris 
1660  Juramento  Hamon  Le  Strange  executoris.  P.C.C.  250  Mabbs.

The  Arms  of  Suckling  in  the  Visitation  of  Norfolk  ( Harl  MS.  1552,  fol.  121)  were 
Per  pale  Gules  and  Azure,  three  bucks  trippant  Or.  The  Crest  was  a  buck  courant  Or,  holding 
in  his  mouth  a  branch  of  honeysuckle  proper. 

The  original  Crest  of  this  family  was  a  stag  courant  Azure,  attired  and  unguled  Or. 
The  colour  was  afterwards  changed  to  Gules,  and  it  is  so  represented  on  some  of  the  family 
monuments.  But  Queen  Elizabeth,  on  one  of  her  progresses  through  Noi’folk,  granted  to  Robert 
Suckling  and  his  heirs  a  stag  courant  Or ;  adding,  in  consideration  of  his  good  and  loyal 

services,  a  sprig  of  honeysuckle  proper  to  be  borne  in  the  stag’s  mouth  (Suckling’s  History  of 
Suffolk,  vol.  i,  p.  41). 

The  family  claims  a  Saxon  origin.  Socling,  as  it  was  anciently  written,  signified  one 

holding  his  estate  by  socage  or  tenure  of  the  plough.  In  Suckling’s  History  of  Suffolk  is  a 
pedigree  compiled  from  original  documents  in  the  possession  of  the  author.  But  he  confined  it 
to  the  Norfolk  line,  persistently  ignoring  the  claims  of  the  more  ancient  possessors  of  the  name 
in  Suffolk,  who,  as  contemporary  records  prove,  had  long  held  lands  in  the  latter  county,  some 
of  which  were  at  no  great  distance  from  Beccles. 

He  makes  casual  mention  in  a  footnote  (vol.  i,  p.  39)  of  one  Robert  Sliding  who  was 
returned  in  the  Hundred  Rolls  as  holding,  in  1274,  a  small  estate  in  Suffolk;  and  of  a  Walter 
Sliding  of  Sapiston.  We  learn  from  other  sources  that  Johannes  Suclling  of  Framlingham 
attended  the  muster  of  the  Hundred  of  Loes  on  Thursday  next  after  the  feast  of  St.  George, 

19th  Edward  II,  1326  (Parliamentary  Writs,  part  i,  p.  745).  In  1331  William,  son  of  William 
Suclyng  of  Cratfield,  bought  lands  of  Richard  Denham  of  Cokeleye  ( Suffolk  Fines,  5  Edward  III ). 
A  William  Sucling  was  Priest  of  Helmingham  in  1349,  and  may  have  been  identical  with 

William  Sucling,  Vicar  of  Darsham,  presented  in  that  year  by  Maria,  Countess  of  Norfolk 
(Suckling’s  Suffolk,  vol.  ii,  p.  222).  In  1381  Margeria,  Johanna  and  Margeria  Succlyng  were 
assessed  at  the  Hay  Subsidy  for  the  township  of  Mildenhall,  and  a  Richard  Sucling  was  living 
at  Fressingfield  (Powell’s  Rising  in  East  Anglia).  Johanna,  wife  of  Philip  Sucling  of  Woodton, 
in  Norfolk,  owned  houses  in  Bally  gate  street  in  the  not  very  distant  town  of  Beccles,  in  1430 
(Suckling’s  Suffolk,  vol.  i,  p  40). 

Henry  Suklyng  of  Oulton,  whose  will  was  proved  in  the  Bishop’s  Court  at  Norwich, 
22  Feb.  145^,  left  a  messuage  in  Ci’atfield  for  the  benefit  of  his  soul.  In  1461  John  Suklyng 
devised  lands  and  tenements  to  his  wife  and  kinsman,  directing  that  his  body  should  be  buried 
in  Framsden  church.  John  Suckling  of  Westylton,  near  Darsham,  gave  his  estate  to  Agnes,  his 
wife,  in  1474  (Will  Cur.  Ep.  Norw.). 

The  name  of  Suckling,  variously  spelt,  often  with  its  ancient  alias  of  Estall  or  Estaw, 
occurs  at  intervals  in  the  Suffolk  Clergy  Lists  at  Norwich,  notably : —

Stephen  Estawe,  appointed  to  the  church  of  Waldringfield  in  1429  ;  and  Walter  de  Estaugh, 
presented  the  same  year  to  Brightwell  by  John  de  Lampyt. 

Giles  Suckeleyne  instituted  to  Nacton,  and  John  Suckling,  formerly  Sacrist  at  Wingfield 
College,  buried  before  the  great  Rood  at  Stratton,  1375. 

Henry  Sucling,  Rector  of  Benhall  and  Master  of  Sudbury  College,  1439. 

John  Suckling,  D.D.,  first  Master  of  Corpus  Christi  College,  Cambridge,  owned  lands  in 
Sudbury  and  Great  Cornard,  which  he  had  apparently  inherited.  He  had  a  godson,  John 
Suckling,  the  son  of  his  brother  Thomas ;  a  brother  George ;  and  two  sisters  named  Joan. 
He  was  President  and  Bursar  of  the  College  and  Proctor  of  the  University  in  1491,  and  again 
in  1501.  In  the  latter  year  he  was  elected  Master  of  Goddeshouse  (Masters’  History  of  the 
College  of  Corpus  Christi).  It  was  in  1506  that  Margaret,  Countess  of  Richmond,  mother  of 
Henry  VII,  removed  the  site  of  this  institution,  re-edified  and  endowed  it  afresh,  and  placed 
him  at  its  head,  He  was  instituted  to  the  Rectory  of  Fen  Drayton  in  1494  (Alcock’s  Reg. 
Alien).  In  his  will,  dated  24  September  1506,  he  directed  his  tenements  in  Sudbury  to  be 
disposed  of  for  the  wealth  of  his  soul. 

The  will  of  Thomas  Sucklyng  of  Southwold,  with  a  wife  Cecilia  and  son  John,  was  proved 

in  March  1477.  Another  Thomas  Sucklyng,  also  of  Southwold,  had  a  wife  Joan.  His  last 

testament  Avas  proved  24th  Sept.  1.586  William  Suckling,  whose  will  was  dated  at  Southwold, 
6th  March  1547,  owned  the  Old  Hall,  with  lands  in  South  Avoid,  Roydon  and  Claydon. 

In  “An  Historical  Account  of  Dunwich,  South  Avoid,  etc.,  by  Thomas  Gardner,  1754," 

Walberswick,  Blithburgh,  is  a  list  of  fishing  craft  at  Walkerswick  in  1451  (29th  year  of  Henry  VI), 

the  owner’s  names  being  Galfryde  Greyve,  and  the  master’s  name  Richard  Suckling.

Will  of  Joint  Suckling,  1461. 

(Translated  from  the  Latin.)  I  John  Suklyng  bequeath  my  Soul  to  God  and  B.  Y.  Mary, 
and  my  body  to  be  buried  in  Framesden  Church.  To  Framesden  high  Altar  xijd  for  tithes 
forgotten.  To  the  High  Altar  at  Pethawe  xijd.  To  repair  of  Framesden  Church  xxs.  To  each 
godson  and  goddaughter  xijd.  To  Margery  my  servant  xijd.  To  the  light  of  the  Blessed  Virgin 
Mary  1  lb.  of  wax.  Residue  to  wife  Margaret  and  to  William  Suklyng,  son  of  John  Suklyng 
junior,  whom  I  appoint  executors.  Robert  Cheke  to  be  supervisor.  Wife  to  have  lands  and 
tenements  for  her  life,  with  remainder  to  the  said  William  Suklyng. 

Dated  Tuesday  after  the  Feast  of  St.  Peter  ad  Vincula.  Proved  5  Sept.  1461. 

Consistory  Court,  Norwich,  Liber  “  Betyngs,”  fol.  56b. 

The  Paston  Letters,  vol.  ii,  p.  60,  of  the  1874  edition,  have  the  following  under  date 
October,  1461  : — “  All  the  great  farmers  have  paid  xx,  and  one  of  Debenham  men,  called 
Sokelyng,  and  his  wife  xxx.”  Framsden,  Pettaugh  and  Debenham  are  almost  adjacent  places.

The  21st  daye  of  December  in  the  yere  of  our  Lord  God  1523,  I  Richard  Sykerlyng  of 

Dunstale,  heyng  of  hole  mynde  and  good  memory  make  this  my  Testament  and  last  Will  in

and  to  all  the  holy  company  of  heven,  my  body  to  be  buryed  within  the  churche  yerde  of 

Seynt  Michell  of  Dunstall  aforesaid.  Also  I  geve  and  bequethe  unto  a  honest  prest  to  synge

decease  x8.  Also  I  geve  and  bequethe  unto  a  secular  prest  for  a  quarter  for  me  xxx8  yf  it 
may  be  born  of  my  goods  after  my  debts  be  paid.  Also  I  bequethe  to  Elizabeth  my  dawther 
all  manner  of  pewter  and  brasse  that  was  her  mother’s  after  the  decease  of  Margaret  my  wiff,

called.

the  Executors. 


Will  of  William  Sucklings,  1547. 

The  6th  day  of  Marche  1547,  and  in  the  seconde  yeare  of  the  reigne  of  Edwarde  the 
Sext  Kinge  of  England,  I  William  Sucklinge  of  Sowthwolde  in  the  countie  of  Suffolk  e* 
Merchaunte,  make  and  ordeyne  this  my  present  Testament  and  last  Wyll  in  this  forme 
following.  First  I  bequethe  my  Sowle  to  Almightie  God,  to  o1'  blyssed  Lady  Seynt  Mary  and 
to  all  the  holye  company  of  hevin,  and  my  body  to  be  buryed  in  the  Churchyerde  of  Sowth¬ 
wolde.  I  give  to  the  pore  people  of  Sowthwolde  after  the  discretion  of  my  Executrix  viu  to 
praye  for  my  Sowle.  I  geve  to  the  pore  people  in  Roy  don  v11  to  praye  for  my  Sowle. 
I  will  that  Elizabeth  my  wyff  shall  have  all  that  my  mease  that  I  dwell  in,  with  the  pyetell 
on  the  lai’ckefelde,  and  the  mast  howse  with  the  bowse  called  the  old  Hall.  Allsoe  myn  inclose 
at  the  see  syde  with  the  capstayn  therin  standinge  for  the  term  of  her  lyff  of  the  saide 
Elizabeth,  my  wyff  kepinge  all  the  saide  howse  in  sufficient  reparacons.  And  after  her  decease 
I  will  that  Robert  my  sonne  shall  have  all  the  saide  mease  and  other  the  premises  as  is 
afforesaide.  And  yf  it  shall  fortune  Robert  my  sonne  to  decease  out  of  this  worlde  my  wyff 
then  beinge  on  lyve,  Than  I  will  that  all  the  saide  mease  and  all  other  the  premises  shalbe 
souled  by  the  said  Elizabeth  my  wyff,  And  the  money  thereof  coming  to  be  equally  parted 
amonge  my  children  and  my  wyffes  children,  that  ys  to  saye,  Ele  and  Felice,  my  dowters,  and 
their  children,  Thomas  Jentylman  and  William  Jentylman  and  their  children.  Item,  I  woll 
that  the  said  Robert  my  sonne  shall  have  my  five  acres  of  lande  after  my  wyffes  decease 
lyinge  on  the  Estayite  of  William  liolbornes  landes.  I  woll  that  Elizabeth  my  wyff  shall  have 
my  mease  that  Jamys  my  sonne  dwellyth  in  withall  the  profittes  thereof  for  the  terme  of  hir 
lyff.  And  after  hir  decease  I  woll  that  the  saide  Jamys  my  sonne  shall  have  yt.  Item,  I

half  of  my  saide  Shippe  and  bote  with  ther  tacling.  Yf  any  chaunce  mysfortune  or  casualtie 
shall  happen  to  the  said  shippe  or  bote,  that  then  the  said  Robert  shall  stande  to  the  chaunce 
of  the  same  for  his  parte.  I  woll  that  my  wyff  shall  have  all  my  catayle  in  Roydon  and 
Sowthwolde,  with  all  my  horse  plowghes,  cartes  and  tumbrelles,  all  my  coles  at  the  woodes 
ende,  and  all  my  come,  both  barley  and  rye,  in  my  berne  called  Watsenes  or  elles  wheare. 
I  give  and  bequeth  to  my  said  wyff,  and  to  Robert  myn  sonne,  my  other  ii  botes.  I  woll 
that  my  saide  wyff  shall  have  the  halfe  of  my  shippe  called  the  “  Edwarde  ”  with  half  hir  bote. 
I  woll  that  Thomas  Jentylman  &  William  his  brother  have  thother  half  of  the  said  shippe  and 
bote.  I  give  to  Richarde  Willot,  my  servant,  viiis  iiiid,  a  manfare  of  xii  scores  with  a  wairrop 
and  two  lynes.  I  woll  that  William  Hoberde  shall  have  my  parte  of  the  crosse,  land  lying  at 
the  Townes  ende.  I  woll  that  my  said  wyff  shall  have  the  longe  howse,  late  Waynfletes,  sett 
and  lying  by  Olyvers  gardinge.  I  woll  that  my  said  wyff  shall  have  the  pyetell  that  Robert 
Rinman  hath  in  occupacon  lyinge  between  Blackkes  and  Dowyes,  and  also  x  acres  of  lande 
which  John  Bealys  hath  in  occupacon.  I  woll  that  Robert  Tanner  shall  paye,  or  do  to  be 
payd,  to  Ele  and  Felecie  my  dawters  iiii8,  which  I  payed  him  for  my  close  nowe  beinge  in 
vowyance  betweene  the  Towne  and  me,  And  so  he  to  enjoye  yt  againe  when  he  hath  recoured 
yt  of  the  Towne.  I  woll  that  my  said  wyff  shall  have  all  myn  inclose  in  Roydon  called 
Baldokkes  for  term  of  hir  lyff,  and  after  hir  decease  I  woll  that  Robert  my  sonne  shall  have 
the  said  close,  and  yf  the  said  Robert  decease  before  my  wyff,  then  I  woll  that  my  wyff  shall 
sell  the  said  close  and  the  mony  therof  comenge  to  be  devided  equally  between  my  two 
dawters  Ele  and  Felecie  and  their  children.  The  said  Elizabeth  my  wyff  shall  have  my 
Tenemente  in  Roydon  with  all  the  landes  both  free  and  houlden  by  copye  of  Court  rolls  in 
Cleydon  aforesaid  for  term  of  hir  lyff,  And  after  hir  decease  I  woll  that  Jamys  my  sonne 
shall  have  (them),  except  the  inclose  called  Baldokkes  which  I  have  given  hertofore  vnto  Robert 
my  sonne  and  to  his  heyres.  The  residue  of  all  my  goodes  I  put  them  holy  to  the  disposal 
of  the  said  Elizabeth  my  wyff,  whom  I  make  my  sole  Executrix,  she  to  dispose  as  she  shall 
thinke  yt  to  be  the  most  pleasure  of  G  od,  and  the  helth  of  my  Sowle ;  and  I  elect  and  chose

The  16th  daye  of  September,  1558,  and  in  the  1st  yere  of  the  reigne  of  our  soueraign 
ladye  Elizabetli  ...  I  Elizabeth  Sucklynge  of  Sowthwolde  in  the  county  of  Suffolke,  wedowe 
.  .  .  make  this  my  presente  Testamente  and  laste  Will  .  .  .  First  1  commend  my  Sowle  to 

Almighty  God  and  my  body  to  be  buryed  in  the  Churchyarde  of  Sowthwolde  next  the  grave 
where  William  Sucklyng,  my  late  husband,  lyeth  buryed.  I  bequeathe  to  Thomas  Jentelman, 
my  sonne,  half  an  acre  of  lands  ...  in  Sowthewolde  ...  To  William  Jentelman,  my  other 
sonne,  my  pycktell  ...  in  Sowthewolde.  ...  I  will  my  longe  house,  late  Waynfletes,  sett 
and  lyinge  by  John  Swaynes  ...  to  be  sold  by  myne  Executors,  and  the  money  shalbe 
devided  amonge  the  children  of  the  said  Thomas  Jentelman  and  William  Jentelman  .  .  . 
I  will  that  my  halfe  sliippe  caled  the  “  Edward  ”  shall  remayne  euenlye  to  the  said  Thomas 
and  William  my  sonnes  .  .  .  yeldynge  and  payenge  therfore  to  the  said  childrene  of  the  sayd 
Thomas  and  William  my  sonnes  fortye  poundes  of  good  English  moneye  ...  1  will  that  my 

halfe  parte  of  my  Corye  called  the  Marye  shall  remayne  to  William  Jentelman  my  sonne  for 
ever.  I  will  that  Elizabeth  Jentelman,  the  daughter  of  the  said  Thomas  shall  have  my  beste 
gyrdle,  my  beste  beades,  and  my  best  taches  ...  I  geve  to  Johan,  the  wife  of  the  said 
Thomas  Jentelman,  my  said  sonne,  my  beste  gowne  and  my  best  kyrtle  ...  To  Margaret,  the 
wief  of  the  said  William,  my  sonne,  my  gown  next  the  beste  ...  To  John  Jentelman,  oldest 
sonne  of  William  Jentelman  ...  To  William  Jentelman  my  sonne  £12.  which  James  Sucklynge 
do  owe  unto  me  ...  I  geve  unto  Thomas  Jentelman,  my  sonne,  my  best  sylver  salte  and  one 
halfe  dozen  of  my  beste  sylver  spones.  I  geve  to  William  Jentelman,  my  sonne,  my  next  beste 
silver  salte  and  fyve  silver  spones  of  the  best  sorte  ...  I  will  that  the  residue  of  my  silver 
spones  .  .  .  thurtye  in  number  be  equally  divided  between  the  children  of  Thomas  Jentelman 
&  William  Jentelman,  my  sonnes  ...  To  Thomas  Jentelman,  sonne  of  Thomas  Jentelman,  my 
sonne,  .  .  .  <tc.,  etc.

There  is  an  abstract  of  this  will  in  the  Rev.  A.  J.  Suckling’s  “  Antique  and  Armorial 
Collections,”  Add.  MS.  18,476 — 18,491.  Richard  Suckling,  the  testator,  was  nephew  to  John 
Suckling  als  Esthall,  who,  on  the  8th  of  July,  1554,  bequeathed  his  messuage  in  Woodton, 
called  Bigottes,  with  a  hundred  acres  of  land,  to  Alice  his  wife,  with  remainder  to  Robert 

Suckling  of  Norwich,  to  whom  he  left  the  rest  of  his  lands  and  houses.  By  a  deed,  dated 

14th  December,  1555,  Alice  Suckling,  the  widow,  released  to  this  Robert  Suckling,  whom  she 
terms  “grandson  of  her  husbands  brother,”  Bigotts  Wood  in  Woodton  with  one  hundred  acres 
of  pasture,  and  Eastgatefield,  containing  forty  acres,  which  her  husband  had  settled  upon  her. 
This  gives  us  a  sure  clue  to  the  relationship  of  the  parties.  John  Suckling  als  Esthall,  who 
seems  to  be  identical  with  the  John  Esthawe  of  Richard  Suckling’s  will,  further  mentions  John 
Suckling  the  son  and  Elizabeth  the  daughter  of  a  certain  John  Suckling,  Robert  Suckling  the 
younger,  the  children  of  Friar  and  of  Mayes  of  East  Bergholt  in  Suffolk,  Stephen  Manclarke 
of  Yarmouth,  Thomas,  Cecilie,  and  .lohn  Manclarke.  And  he  gives  substantial  legacies  to 
Mistress  Marie  Windham  and  Mistress  Katherine  Heydon,  daughters  of  Sir  Christopher  Heydon, 
to  the  “good  ladie  Heydon,”  Mistress  Elizabeth  Heveningham,  Mistress  Anne  Palgrave,  Alice 
Seevar,  Agnes  Seman,  Dorothie  Roodes,  and  others. 

A  curious  old  paper,  entitled  the  “Disposition  of  John  Manclerk,  1556,”  formerly  in  the 
possession  of  the  Rev.  A.  J.  Suckling,  the  Suffolk  Historian,  states  that  Eastgatefield  in  Woodton 
was  purchased  by  John  Suckling  the  elder,  the  father  of  John  Esthall  the  younger,  who  settled 
it,  as  above  said,  upon  Alice  his  wife.

Sir  John  Suckling,  youngest  son  of  Robert  Suckling,  Mayor  of  Norwich,  by  Elizabeth, 
his  wife,  daughter  of  Adam  Barwick,  of  East  Bergholt,  in  Suffolk,  was  born  in  1569.  He 
married,  first,  Martha,  sister  of  Lionel  Cranfield,  Earl  of  Middlesex,  the  mother  of  his  children, 
and  secondly  Jane,  daughter  of  John  Reve,  of  London.  His  eldest  son,  Sir  John  Suckling,  the 
Cavalier  Poet,  was  born  in  1609.  He  purchased  the  Manor  of  Roos  Hall  in  Beccles,  where  he 
resided  at  times,  in  1600,  and  that  of  Barsham  in  1613.  In  a  letter  written  in  the  latter 
year  to  his  brother  Charles  Suckling  of  Woodton,  he  says: — “I  ame  nowe  nowe  gone  through 
for  Barsham,  and  have  had  a  line  recoverie  acknowledged  to  my  use  before  my  Lord  Hubbard, 

A  to-morrow  the  indentures  are  to  be  sealed . It  is  nowe  myne  A  I  trust  that  the 

name  of  Sucklings  shall  inheritt  A  possess  it  when  I  am  dead  A  rotten.”  Sir  John  was 
Secretary  of  State,  Comptroller  of  the  Household,  and  Privy  Counsellor  to  James  I  and  his 
unfortunate  successor,  and  M.P.  for  Dunwich  in  Suffolk.  Jane,  his  widow,  subsequently  remarried 
Sir  Edwin  Rich,  with  whom  she  resided  at  her  dower  House  of  Roos  Hall  through  the 
troublous  times  of  the  Rebellion.  See  Sir  John’s  Suckling’s  life  in  the  Dictionary  of  National 
Bioyraphy. 

His  three  daughters  are  buried  in  Pangbourne  Church,  Berkshire,  beneath  a  monument 
thus  inscribed  “  Within  a  vault,  under  the  marble  stones  hereunto  adjoining,  resteth  the  bodies 

of  three  sisters . Martha  was  first  marrayed  unto  Sir  George  Sowthcott  of  Shillingford  in 

the  County  of  Devon,  Knight ;  A  dyed  the  wife  of  William  Clagett,  of  Iselworth  in  the  County 
of  Middlesex,  Esquire.  She  dyed  at  the  Bathe,  29  June  1661.  Anne  was  marryed  unto  Sir 
John  Davis,  son  of  Sir  John  Davis,  both  lords  of  this  Manor,  A  dyed  the  24th  of  July  1659. 
Mary  Sucklinge  dyed  a  virgine  the  17th  of  October  1658.”

Joint  buckling,  1609 — 1641. 


Sir  John  Suckling,  the  Cavalier  Poet,  was  born  at  Whitton,  and  baptized  in  Twickenham 
Church  10th  February  1609.  He  succeeded  to  his  father’s  estates  of  Whitton  Park  and  Barsham 
Hall  in  1627.  The  following  year  he  started  on  his  travels  to  Italy,  France  and  Germany, 
afterwards  joining  the  English  volunteers  under  Gustavus  Adolphus  for  the  relief  of  the  Prince 
Palatine.  He  served  with  distinction  at  the  battle  of  Leipsic,  7th  September  1631,  and  was 
present  at  the  sieges  of  Crossen,  Guben,  Glognan  and  Madgeburg.  Returning  to  England,  he 
entered  upon  a  brilliant  social  and  literary  career.  In  1637  he  published  his  “Sessions  of  the 

Poets”  and  “Socimanism,  an  account  of  Religion  and  Reason.”  In  1638  he  produced,  at  his 
own  cost,  “  Aglaura,”  said  to  have  been  the  first  play  acted  with  scenes  in  this  Kingdom. 
Being  in  high  favour  at  Court,  especially  with  Queen  Henrietta  Maria,  their  Majesties  were 
present  at  the  first  representation.  The  gathering  of  political  clouds  was  shadowed  forth  by  the 
publication  of  “  Brennoralt  ”  in  1639,  and  when  the  national  supplies  were  refused  to  the  King, 
Sir  John  presented  His  Majesty  with  a  troop  of  a  hundred  horsemen,  clothed  and  maintained 
from  his  own  purse.  The  uniform  was  white  doublets  with  scarlet  coats  and  breeches.  ( State 

Papers,  Domestic  Series,  January  1632-9).  This  body  cost  him  XI 2,000,  which  he  raised  by  the 
sale  of  his  manor  of  Barsham  to  his  uncle,  Charles  Suckling,  of  Woodton.  With  these  men  he 
joined  the  expedition  to  the  North,  but  on  its  failure  they  were  disbanded.  Combining  with 
Henry  Percy  and  Henry  Jermyn  (afterwards  Earl  of  St.  Alban’s),  Sir  John  entered  into  a 

Royalist  plot  on  behalf  of  the  Queen,  and  by  a  Parliamentary  Proclamation,  issued  in  May 
1641,  they  were  charged  with  high  treason.  Jermyn  and  Suckling  fled  to  the  Continent,  where 
the  latter  died,  murdered  by  his  valet,  and  was  buried  in  the  Protestant  Cemetery  of  Paris, 
1641-2.  Selections  from  Sir  John  Suckling’s  works,  with  a  life  of  the  author,  by  the  Rev. 
Alfred  Suckling,  were  published  by  Longman  in  1836. 

“  The  Desposition  of  Christopher  Barrett,”  which  has  been  preserved  in  the  Muniment 
Room  at  Norwich  Castle,  throws  inteiesting  side  lights  upon  the  sale  of  Barsham  Hall.  Charles 
Suckling,  the  uncle,  found  that  he  had  paid  too  high  a  price  for  it,  the  rent  charges  and 


SUCKLING  OF  BARSHAM. 


193 


.annuities  considered.  Sir  John  urged  that  “one  Mr.  Riche,  who  had  married  the  Lady 
Suckling,”  would  have  procured  him  more.  But  this  was  disproved  by  a  letter  of  Mr.,  afterwards 
Sir  Edwin,  Rich.  He,  too,  had  found  the  incumbrances  upon  the  property  too  heavy.  Christopher 
Barrett’s  deposition,  taken  8th  September  1645,  gives  a  minute  account  of  a  meeting  between 
Sir  John  and  his  uncle,  at  which  he  was  invited  to  assist.  The  good  feeling  of  the  knight, 
who  was  anxious  to  end  all  matters  of  unkindness,  is  most  evident.  Mention  is  made  of 
Lionel  Suckling,  the  poet’s  younger  brother,  and  of  William  Barrett,  the  executor  of  his  father’s 
will.  The  Barretts  and  the  Sucklings  were  nearly  connected  by  the  marriage  of  Alderman 
Suckling,  of  Norwich,  with  the  widow  of  William  Barrett,  of  Westhall,  in  Suffolk.  Their 
respective  children  called  one  another  brother  and  sister,  the  Christopher  Barrett  of  the

Walpole,  the  respective  sums  of  £100  apiece.  To  the  Hon:  Robert  Walpole,  youngest  brother 
of  the  said  Lord  Walpole,  £1000;  and  to  the  Hon:  Miss  Catherine  Walpole,  eldest  daughter  of 
the  said  Lord  Walpole,  £1500.  If  any  of  these  legaties  die,  the  legacy  to  be  given  to  my 
brother  William  Suck  line 

I  give  unto  ....  Nelson,  ....  Nelson  ....  and  ....  Nelson  (so  in  the  will) 

the  sum  of  £1000  apiece  when  they  shall  attain  their  ages  of  twenty  one  years.  To  my 

nephew,  Maurice  Nelson,  eldest  son  of  my  late  sister  Nelson.  To  all  other  the  sons  of  my  late 
sister  Nelson  that  shall  be  living  at  my  decease  the  respective  sums  of  £500  apiece,  and  £150 
apiece  at  the  age  of  twenty  one  years.  I  bequeath  the  reside  of  my  estate  to  my  brother 
William  Suckling. 

Lord  Walpole  of  Wolterton  and  William  Suckling  are  named  as  executors. 

Captain  Maurice  Suckling  was  M.P.  for  Portsmouth  and  Comptroller  of  the  Navy  when 
he  died  in  17/8.  He  was  eldest  son  of  Maurice  Suckling,  D.D.,  by  Anne,  daughter  of  Sir 
Charles  turner,  Bart.,  and  was  born  at  the  Rectory  House  of  Barsham  in  1726.  Entering  the 
navy  under  the  auspices  of  his  mother’s  kinsman,  George  Townshend  (of  the  siege  of  Bastia 
fame),  he  early  rose  in  the  service.  When  in  command  of  the  “  Dreadnought,”  attended  by 
the  “Augusta”  and  “Edinburgh,”  he  fought  an  action  off  Cape  St.  Francois,  in  1757,  paralleled 


SUCKLING  OF  BARSHAM. 


199 


only  by  his  nephew  Nelson’s  achievements.  This  took  place  on  the  21st  of  October,  the  day 
of  the  great  victory  of  Trafalgar,  and  Nelson  alluded  to  it  at  the  commencement  of  that 
memorable  engagement. 

Anne  Suckling,  Captain  Suckling’s  mother,  and  Catherine  Nelson,  his  sister,  died  within 
a  few  days  of  one  another.  The  Captain,  at  this  time  of  double  mourning,  promised  to  take 
care  of  one  of  the  Nelson  boys.  Three  years  afterwards  Horatio,  being  home  for  the  Christmas 
holidays,  saw  his  uncle’s  appointment  to  the  “  Raisonable  ”  of  64  guns  in  the  county  paper. 
“Do,  William,”  he  said  to  his  brother,  “write  to  my  father  and  tell  him  I  should  like  to  go 
to  sea  with  uncle  Maurice.” 

Captain  Suckling  was  written  to.  “What,”  said  he  in  answer,  “has  poor  Horatio  done, 
who  is  so  weak,  that  he  above  all  the  rest  should  be  sent  to  rough  it  at  sea  1  But  bid  him 

come,  and  the  first  time  we  go  into  action  a  cannon  ball  may  knock  off  his  head,  and  provide 

for  him  at  once.” 

In  the  desperate  boat  action  off  Santa  Cruz,  in  which  Nelson  lost  his  arm,  he  received 
a  shot  through  the  right  elbow,  but  as  he  fell  he  caught  the  sword,  which  he  had  just  drawn, 

in  his  left  hand,  determined  never  to  part  with  it,  for  it  had  belonged  to  his  uncle,  Captain 

Maurice  Suckling.  And  writing  to  his  uncle  William  Suckling,  Comptroller  of  Customs,  on 
July  5th,  1788,  Horatio  says,  “I  trust  I  shall  prove  myself  worthy  of  the  place  in  the  service 
of  nry  country  which  my  dear  uncle  (Maurice)  left  me.  I  feel  myself  to  my  country  his  heir, 
and  it  shall,  I  am  bold  to  say,  never  lack  the  want  of  his  council.” 

When  the  bells  of  Barsham  church  were  re-hung  in  1896,  a  new  one,  bearing  a  suitable 
inscription,  was  added  in  memory  of  Captain  Maurice  Suckling  at  the  joint  expense  of  the 
Rev.  Robert  Alfred  Suckling,  lord  of  the  manor,  Horatio,  third  Earl  Nelson,  and  Captain 
Thomas  Suckling,  R  N.

This  is  the  last  Will  and  Testament  of  Anne  Suckling  of  Burnham  Thorpe,  widow, 
20th  Dec.  1767.  I  desire  to  be  buried  in  a  plain  manner,  without  pall  bearers,  in  the  Chancel 
(of)  Barsham  near  Beccles,  in  the  county  of  Suffolk,  and  under  the  same  stone  where  the 

remains  of  the  Reverend  Doctor  Suckling,  my  late  husband,  are  interred.  My  funerall  expenses- 
and  all  my  just  debts  to  be  paid  as  soon  after  my  death  as  possible.  The  remainder  of  the 
£300  in  the  hands  of  William  Suckling,  my  sonne,  I  bequeath  as  follows : — The  income  arising 
therefrom  to  be  paid  to  my  daughter,  Catherine  Nelson,  for  her  sole  use  during  her  life,  and 
after  her  decease  to  be  equally  divided  among  my  granddaughters  Susannah,  Anne  and  Catherine 
Nelson.  I  give  to  my  grandson  Maurice  Nelson,  my  pearl  backed  watch ;  to  Susannah  Nelson 
my  six  gilt  tea  spoons ;  to  my  granddaughter  Anne  my  old  purse  containing  some  gold  medals. 
Also  to  my  son  William  Suckling  a  parcel  of  freehold  land  containing  five  acres  in  or  near 

Beccles.  My  household  furniture,  plate,  china,  and  wearing  apparel  I  give  to  my  daughter 

Catherine  Nelson.  The  rest  of  my  real  and  personal  estate  (I  give)  to  my  three  children, 

William  Suckling,  Maurice  Suckling,  and  Catherine  Nelson,  share  and  share  alike.  And  I 
appoint  my  son  William  Suckling  Executor  and  Trustee.  Witnesses : — Sarah  Bowers,  Richard 
Raven,  John  Smith  Junr.

Amongst  the  monumental  inscriptions  in  Barsham  chancel,  where  so  many  of  the  Sucklings  lie  buried,  is  the 
following : — 

“  Sacred  to  the  memory  of  William  Suckling,  Esqr,  late  of  Kentish  Town  in  the  County  of  Middlesex,  who  departed 
this  life  December  15th  1798,  aged  83.” 

“Against  the  wall  is  a  Hatchment  with  the  arms  of  this  gentleman  with  Rumsey,”  Quarterly,  1st  and  4th,  Argent 
a  fesse  Gules,  in  chief  a  label  of  four  points  Azure ;  2d  and  3d,  Azure  a  cinquefoil  within  a  bordure  Ermine. 

Add.  MS.  18,476,  page  52.

Amongst  the  existing  portraits  of  the  Sucklings  and  their  kinsmen  are  those  of  Robert  Suckling,  M.P.  for  Norwich, 
on  panel,  dated  1583;  Sir  John  Suckling,  who  purchased  Barsham;  Sir  John  Suckling,  his  son,  the  poet,  by  Vandyke  (of 
which  engravings  will  be  found  in  his  life  by  the  Rev.  A.  J.  Suckling,  and  the  latter’s  History  of  Suffolk);  Robert 
Suckling,  High  Sheriff  of  Norfolk,  and  Anne  Wodehouse,  his  wife,  dated  1645;  Sir  Robert  Walpole,  Earl  of  Orford,  by  Van 
Loo ;  Nelson’s  grandparents,  Maurice  Suckling,  II. D.,  in  wig  and  gown,  and  his  wife,  Anne  Turner,  in  her  widow’s  weeds 
(dated  1745,  J.  T.  Heins)  ;  their  daughter,  Catherine  (Heins  1745),  afterwards  Nelson’s  mother.  These  and  many  other 
Suckling,  Walpole,  and  Townshend  portraits  are  now  in  the  possession  of  the  present  lord  and  patron  of  Barsham  Manor. 

A  large  oil  painting,  by  Bardwell  1764,  of  Captain  Maurice  Suckling,  R.N.,  once  the  property  of  Nelson  himself,  is 
now  at  High  wood  in  the  possession  of  Captain  Thomas  Suckling,  R.N.
