Through  their  ancestors,  the  Boltons  of  Woodbridge,  the  Earls  Nelson  can  claim  yet  another  line  of  descent  from 
Edward  1.  Thomas  Bolton,  of  that  town,  about  the  beginning  of  the  seventeenth  century,  married  Mary,  sister  of  Sir 
William  Wiseman,  of  Canfield,  in  Essex,  Baronet,  whose  great  grandfather, |  Sir  William  Waldegrave,  of  Smalbridge,  died  in 
1554.  Sir  William  Waldegrave  who  died  in  1524,  the  grandfather  of  this  Sir  William,  married  Margery,  grand-daughter  of 
Roger  Wentworth,  of  Nettlested,  by  Margery,  widow  of  Lord  Roos  and  daughter  of  Sir  Philip  le  Spencer.  Sir  Philip  was 
fourth  in  descent  from  Hugh  le  Despencer,  Earl  of  Gloucester,  the  husband  of  Eleanor  de  Clare,  daughter  and  coheir  to 
the  Princess  Joan  of  Acre,  King  Edward  I’s  daughter  by  Eleanor  of  Castile.  The  Royal  lineage  of  Margery  Wentworth, 
wife  of  Sir  William  Waldegrave,  is  given  more  at  length  and  in  pedigree 1  form  in  vol  i,  page  313,  of  this  work.

Trinitie,  and  my  boddie  to  be  buried  within  the  Parrishe  church  of  Sainte  Marie  in  Thetforde. 

The  ffunerall  whereof  I  will  shalbe  doon  in  suche  order  as  by  the  Lawes  of  this  Realme  is 

to  be  used.  I  will  haue  a  Conveniente  Tombe  of  ffreston  erected  over  me  and  my  wief.

withe  my  provisions  remeyning  in  my  saide  howse  &  pastures.  So  as  in  that  time  my  §untes

P.C.C.  33  Stonard. 

From  1537  downwards  the  testator,  then  Richard  Fulmerston  of  Ipswich,  gentleman,  made 
large  purchases  of  abbey  buildings  and  church  lands.  We  learn  from  his  Inquisition  post-mortem 
that  he  held  the  Manor  of  Thetford  Finches  in  Norfolk  and  Suffolk,  the  late  Monastery  of  the 
Canons  of  the  Holy  Sepulchre,  the  site  of  the  Dominican  Monastery  with  the  Hospital  of  God’s 

House,  the  Rectories  and  Churches  of  Holy  Trinity,  St.  Cuthbert,  and  St.  Andrew,  and  the 

Benedictine  Nunnery,  all  in  that  town ;  also  the  Manors  of  Monk’s  Hall  and  Staines  in  Elveden 


MAY,  FULMERSTON,  HEYWARD. 


211 


and  the  Rectory  there,  together  with  lands  in  Brandon  Ferry,  the  Barnhams,  Downham,  Croxton, 
and  Westwicke.  In  ancient  times  the  greater  part  of  Thetford,  where  these  abbeys  where,  was 
on  the  Suffolk  side  of  the  river,  now  forming  St.  Mary’s  parish.  He  converted  the  Nunnery 
into  his  residence,  and  lived  and  died,  so  far  as  domicile  went,  a  Suffolk  man.  He  was  buried 
in  St.  Mary’s  Church,  where  a  sumptuous  monument,  now  greatly  delapidated,  was  erected  to 
his  memory.  The  Grammar  School  and  Hospital  for  the  Poor,  his  benefactions  to  the  town, 
were  also  in  Suffolk.  The  Arms  granted  him  by  Sir  Gilbert  Dethick,  in  the  reign  of  Queen 
Mary,  are  variously  described.  Burke  gives  them  as  Or,  on  a  fesse  between  three  doves  Azure, 
a  rose  between  two  garbs  of  the  first.  Davy  describes  the  birds  as  sea  mews.  The  Crest  is 
a  goat’s  head  erased  Gules,  platee,  armed  Or,  holding  in  its  mouth  a  branch  with  roses.  “  An 
eglantine  branch  vert,”  says  Davy,  flowered  argent.  Eglantine  is  an  old  world  name  for  the 
sweetbriar,  and  occasionally  for  the  wild  rose.  Halliwell.

holie  Trinitie.  My  foure  sonnes  Thomas,  Charles,  John  and  Frauncis  Heywarde  ar  all  vnder  age. 
I  giue  to  everye  of  theim  a  hundreth  pounds  a  piece  at  his  age  of  twentie  and  five  yeares. 
Children  of  mie  sonne  William  Heiwarde.  Children  of  mie  daughter  Alice  Fulmerston.  My

June  11th  1589.  Your  pore  orators  Thomas  Heyward  and  Agnes  his  wyfe,  Arthur  Wilton 
and  Martha  his  wyfe,  and  Margaret  Gostling,  complayn  that  one  Martha  Gostlinge,  late  of 
Topcroft,  co.  Norfolk,  wydowe,  grandmother  to  the  said  Agnes,  Martha  and  Margarett,  by  her 
last  testament,  dated  about  May  11th  in  the  27th  year  of  Queen  Elizabeth  (1585)  willed  them 
legacies,  to  be  paid  when  they  severally  became  of  age.  She  left  lands  called  Parkfield  in 
Hempnall,  in  all  about  fifty  acres,  to  one  Robert  Gostlinge  to  fulfill  the  said  will,  appointing 
him  and  Myles  Warde  executors.  The  widow  dyed,  having  previously  sold  the  lands  for  £440. 
Your  orators  have  long  since  attained  their  ages  of  one  and  twenty  years ;  but  their  legacies 
are  unpaid.  Eliz.  B.  &  A  ,  H.  H.  2,  20. 

The  pedigree  of  the  Thetford  Heywards  which  found  its  way  into  the  collection  of 
Norfolk  genealogies,  made  by  R.  Mundy  in  1620,  known  as  Harleian  MS.  1552,  practically  assigns 
to  Thomas  Heyward  and  Anne  Gostling.  the  children  of  Thomas  Heyward,  his  father,  and  Anne 
Woodshaw — a  by  no  means  unprecedented  blunder.  They  are  all  named  in  the  will  which 
Anne  Woodshaw’s  husband  made  in  1586,  the  year  of  his  death. 

This  Chancery  Bill  of  1589,  shows  that  Thomas  Heyward  and  Ann  Gostling,  who  were 
then  comparatively  young,  lived  a  generation  later  than  the  father  of  Alice  Heyward— successively 
the  wife  of  Richard  Fulmerston,  John  Lawe,  and  Dean  Suckling.

(grant  of  <3lrms* 

To  all  and  singular  to  whom  this  present  shall  come  William  Camden  Esquier,  also 
Clarencieux  principle  herald  A  King  of  Arms  of  the  East,  West  &  South  parts  of  England  from 
the  river  of  Trent  southward,  sendeth  due  commendation  in  our  Lord  God  everlasting.  Forasmuch 
as  anciently  from  ye  beginning  it  was  ordained  that  men  of  wisdom,  virtuous  life  &  noble  courage, 
A  such  as  for  their  learning,  justice  A  discretion  are  made  Magistrates  in  their  native  Country 
A  Commonwealth,  have  been  worthily  commended  to  the  world  by  monuments  and  remembrances 
of  their  good  deserts,  amongst  which  ye  chiefest  and  most  usual  hath  been  the  bearing  of  Signs 
in  Shields  called  Arms.  In  which  respect  being  required  by  Thomas  Bolton  of  Woodbridge  in 
the  County  of  Suff.  Esq1'  to  search  in  the  Registers  A  Records  of  toy  office  for  such  ancient 
arms  as  pertain  to  y°  house,  name  &  family  whereof  he  is  descended,  as  also  to  ratifie  &  confirm 
the  samo  unto  him  with  the  Crest  belonging,  with  such  congruent  difference  as  he  may  lawfully 
bear  without  prejudice  of  any  other.  All  whose  gentle  A  reasonable  requests  upon  due 
consideration  of  his  good  desert  &  ability,  and  withall  being  credibly  informed  that  ye  said 
Thomas  is  lineally  descended  from  the  Boltons  of  Bolton  in  Lancashire,  I  the  sd  Clarencieux 
King  of  Arms  have  ratified  &  confirmed  unto  him  these  his  antient  Arms  following :  that  is  to 
say,  two  coats,  quarterly,  The  first,  sa.  a  falcon  arg4  beaked,  membred  A  bells,  gold ;  The  2d  gules, 
3  wolves’  heads  erased,  gold,  the  3d,  as  the  2d,  the  4th  as  the  1st : — for  his  difference,  a  trefoil 
vert : — A  for  his  Crest,  or  Cognizance,  On  a  wreath  of  his  colours,  a  falcon  arg4  with  like 
difference,  mantled  gules,  doubled  arg4  as  more  plainly  appeareth  depicted  on  the  Margent.  Which 
Arms  A  Crest  I  the  said  King  of  Arms  (by  power  A  authority  under  the  great  seal  of  England 

unto  my  office  annexed)  do  by  these  prsts  ratify  &  confirm  unto  the  said  Thomas  Bolton  Esqr  A 

to  his  posterity,  with  their  due  differences,  to  use  &  shew  forth,  in  shield,  Coat  Armour  or 
otherwise  (according  to  the  antient  laws  of  armes),  without  any  contradiction  of  any  Manner  of 
person.  In  witness  whereof,  I  the  said  King  of  Arms  have  hereunto  sett  my  hand  &  seale  of 
my  office.  Dated  at  London,  ye  25th  day  of  Aug4  1610.  and  in  the  13th  year  of  our  Sovereign  Lord, 
King  James.  William  Camden,  Clarenceux  King  of  Arms. 

This  Grant,  relieved  of  some  of  its  redundant  verbiage,  is  taken  from  the  records  of  the 
Heralds’  College.  In  1803  Thomas  Bolton,  the  nephew  of  the  Hero  of  the  Nile,  served  as  one 
of  the  Esquires  at  Nelson’s  installation  as  a  Knight  of  the  Bath,  when  he  had  to  prove  his  right 

to  Arms.  He  memorialised  the  Earl  Marshal  for  a  grant,  stating  that  the  family  had  borne  the 

insignia  granted  by  Camden  in  1610  to  Thomas  Bolton  of  Woodbridge,  from  whom  he  was  by 
family  tradition  descended  ;  but  that  he  had  not  time  to  investigate  the  descent.  The  coat  allowed 
him  was  Sable,  on  a  mount  "Vert  in  base,  a  falcon  Ermine,  beak  and  bells  Or ;  in  the  mouth  a 
trefoil  slipped  of  the  second.  Crest,  on  a  mount  Yert,  a  falcon,  as  in  the  Arms.

I,  Thomas  Bolton  of  Woodbridge  in  the  Countie  of  Suff :  gentleman,  vppon  the  fower 
and  twentith  daye  of  Januarye,  1616,  do  ordayne  and  declare  this  my  last  will  and  testament. 
First  I  commend  my  soule  into  the  mercifull  hand68  of  the  Almightie  god,  trusting  throughe  the 
meritts  of  his  sonne  Christe  Jesus  to  be  made  partaker  of  the  Kingdome  of  heaven.  I  give  to 
the  poore  of  Woodbridge,  with  other  poore  that  shall  come  to  my  Buriall,  six  poundes.  I  give 

to  Alice  my  wife  all  my  mesuage  and  landes  in  Melton  in  lieu  of  her  thirdes  and  dowry,  and 

therewith  also  to  bring  vp  in  the  feare  of  god  and  good  nourture  my  three  younge  children  Josias, 
Daniell  and  Sara.  And  I  will  that  Alice  my  wife  shall  paye  to  Josias  my  sonne  twentie  poundes 
a  yere  during  her  naturall  life.  And  after  her  decease  Josias  and  Daniell  my  twoe  youngest 
sonnes  shall  have  ioyntlie  togeather  my  (said)  mesuage.  I  bequeathe  to  Alice  my  wife,  during 
all  the  tyme  she  shall  liue  a  widowe,  the  moytie  of  my  mesuage  and  howse  wherein  I  nowe  dwell 
with  halfe  the  garden  &c.  Vnto  Thomas  my  sonne  my  mesuage,  howses,  landes  and  tenement 
in  Martellsham,  Belinges  magna,  Beling  parua,  Barkinston  or  elswhere,  vppon  Condition  that  he 
shall  perform  all  guiftes,  bequeathes  and  legaceys  appoynted  in  this  my  will.  Vnto  Thomas  my 
sonne  my  mesuage  and  lande  in  Fevertou  als  Teverton,  and  all  other  tenements,  remaynders  and 

titles  that  I  may  haue  righte  to.  Vnto  Thomas  my  sonne  all  my  partes  of  shipps  and  car  veils. 

I  bequeathe  to  John  my  sonne  fyve  poundes  to  be  paid  euery  quarter  of  the  yere  towardes  his 
mayntennce  at  Cambridge,  (and)  fifteene  poundes  when  he  shall  accomplishe  his  age  of  one  and 
twentie  yeres,  to  discharge  the  chardges  of  his  Commencement.  I  giue  him,  after  he  shall 
accomplish  his  full  age,  three  hundred  poundes,  vppon  condition  that  he  do  not  forsake  his 
begonne  Calling  of  a  Divine  for  seaven  yeres  next  folowing  the  date  hereof.  I  give  to  Alice  my 
daughter  twoe  hundred  poundes.  To  my  three  youngest  daughtrs,  Martha,  Susan  and  Sara,  to 
every  one  of  them  twoe  hundred  poundes,  when  they  shall  accomplish  the  seuerall  ages  of 
nynteene  yeres.  To  my  sonne  in'  lawe  William  Carye  and  Mary  his  wife  twentie  poundes.  To 
Thomas  Carye  my  graund  childe  twentie  markes  when  he  shall  accomplish  his  full  age.  I  make 
my  sole  executor  Thomas  my  sonne.  Yf  he  departe  this  life  before  my  three  youngest  children 
shall  accomplish  theire  seuerall  ages  of  one  and  twentie  yeres,  then  I  will  that  John  my  sonne 
shall  enter  into  the  landes  and  bring  vp  my  three  youngest  children.  Witnesse  Thomas  Ritcher 
and  John  Bolton.

past,  a  day  or  twoe  before  his  death,  with  an  intent  to  settle  and  dispose  of  his  estate,  did 
by  word  of  mouth  declare  the  same  in  these  words.  “  £  giue  vnto  my  brother  William  Bolton 
all  my  estate  whatsoever  And  I  make  him  my  Executor.  Or  the  said  Wisman  [sic]  Bolton  did 
declare  his  Will  and  Testament  in  words  to  the  like  effect.  In  the  presence  of  Robert 
Sparham,  Apothecary,  Anthony  Applewhite,  habbed  of  small  wares  and  others. 

This  will  was  proved  at  London  the  15th  day  of  June  1558  by  the  oathe  of  William 
Bolton,  the  brother  and  Executor.  P.C.C.,  494  Wootton. 


Mill  of  jitary  Bolton,  1685. 

Mary  Bolton  of  Woodbridge  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolke,  widowe,  the  eighth  day  of 
September,  1683.  To  be  decently  buried  vnder  the  Gravestone  where  the  Body  of  my  late 
Husband  lies  interred,  hopeing  of  a  glorious  Resurrection.  1  give  vnto  Thomas  Bolton  my  sonne 
a  Birded  Coverlett,  as  it  now  stands  in  my  Roome,  my  Riding  Hood,  Muffe,  and  all  my  other 
Hoods,  both  Silke  and  Linnen,  and  a  Painted  Boxe  with  Lock  and  Key.  Vnto  William  Bolton, 
my  grandchild,  the  Trendle  Bed,  &c.,  wch  I  formerly  lent  my  son  Wittm  his  father,  and  two 
Paire  of  my  narrowest  hemping  Sheets.  Vnto  my  grandchild  Thomas  Hervey  one  Velvett 
Grogerin  covered  back  chaire.  Vnto  Edmund  Bolton  my  sonne  the  two  Bucketts  hanging  vpon 
iron  Chains  vsed  and  belonging  to  the  Well.  I  give  vnto  Wiffm  Bolton  my  sonne  all  my 
ready  money  and  other  my  Goods  not  otherwise  bequeathed  wch  of  Right  doe  belong  vnto  mee. 
Which  sayd  William  my  sonne  I  doe  Ordaine  to  be  my  Sole  Executor.  Probatum  apud  Gippm 
decimo  quinti  die  mensis  Augusti  1687.  Arch.  Suff.  Liber  “  Prideaux,”  fol.  260b. 

Thomas  Bolton,  of  Woodbridge,  gentleman,  the  testator’s  husband,  in  a  brief  will,  dated 
18th  April  1663,  devised  his  lands  to  Thomas  Bolton  his  son,  and  the  rest  of  his  estate  to 
Mary  his  wife,  whom  he  appointed  his  executrix.  It  was  proved  27th  January  1666  by  Thomas 
Bolton,  the  son,  his  widow  having  renounced.  Arch.  Suff,  Original  Wills,  1666,  No.  181.

® banary  flrom'tihtgs,  IBolton  r.  Carry,  1708. 

Samuel  Bolton  of  Woodbridge,  Surgeon,  and  Alice  bis  wife,  and  Mary  Cary  of  Ipswich, 
spinster,  shew  that  William  Cary  of  Halesworth,  co.  Suffolke,  gent.,  made  his  last  will  about 

the  first  day  of  May  1686  in  these  words.  “  I  give  unto  Thomas  Cary  my  nephew  all  my 

lands  which  I  had  upon  mortgage  from  Miles  Gardner,  lying  in  Bulchamp,  and  my  fields  in 
Blyford  and  the  messuage  and  tenement  wherein  I  do  now  inhabitt  in  Halesworth  and  the 
messuage  &  lands  which  I  purchased  of  one  Drane,  and  the  messuage  which  I  had  of  Thomas 
Cary  my  brother  of  Woodbridge,  Gent.,  and  the  messuage  which  I  had  of  W alter  l’rowd  in 
Halesworth,  and  my  lease  off  two  tenements  in  Great  Tower  Hill,  London;  he,  the  said  Thomas 
Cary  my  nephew,  paying  out  of  the  same  to  his  fower  sisters  £800 : — (that  is  to  say)  to 
Katherine  his  sister  and  her  child  £200 ;  and  to  his  sister  Sarah  £200  and  to  each  of  his 
other  two  sisters  Alice  Cary  and  Mary  Cary  the  sum  of  £200  a  peice  at  their  several  ages  of 
one  and  twenty  yeares,  and  to  Sr  Henry  Beddingfeild,  Lord  Chief  Justice  of  the  Common  Pleas, 
twenty  guineas.  And  my  will  and  mind  is  that  the  residue  of  my  money  due  upon  mortgages, 
and  other  securities  taken  in  my  owne  brother  Thomas  or  nephew  Thomas  name,  shall  be  laid 
out  upon  purchases  of  land  in  trust  to  the  use  of  Thomas  Cary  my  brother  for  his  life,  and 

after  his  decease  remain  to  my  nephew  Thomas  Cary,  whom  I  make  my  Executors.”  Within  a 

few  years  after  the  death  of  the  said  William  Cary,  Thomas  Cary  the  elder,  his  brother, 
departed  this  life  intestate,  leaving  Thomas  Cary  the  younger,  his  eldest  sonn  and  heir,  and 
soon  after  Katherine,  his  widdow,  tooke  out  letters  of  Administration  and  possessed  herself  of 
the  personall  estate  of  the  said  Thomas  Cary  the  elder.  The  said  Thomas  Cary  the  younger 
received  to  his  owne  use  the  issues  of  the  lands  of  William  Cary  and  was  duly  admitted  to 
the  copyholds  and  paid  the  legacy  of  twenty  guineas  to  Dame  .  .  .  Beddingfield,  the  executrix 
of  Sr  Henry  Beddingfield.  Katherine,  one  of  the  four  sisters  of  the  said  Thomas  Cary,  was 
then  married  to  one  Thomas  Summerlay  of  London,  Scrivener,  long  since  dead,  and  her  child 
named  in  the  will  was  her  youngest  daughter  Mary,  since  mai'ried  to  Thomas  Fuller  of 
Hintlesham,  and  is  now  living.  Sara,  one  other  of  the  said  four  sisters,  is  married  to  Thomas 
Wade  of  Woodbridge  ;  your  Oratrices,  Alice,  now  the  wife  of  Samuell  Bolton,  and  Mary  Cary 
being  two  other  of  the  said  sisters  of  Thomas  Cary  the  younger  and  devisees  in  the  said  will. 
The  said  Alice  attained  her  age  of  one  and  twenty  years  about  the  26th  of  October  1691, 
being  since  married  to  your  Orator  Samuell  Bolton.  And  Mary  Cary  attained  her  said  age  in 
July  1701.  But  Thomas  Cary  junior  confederating  with  Thomas  Miller  and  Mary  his  wife, 
Thomas  Wade  and  Sarah  his  wife,  William  Perkins  of  Blyford,  co.  Suffolke,  Hone  Setter,  and 
others  doth  refuse  to  pay  the  respective  legacies. 

Answers  of  Thomas  Cary,  gent.,  &  others.  Complicated  statements. 

Chan.  Proc.,  Mitford  D.C.V.  31. 

In  the  Hawes  MS.,  written  circa  1712,  and  described  by  Page  in  his  History  of  Suffolk, 
pp.  83,  133,  are  notices  of  the  “Gentry  sometime  residing  in  Woodbridge,”  and  coloured 
drawings  of  their  Arms.  It  mentions  “  Thomas  Bolton,  Esqr,  who  dwelt  in  this  Parish  in  the 
reign  of  K.  Ja8  I  and  was  buried  there  1616.  From  him,”  it  adds,  “  Mr  Samuel  Bolton,  now 
living  in  Wroodbridge,  is  descended.”  Mr.  Bobert  Hawes,  the  compiler,  presented  an  autograph 
copy  of  this  manuscript  to  the  Master  and  Fellows  of  Pembroke  Hall,  Cambridge.

The  first  day  of  May,  1686,  I  William  Cary  of  Halesworth  in  the  County  of  Sufi'., 
gent.,  doe  make  this  my  last  will  and  Testament.  I  give  my  soule  into  the  hands  of  Allmighty 
God,  and  my  body  to  be  decently  interred  in  the  Church  of  Halesworth  1  bequeath  unto 
Thomas  Cary  my  nephew  all  my  lands  and  tenements  in  Bulcampe  ;  and  my  lands  in  Blyford, 
which  I  hold  by  the  conditional  surrender  of  Philip  Partrich,  late  deceased ;  and  all  the  messuage 
and  tenement  wherein  I  now  inhabit  in  Halesworth ;  and  that  messuage  which  I  late  purchased 
of  one  Drane,  holden  of  severall  mannors ;  and  that  messuage  and  lands  which  1  had  of  the 
surrender  of  Thomas  Cary  my  brother  in  Woodbridge;  and  the  messuage  which  I  hold  of  the 
surrender  of  Walter  Proud  in  Halesworth ;  and  my  lease  and  terme  of  yeares  to  come  of  my 
two  tenements  scituate  on  great  Tower  Hill,  London,  to  hold  to  the  said  Thomas  Cary,  my 

nephew,  and  his  heires  for  ever,  he  paying  out  of  the  same  to  his  foure  sisters  eight  hundred 
pounds,  in  this  manner  (that  is  to  say),  to  Katherine  his  sister,  £200,  which  shall  be  secured 
for  her  maintenance  dureing  her  life,  and  after  the  principall  for  her  child  now  with  her ;  my 
said  nephew  paying  unto  his  sister  Sarah  £200,  within  one  year  after  my  decease,  and  to  each 

of  his  two  other  sisters,  Alice  Cary  and  Mary  Cary,  £200,  at  their  sevei-all  ages  of  one  and 

twenty  yeares ;  my  nephew  Thomas  Cary  alsoe  paying  out  of  aforesaid  demised  lands,  to  my 
most  honoured  friend,  Sr  Harry  Bedingfeild,  now  Lord  Cheife  Justice  of  the  common  Pleas, 
whome  I  name  supervisor  of  this  my  will,  twenty  guineas  towards  his  advise  and  trouble  in 
the  settlements  of  the  severall  lands  in  this  my  will  devised.  I  give  to  my  couzin,  Prancis 
Barker,  five  pounds  to  buy  him  mourning,  and  to  my  two  Godsonnes,  Mr  John  Wheeler  and 
Mr  William  Nuthall,  twenty  shillings  a  piece  to  buy  them  rings  with  a  memento  mori.  To 

the  poore  of  Woodbridge  five  pounds.  To  the  poore  of  Hallesworth  tenn  pounds ;  six  pounds 
to  be  distributed  the  day  after  my  Interment,  and  foure  pounds  on  St.  Thomas  Hay  next  after 
my  decease,  in  such  manner  as  for  many  years  in  my  life  time  I  distributed  my  charity. 
Executors  shall  purchase  a  small  parcell  of  ground  of  the  Lord’s  wast  in  Halesworth,  at  the 
south  entrance  into  the  Towne,  nere  where  the  Lord’s  pound  now  standeth,  and  thereupon  to 
erect  a  house  for  the  poore,  to  conteyne  twelve  roomes,  besides  garretts,  foure  yards  and  a  halfe 
square  and  eight  foot  high,  all  to  be  bricke  from  the  foundation  to  the  roofe,  two  to  be  tiled 
Gabell  endes  with  double  chimneys,  and  two  chimneys  of  equal  distances  betweene  each ;  foure 
fire  hearths  supplyes  twelve  roomes  ;  one  pump  or  well  in  the  middle  behind  the  house  comon 

to  all.  This  I  intend  for  ever  a  habitation  for  twelve  or  more  aged  poore  single  woemen  and 

single  men,  of  honest  and  good  reputation,  coming  to  divine  service.  And  where  of  such  that 
number  be  wanting,  I  will  it  to  be  supplied  by  poore  widdowes  without  children  at  the  discre¬ 
tion  of  the  Churchwardens  for  the  time  being.  Every  person  that  shall  inhabit  in  the  poore’s 

house  shall  ware  a  badge  of  silver  as  thicke  as  a  halfe  crowne  and  broader  then  a  Crowne,

The  Kempes  of  Beccles,  whose  pedigree  is  given  in  Camden’s  Visitation  of  Suffolk,  1612, 
were  a  branch  of  the  Kempes  of  Gissing,  in  Norfolk.  They  bore  ( Harl .  MS.  1552,  fol.  181) 
Quartet ly  of  8  : — 

1,  Kempe — Gules,  three  garbs  within  a  bordure  engrailed  Or. 

2,  — Azure,  a  lion  rampant  Argent. 

3,  — Sable,  three  bars  Argent ;  on  a  canton  Gules,  a  saltire  of  the  second, 

4,  Hastings — Or,  a  maunch  Gules. 

5,  Duke — Azure,  a  chevron  between  three  birds  close  Argent,  beaked  and  legged  Gules. 

6,  Butvillain — Argent,  three  crescents  Gules. 

7,  Bardolph  (Harl.  MS.  1561) — Azure,  three  cinquefoils  Or. 

8,  — Argent,  two  chevrons  Sable. 

Their  crest  was  an  eagle  with  wings  endorsed,  standing  on  a  garb  lying  fessways,  all  Or. 

In  the  Visitation  of  London,  1568  [Harl.  MS.  1^63),  the  arms  of  Margaret,  daughter  of 
Edmund  Kempe,  and  wife  of  William  Dane,  Alderman  of  that  city,  are  Quarterly  of  6 
1,  Kempe,  as  above;  2,  Butvillain,  as  above;  3,  Argent,  two  chevrons  Sable;  4,  Sable,  a  lion 
rampant  Argent ;  5,  Sable,  three  bars  Argent,  on  a  canton  Gules  a  saltire  of  the  second ;  6, 

Ermine,  a  bend  chequy  Sable  and  Argent. 

In  the  Norfolk  Visitation  of  1664  (Harl.  MS.  1085)  the  arms  of  Sir  Robert  Kempe,  of 
Gissing  (and  afterwards  of  Ubbeston,  co.  Suffolk),  Baronet,  who  married  the  daughter  and  heir 
of  Sone,  differ  somewhat  from  those  tricked  in  Harl.  MS.  1552.  The  escutcheon  is  Quarterly  of 
Nine.  The  fifth  or  central  quarter,  apparently  Gules,  a  bend  Argent,  is  almost  obliterated  by 
the  shield  of  pretence  for  Sone  (per  pale  Or  and  Azure,  on  a  fess  wavy  two  crescents  between 
four  quatrefoils,  all  counterchanged) ;  and  the  two  last  quarterings  have  changed  places. 

For  further  particulars  respecting  the  Kempes  of  Suffolk,  Norfolk  and  Essex,  the  reader 
is  referred  to  the  “  General  History  of  the  Kempe  Families  of  Great  Britain  and  her  Colonies,” 
by  Frederick  Hitchin-Kemp,  an  illustrated  quarto  volume,  the  outcome  of  years  of  research.  It 
treats  largely  of  earlier  generations,  whose  connection  with  the  family  tree  is  not  as  yet  quite 
proven  or  understood,  and  its  illustrations,  especially  the  portraits  of  the  Gissing  baronets  and 
their  kindred,  are  excellent. 

It  cannot  be  denied  that  the  descents  in  the  visitation  pedigree  of  the  Weston  and 
Gissing  Kempes,  as  given  in  Harl.  MS.  1552,  are,  prior  to  the  real  marriage  of  the  coheiress 
of  the  Butvileins,  traditionary  and  inexact.  It  was  in  1460  that  her  son,  Robert  Kempe,  of 
Weston,  in  the  county  of  Suffolk,  gentleman,  inherited  his  Gissing  manors,  on  the  division  of 
the  estates  of  his  late  uncle,  Sir  Robert  Butvillein,  of  Northamptonshire.  See  Bridge’s  History 
of  that  County,  vol.  i,  p.  554,  and  the  Indenture,  38  H.  6,  given  on  p.  226.

In  his  Inquisition  post  mortem,  taken  20th  September,  19th  Henry  VIII,  it  is  stated 
that  Robert  Kempe  died  seized  of  the  Manors  of  Butvelyns,  Dallynges  and  Hastyngs  in  Gissing, 
and  lands  in  Florden  and  Brakon  in  the  county  of  Norfolk.  Bartholomew  Kempe,  Esqr.,  his 
son  and  heir,  was  of  the  age  of  thirty  years  and  upwards.  The  testator  was  already  married 
to  Anne  Clifford,  his  second  wife,  in  1490  (4th  Henry  VII)  when  a  settlement  was  made  upon 
her.  Another  Inquisition  had  been  taken  a  few  days  earlier  (16th  September)  respecting  his 
Suffolk  lands,  in  Weston,  Ellough,  Worlingham,  and  Reddisham.  He  had  died  on  the  5th  of 
December  1526.

In  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1612  the  testator  is  said  to  have  been  of  Washbrook  in 
that  county.  It  was  Thomas,  his  third  son,  who  settled  at  Beccles  and  succeeded  to  his  Suffolk 
estates  in  Weston  and  Ellough.  For  the  brother  Anthony  Drury,  of  Besthorpe,  and  niece 
Elizabeth  Harborne,  see  their  pedigree  vol.  i,  p.  355. 


Jlobcrt  of  Sira  S>t.  (Sdtmmta,  1595. 

In  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1612,  Robert,  the  fourth  son  of  Robert  Kempe,  of  Gissing,  is 
stated  to  have  married  Ann,  daughter  of  William  Stanton,  of  Westmoreland  ('!  Weston).  His  mother 
was  Elizabeth,  daughter  of  Edmund  Grey.  We  first  hear  of  him  in  1593,  in  the  will  of  his 
great  aunt,  Elizabeth  Spelman  (Cur.  Ep.  Norw.,  book  91,  fol.  294),  whose  niece  married  Edmund 
Grey,  of  Merton.  She  bequeaths  to  her  “cousin”  (or  nephew)  Robert  Kempe,  of  Bury  St. 
Edmunds,  the  “pycture  in  my  plor  of  the  iudgement  of  Solomon,”  and  makes  him  one  of  her 
executors.  Later  on,  in  his  will  in  1599,  Richard  Kempe,  of  Gissing,  his  eldest  brother,  speaks 
of  a  “  cousin,”  Robert  Kempe,  of  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  and  a  nephew  Robert  Kempe,  son  of  his 
brother  Robert,  who  are,  apparently  identical.  In  1610  John  Kempe,  of  Antingham,  another 
brother,  bequeaths  money  to  his  nephew  Thomas  Kempe,  son  of  Robert  his  brother.  Very  little 
is  known  of  this  brother  Robert  Kempe,  who  made  no  will.  In  1588  and  1595  the  Adminis¬ 
tration  Books  in  the  Bury  Probate  Registry  describe  him  as  a  notary  public.  As  “  Robert 
Kempe  of  Bury,  gentleman,”  he  was  assessed  at  three  pounds  in  the  Suffolk  Subsidy  of  1610, 
42nd  Elizabeth,  i|~|.  His  name  does  not  occur  in  the  parish  registers  at  Bury.  What  became 
of  him,  his  wife,  and  his  sons,  Robert  and  Thomas,  or  what  other  issue,  if  any,  he  had,  has 
never,  as  yet,  been  ascertained.  It  is  not  improbable  that  Elizabeth  Kempe,  who  married  Oliver 
Hovell,  of  Bury,  and  whose  daughters  mated  with  members  of  the  Visitation  families  of  Clench, 
Chaplyn,  and  Vesey,  may  have  been  his  child.  See  their  pedigree,  vol.  ii,  p.  103.

The  29th  of  April,  1646,  I  Sr  Robert  Kemp  of  Gissing  co.  Norff.  K4  &  Baronet,  doe  ordaine 

and  make  this  my  last  will  written  with  myne  owne  hand.  First  I  comend  my  soule  into  ye

thro’  the  meritts  of  whose  most  bitter  death  and  passion,  I  stedfastly  beleeve  to  have  remission 

of  my  sinnes.  My  body,  I  will,  shall  be  buried  in  my  Chappell  in  Gissing  Church. 

To  Robert  Kemp,  my  eldest  son,  all  my  books  and  my  yellow  diamond  ringe  and  an 
annuity  of  £80  a  year,  during  his  minority,  charged  on  Antingham  Manor  and  lands  there.  To

Matthew  Kemp,  my  third  son,  £50  a  yere  for  life,  out  of  Flordon  Manor  and  lands,  to  begin 
when  he  is  sixteen.  To  Richard  Kemp,  my  fourth  son,  £50  a  yere,  when  sixteene  years  of 
age.  To  Maurice  Shelton  4  and  his  wife,2  to  each  of  them  £10,  to  buy  “  moorninge  clothes.”

it  be  with  the  consent  of  my  executor,  or  of  my  sister  the  Lady  Kemp  in  Essex. 

To  my  loving  brother,  Sir  Robert  Kempe  of  Finchingfield  in  Essex,  and  to  my  sister  his 
wife,  and  to  every  one  of  my  own  brothers,  and  to  my  son  Thomas  Waldegrave  and  his  wife 

£10  a  peice,  to  buy  them  “  moorninge  clothes.”  To  my  grandchild  Jane  Waldegrave  £20.

and  Thomas  Wallgrave  for  five  hundred  years,  in  trust,  to  raise  £2,500  portion  for  my  daughter 
in  case  of  failure  of  issue  male  by  me,  the  remainder  being  settled  by  the  first  named  Indenture.

of  fiolml  Hemp,  1734* 

The  7th  day  of  December,  1734,  I  Sir  Robert  Kemp  of  Ubbeston  in  the  County  of 
Suffolk,  Baronet,  do  make  and  declare  this  my  last  will.  My  body  I  commit  to  the  earth,  to 
be  buried  in  my  vault  at  Gissing,  between  my  two  former  wives,  and  right  over  my  late 
deceased  wife.  1  will  it  be  put  into  two  Coffins,  a  timber  one  within  the  leaden  one,  by  the 
person  in  Norwich  that  made  my  late  dear  wife’s.  I  give  unto  my  eldest  son,  Robert  Kemp 
Esqr,  all  my  mannors,  messuages  and  lands  in  the  Kingdom  of  Great  Britain ;  he  to  pay 
annuities  and  bequests.  Unto  Dame  Amy,  my  loving  wife,  the  £300  a  year  which  I  settled 
upon  her  before  marriage.  I  bequeath  (sums  of  money,  some  of  them  the  gift  of  their  uncle 
Isaac  Brand)  to  my  daughter  Elizabeth  Kemp ;  my  sons  Thomas,  Benjamin  and  William  Kemp. 
Dame  Amy  Kemp,  my  loving  wife,  to  have  the  care  of  my  daughter  Martha  until  she  marry 

or  come  of  age.  Annuity  to  my  son  John  Kemp,  he  having  hitherto  been  unfortunate  in  the 

world.  My  son  Isaac  has  spent  most  of  the  money  his  uncle  Brand  left  him.  My  mother  in 
law,  Mrs  Elizabeth  Spencer.  To  the  poor  of  Edwardston,  according  to  the  will  of  John  Brand 
Esqr,  my  late  father  in  law.  To  Dame  Amy  my  wife,  my  picture  that  hangs  up  in  her 
dressing  room.  To  my  daughter  Blois  and  my  brother,  William  Kemp  Esqr.  My  son  Robert 
shall  erect  a  monument  in  my  Isle  in  Gissing  Church,  where  my  vault  is.  Dame  Amy  Kemp, 

and  Robert  and  John  Kemp,  my  sons,  to  be  executors.  This  will  was  proved,  10th  May,  1735t 

by  Sir  Robert  Kemp,  Baronet,  and  John  Kemp  Esqr,  two  of  the  executors.

only  child  Amy,  who  married  Robert  Blois,  eldest  son  of  Sir  Charles  Blois,  Baronet.  Her  will 
and  that  of  her  daughter,  Amy  Blois,  who  was  buried  in  Westminster  Abbey,  will  be  found

In  consideration  of  Nelson’s  Suffolk  ancestry,  and  especially  of  his  descent,  through  the 
Sucklings  and  the  Sheltons,  from  the  first  Baronet  of  their  name,  the  Kemps  offered  to  sell 
Ubbeston  to  the  Nation  as  a  suitable  seat  for  Earl  Nelson  and  his  family.  Much  concerning 
this  proposal  and  its  consideration  by  Parliament  will  be  found  in  the  “  Historical  Chronicle  ” 
of  1815  and  Mr.  Hitchin-Kemp’s  “  History  of  the  Kempe  Families.” 

By  the  marriage  of  Sir  Robert  Kemp  with  Jane,  daughter  of  Sir  Matthew  Browne,  of 
Beechworth  Castle,  and  other  matches,  the  Kemps  and  their  descendants  derive  a  number  of 
Royal  descents,  the  most  remarkable,  perhaps,  being  that  from  King  Henry  the  Third,  through 
the  Fitz  Alans  and  the  Earls  of  Lancaster.  See  the  Browne’s  pedigree  in  the  volume  of  Surrey 
Visitations  published  by  the  Harleian  Society.

Edward  Kempe,  Priest  of  Holy  Church  and  Fellow  of  Queen’s  Colledge  in  the  Vniversity 
of  Cambridge,  the  23d  day  of  October  1671.  My  frequent  infirmities  and  (great)  age  call  upon 
me  to  prepare  for  my  last  end.  I  doe  professe  my  selfe  a  sonne,  though  very  vnworthy,  of 
the  Church  of  England.  I  would  not,  for  any  thing  in  this  world,  dissent  from  what  the 
Catholick  Church  of  Christ  (doth)  hold  and  believe.  I  hope  I  shall  not  dye  soe  sodainely  but 
that  I  shall  haue  tyme  to  receive  my  absolution  from  some  Priest  of  Ploly  Church.  I  forgive 
all  the  world  any  injuries,  whatsoever  haue  beene  offered  me,  and  I  desire  all  men’s  forgivenesse 
in  what  I  may  haue  offended  them.  My  body  I  desire  may  be  interred  in  holy  ground,  there 
to  expect  a  glorious  resurrection,  when  God  shall  raise  it  from  its  dust.  I  doe  giue  vnto  the 
said  Queen’s  Colledge  the  sume  of  three  hundred  powndes  to  purchase  land,  or  a  rent  charge 
vpon  land,  in  vsum  sacelli,  for  the  maintenance  of  God’s  solemne  service  and  worshipp  in  the 
Chappell  of  the  saide  Colledge,  according  to  the  Rites  now  practiced  by  the  Church  of  England. 
I  giue  vnto  my  nephew,  Sr  Robert  Kempe,  the  sume  of  two  hundred  pownds,  out  of  the  five 
hundreds  of  mine  now  in  the  hands  of  Mr  Charles  Baron  of  Little  Eversden  in  the  County  of 
Cambridge.  I  nominate  Mr  Charles  Smyth,  ffellow  of  Queen’s  Colledge,  my  sole  executor. 
Surplusage  of  moneys  I  giue  vnto  my  said  nephew  Sr  Robert  Kempe.  My  will  to  be  entered 
into  the  Register  of  said  Colledge.  Probatum  28°  Nov.  1671,  coram  Deputat  Procancellarii 
Almas  Universitatis  Cantebr,  Comiss  adfti  Carolo  Smith  executori.

The  best,  perhaps,  of  the  older  Kempe  pedigrees  is  that  in  Harl.  MS.  1154,  fo.  69b.  It 
gives  the  lineage  of  the  Butvilleins  and  Cliffords,  the  descendants  of  Edmund  Kempe  of  London 
and  Bridget  Style,  and  the  eldest  sons  of  Robert  Kempe  of  Bury  and  his  brother,  William  Kempe — 
details  not  to  be  found  in  better  known  genealogies  of  the  family.  It  also  shows  that  Alexander 
Kempe  of  Weston,  1327,  was  another  of  the  children  of  Allan  Kempe  of  that  parish. 

It  has  drawings  too  (fo.  lc)  of  a  number  of  Kempe  shields  “  in  the  windowes  at  Mr.  Fawether,” 
as  Kempe  impaling  Stanton;  Kempe,  with  a  mullet  for  difference,  impaling  Moore  of  Ipswich  ; 
the  arms  of  “  Moore  ''wnn  a  Mantell  over  the  chimlie  peece ;  ”  and,  probably  by  way  of  a  pleasantry, 
“  his  woord,”  or  motto,  “  Memento  Mori.”

Armorial  Scarings. 

The  Arms  of  Barrow  of  Westhorpe,  as  sketched  in  that  admirable  collection  of  Suffolk 
pedigrees,  Harl.  MS.  1560,  were  Quarterly  of  six,  1,  Barrow,  Sable  two  swords  in  saltire 
Argent,  hilts  and  pomels  Or,  between  four  fleurs-de-lys,  all  within  a  bordure  of  the  third ;  2, 
Bures,  Ermine,  on  a  chief  dancette  Sable,  two  lions  rampant  Or ;  3,  Roydon,  chequy  Argent 
and  Gules,  a  cross  Azure;  4,  (1)  Morieux,  Azure,  three  leaves  Or;  5,  Farmor,  Ermine,  a  chevron 
Sable  between  three  roses  Gules ;  6,  Party  per  bend  wavy  Sable  and  Or.  The  Crest  which 
heads  the  pedigree  of  Barrow  in  Harl.  MS.  1552,  a  similar  volume  which  treats  of  Norfolk,  is 
a  hind’s  head  couped  Argent.  In  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664  (Harl.  MS.  1085)  a  shield, 
with  two  swords  in  saltire  between  four  fleurs-de-lys,  accompanies  the  name  of  “  Morris  Barrow 
of  Barningham  Esq.,”  but  no  tinctures  are  indicated. 

The  arms  of  the  Sheltons  of  Barningham,  who  inherited  most  of  the  Barrow  estates,  were 
Or,  a  cross  Azure. 


Mill  of  Milliam  Sarroio,  1615. 

Wiiim  Barrow  of  Westhorpe  co.  Suff.  Esq.  23  Dec.  1613.  To  be  buried  in  Westhorpe 
church.  Estate  to  executor  vntill  Maurice,  my  only  sonne,  come  to  the  age  of  twentie  and  ffower 
yeres.  Vnto  my  daughter  £1600  at  her  age  of  eighteene  yeares,  whether  married  or  no.  Vnto 
Jane  Hunte,  my  goddaughter  of  my  neece  Hunte  £100.  Vnto  my  nephewe,  Henry  Shelton,  rent 
chardge  out  of  my  Mannor  of  Reydon  hall  in  Suffolk  during  his  life.  If  my  sonne  and 
daughter  dye  wthout  heires  of  their  bodies,  the  one  moytie  of  my  Mannor  of  Newton  in 
Suffolke  shall  remayne  vnto  my  nephewe,  John  Claxton,  and  the  other  vnto  Anne  Claxton,  my 
neece ;  and  my  (other)  manors  and  lands  vnto  my  nephewe  Henry  Shelton  and  the  heires  of 
his  body ;  and  for  default  of  such  issue,  unto  the  right  heires  of  me,  William  Barrow  for  ever. 
I  appoint  Elizabeth,  my  now  wife,  sole  executor.  Probatum  xxi°  die  Januarij  1613,  juramento 
Elizabeth*  Barrowe,  relicte.  P.C.C. 


Mill  of  JRauritt  IBarrohi,  1665. 

Maurice  Barrow  of  Barningham  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolk  Esq.,  16tl‘  Nov.  1665.  To  be 
buried  in  a  vault  I  built  at  the  end  of  the  north  side  of  Westhorpe  church  for  myself  and 
Mary,  Lady  Pointz,  my  wife.  She  is  already  well  endowed.  I  bequeath  her  nine  pieces  of 


BARROW  OF  WESTHORPE. 


239 


Arras  hangings  given  me  by  Mr  Richard  Smith,  my  father  in  law,  and  lands  in  Reydon  and 
Newton  near  Sudbury  during  her  life.  For  the  advancement  of  the  ancient  family  of  the  Sheltons, 
being  of  noble  extraction,  I  give  my  Manors,  Ac.,  of  Roydon  Hall,  Newton,  Westhorpe  and 
Coneyweston,  to  Maurice  Shelton  the  elder  and  the  heirs  of  his  body.  In  default  of  such,  I 
give  my  Manor  and  Advowson  of  Newton  unto  my  loving  couzin  Hamond  Claxton  :  and  one 
third  of  my  Manor  and  Advowson  of  Westhorpe  to  my  couzin  Charles  Fitch,  Esq.,  son  and  heir  of 
Sir  William  Fitch,  Kfc,  deceased.  Maurice  Shelton,  eldest  son  of  said  Maurice,  whose  father  (my 
entirely  beloved  cousin)  entrusted  me  with  his  and  his  two  sisters’  education.  My  Manor  of 
Packmaston  in  Kent  to  said  cousin  Hamond  Claxton.  Lands  in  Erith,  Plumsted  and  Lesnes, 
co.  Kent,  to  be  sold.  William  Barrow,  Esq.,  my  late  father;  his  eldest  sister,  wife  of  John 
Claxton,  Esq.,  my  late  uncle.  Thomas  Dandy,  son  and  heir  of  Thomas  Dandy,  deceased,  my 
kinsman.  Edmund  Ferneley,  Esq.,  my  kinsman,  and  Edmund,  Elizabeth  and  Mary,  his  children. 
Kinsmen  John  Sothebie,  James  Sothebie  of  London  and  Roger  Sothebie.  My  cousins  Francis 
Quarles,  Rector  of  Newton,  and  William  Quarles  of  Norwich.  My  cousins  Mary,  wife  of  Mr 
Richard  Humfrey,  and  Elizabeth,  wife  of  Mr  Charles  Humfrey,  deceased.  My  kinsman,  Sir 
Edmund  Bacon,  deceased.  Charles  Fitch,  Esq.,  my  cousin,  Barrow  Fitch  his  eldest  son  and 
Elizabeth,  Lady  Moore,  his  sister.  Lands  in  Hopton,  Weston,  Euston,  Knettishall,  Barningham, 
Ac.,  co.  Suffolk.  Farm  called  Brakland  Parke  in  Bardwell  and  Fakenham  Wood,  containing 
three  hundred  and  fifty  acres.  Indentures  recapitulated.  Maurice  Shelton  the  elder,  Hamond 
Claxton  and  John  Sothebie  to  be  executors.  For  the  finishing  of  the  vault  at  Westhorpe,  and 
the  erecting  of  an  iron  gate  for  its  preservation  I  appoint  the  sum  of  £500.  Blacks  and  rings 
to  be  given  to  my  kindred  and  friends,  and  blacks  to  my  servants,  to  the  value  of  £600,  my 
body  being  buried  with  all  decency  and  privacy.  To  the  Lady  Pointz,  my  dear  wife,  my  best 
fasset  diamond  Ring  (valued  at  a  hundred  pounds)  during  her  life,  and  after  her  decease,  to 
Maurice  Shelton  the  elder  Esqr  my  godson ;  to  whom  I  give  my  blue  saphir  ring,  and  my 
Guilt  Cup  and  cover  thereunto,  desiring  they  may  be  left  by  him  to  Maurice  Shelton  his  son 
(and  my  godson),  and  so  to  the  successive  heirs  of  the  ancient  family  of  the  Sheltons  for  ever. 
As  for  the  Mannors  of  Sfc  Cleers  &  Netherhall  &  my  Mansion  house  wherein  I  dwell  called 
Barningham  Hall  and  my  parke  called  Brakland  Parke,  I  limit  the  same  to  Maurice  Shelton 
the  elder  and  to  the  heirs  of  his  body.  Nevertheless,  if  Mary  Lady  Pointz,  my  dear  wife,  by 
reason  of  her  inability  to  travell,  be  desirous  to  dwell  there  at  a  reasonable  rent,  the  said 
Maurice  Shelton  (for  my  sake)  to  yield  her  all  due  respect  and  assistance.  My  will  is  that 
she  shall  have  yearly,  during  her  life,  four  brace  of  bucks  and  four  brace  of  does,  out  of  the 
said  parke.  All  other  my  Manors  and  lands  shall  remain  and  stand  to  the  use  of  Hamond 
Claxton  of  Great  Livermere  Esqr  A  John  Sothebie  of  Bury  S1,  Edmunds  Esqr  and  their  executors 
for  the  space  of  twenty  years  after  my  decease,  who  shall  out  of  the  rents  thereof  pay  all 
my  debts,  mortgages,  funeral  expenses  and  legacies.  My  dear  father,  William  Barrow  Esq.  did 
constantly  intend,  in  case  he  died  without  issue,  the  greatest  part  of  his  estate  to  the  issue 
of  his  eldest  sister.  The  posterity  of  his  second  sister  is  fairly  enabled  by  lands  descended 
from  John  Claxton  Esqr  my  late  uncle,  and  by  gifts  of  Hamond  Claxton,  deceased.  To  Maurice 
Shelton,  eldest  son  of  Maurice  Shelton  the  elder,  my  chamber  in  Graye’s  Inne  in  the  county 
of  Middx.  This  lengthy  will  concludes  with  numerous  bequests  to  friends,  annuities  to  old 
servants,  and  substantial  gifts  to  the  poor.

1  “  1  make  the  righte  honorable  and  my  verie  good  lord,  the  lord  Burghlie,  lord  highe  Treasurer  of  england  [my 
supervisor],  most  humblie  beseechinge  his  honor,  for  the  dutie,  love  and  good  will  that  1  haue  eu’  borne  vnto  him,  and  for 
the  great  attiaun’ce  that  I  haue  that  Giles  Alington,  my  yonge  nephew  and  now  my  heire  apparent,  should  match  in  his 
Lordshippes  howse  with  one  of  the  daughters  of  his  Lordshippes  sonne  and  heire,  Sir  Thomas  Cecill,  Knight ;  that  he  will 
not  only  be  aidinge  vnto  my  executors  in  the  due  execucion  of  this  my  Testament,  but  allso  that  his  Lordshippe  will  haue 
a  speciall  care  to  bringe  the  said  marriage  to  passe;  and  duringe  the  minoritie  of  my  said  heire  to  see  his  woodes  pre- 
serued,  his  howses  well  repaired,  and  his  poore  tennaun’tes  vyell  and  charitablie  ordered.” 

From  the  will  of  Sir  Giles  Allington,  1586.  P.C.C.  49  Windsor.

Jlrmorial  Sea rings. 

The  arms  which  accompany  the  Jermyn  pedigree  in  Harl.  MS.  1560  are  Quarterly  of  niner 
1,  Jermyn,  Sable  a  crescent  between  two  mullets  in  pale  Argent;  2,  Rushbrook,  Gules  (Burke 
says  Sable)  a  fess  between  three  roses  Or ;  3,  Heveningham,  Per  cross  Or  and  Gules ;  on  a 
bordure  engrailed  Sable  eight  escallops  Argent ;  4,  Jarvile,  Paly  of  six  Or  and  Azure  ;  5.  Gissing, 
Argent  on  a  bend  Azure  three  eagles  displayed  Or ;  6,  Redesham,  Argent,  semee  of  fleurs  de  lys 
Gules  ;  7,  Reppes,  Ermine  three  chevrons  Gules  (Sable,  Burke)  ;  8,  Burgon,  Azure  a  hound  passant 
Argent ;  9,  Bozun,  Gules  (Sable,  Burke)  three  bird  bolts  in  fess  Argent. 

These  arms,  the  third  quartering  excepted,  appear  upon  the  monument  in  Rushbrook  church 
to  Thomas  Jermyn  Esqr,  who  died  in  1659.  When  Anne,  the  daughter  of  George  Heveningham, 
married  Sir  Ambrose  Jermyn,  she  added,  as  coheiress,  the  shields  of  Heveningham,  Jarvill,  Gissing, 
Redesham,  Reppes,  Burgon  and  Bozun  to  the  family  escutcheon. 

The  Crest  in  Harl.  MS.  1560  is  a  greyhound  passant  Argent,  collared  Or  and  eared  Sable. 
Two  variants  are  given  in  Burke’s  Armoury ;  a  greyhound’s  head  Sable  gorged  with  a  bar  gemelle 
Or ;  and  a  greyhound’s  head  proper  collared  Or. 

In  his  “  Rushbrook  Parish  Registers,”  the  Rev  Sydenham  H.  A.  Hervey  has  given  us  a 
delightful  history  of  the  Jermyns,  absolutely  readable,  with  endless  quotations  from  the  quaint  yet 
racy  manuscripts  upon  which  it  is  founded.  He  has  added  the  wills  and  many  portraits  of  the 
knights,  the  gentlemen,  the  esquires  and  the  peers  who  form  the  main  line  of  this  most  interesting 
family.  The  illustrations  of  Rushbrook  Hall,  the  fine  old  mansion  which  the  Jermyns  built,  add 
greatly  to  the  value  of  the  work. 

Like  most  early  descents,  the  pedigree  in  Harl.  MS.  1560,  said  to  be  based  upon  the 
Registers  of  the  Abbey  of  St.  Edmundsbury,  is  largely  conjectural.  That  the  families  of  Jermyn 
and  Rushbrook  were  closely  connected  is  rendered  probable  by  Rushbrook  wills  and  fines.  It 
would  almost  seem  that  the  John  Rushbrook,  who  calls  Jane  Jermyn  his  cousin  in  1514,  was 
identical  with  the  attorney  who  acted  for  Thomas  Jermyn  when  he  purchased  bis  Rushbrook 
estates.  These  and  other  evidences  which  we  subjoin,  relating  to  the  undoubted  descendants  of  this 
Thomas  Jermyn,  are  supplementary  to  those  printed  by  Mr.  Hervey.

By  an  Inquisition  taken  at  Swafham  Market,  in  Norfolk,  14th  May  21  H.  7,  it  was  found 

that  a  long  time  before  the  death  of  Thomas  Jermyn  named  in  the  brief  a  certain  Thomas  Darell 

* 

was  seized  of  the  Manor  of  Marham  in  the  same  county.  By  a  charter,  which  was  produced  in 
evidence,  he  settled  this  to  the  use  of  the  said  Thomas  Jermyn,  and  to  fulfil  the  intention  of 
his  last  will.  It  was  found  too  that  Thomas  Leeffe  and  Robert  Rolff,  who  were  seized  of  the 
Manor  of  Barowes  and  lands  in  West  Toftes,  co.  Norfolk,  by  their  charter,  also  produced,  enfeoffed 
them  to  Thomas  Jermyn  aforesaid.  Afterwards,  on  the  12th  of  January  1496,  Thomas  Jermyn 
made  his  will  at  Rushbrook,  devising  Manors  and  lands  to  his  executors  for  thirteen  years ;  the 
Manor  of  Marham  then  passing  to  Robert  Jermyn  and  Francis  Jermyn  his  sons  for  their  lives, 
with  remainder  to  Beatrice  and  Anastacia  Dorell,  the  daughters  and  heirs  of  the  abovenamed 
Thomas  Darell;  whilst  the  Manor  of  Barowes  and  the  lands  in  West  Tofts  were  to  devolve  on 
St.  Michael’s  Day  1506  upon  Thomas  Jermyn,  his  eldest  son.  Marham  was  held  of  the  King, 
as  of  his  Honour  of  Hagenet,  and  Barowes  and  the  West  Tofts  lands  of  the  Priory  of  Thetford. 
Thomas  Jermyn  the  father  died  on  the  tenth  of  October  last  past,  and  Thomas  Jermyn  his  son 
and  heir  was  then  of  the  age  of  twenty  three  years. 

Inquisitions  Post  Mortem,  C.,  Vol.  19,  96. 

At  a  similar  Inquisition  taken  in  Suffolk  in  the  same  year,  it  was  deposed  that  Thomas 
Jermyn  had  died  possessed  of  lands  and  tenements  in  lx  worth  and  Brorne  held  of  the  Priory 
of  Ixworth ;  a  piece  of  land  in  Bury  St.  Edmunds  called  Greenehough ;  lands  in  Oakley  held  of 
the  Abbey  of  Bury ;  lands  in  Hoxne  held  of  the  Bishop  of  Norwich ;  lands  in  Thurston  held  of 
John  Wodell ;  a  tenement  called  Harvies  held  of  the  Prior  of  Thetford ;  and  a  third  part  of 
the  Manor  of  Braham  held  of  the  King  as  of  his  Honour  of  Clare.  His  will  is  mentioned  in 
part;  but  the  document  is  much  defaced,  and  is  in  places  altogether  illegible. 

Inquisitions  Post  Mortem,  C.,  Yol.  19,  No.  95.

Inquisition  on  tb t  Dratlj  of  S>ix  Jlntbrose  Jn*ntgn,  1577. 

By  his  Inquisition  taken  at  Bury  9th  Aug.  19th  Elizabeth,  it  was  found  that  Sir  Ambrose 
Jermyn,  long  before  his  decease,  had  held  the  Manor  of  Rushbrook  in  Suffolk,  with  twenty 
messuages,  ten  tofts,  four  hundred  acres  of  arable  land,  &c.,  which  Thomas  Jermyn  (his  grand¬ 
father)  by  John  Rushbrook  his  attorney,  had  purchased  of  Henry  Tey  and  Margaret  his  wife.  He 
had  also  held  the  Manor  of  Little  Whelnetham  which  Robert  Sexteyn  had  bought  of  John 
Awdeley  and  then  passed  on  to  him.  The  said  Thomas  Jermyn,  by  his  will  dated  6th  July,  1503, 
devised  Little  Whelnetham  to  Thomas  Jermyn  his  son,  with  remainder,  failing  heirs  male  of  their 
bodies,  successively  to  Robert  Jermyn  and  Francis  Jermyn  his  sons,  and  to  his  next  heirs  without 
end  He  died  on  the  6th  day  of  July  aforesaid.  By  a  statute  of  uses  at  Westminster  4th  Feb. 
27th  Henry  VIII,  the  Manor  of  Rushbrook,  previously  held  by  trustees,  was  transferred  to  Thomas 
Jermyn,  then  a  Knight,  the  son  of  the  testator.  Sir  Thomas  Jermyn  died  13th  Octr,  7th  Edward  VI, 
and  the  premises  descended  to  Sir  Ambrose  Jermyn  as  his  son  and  heir.  Sir  Ambrose  acquired 
the  Advowson  of  Rushbrook  by  feoffment  of  William  Cordell  Esqr,  Solicitor  General  of  King  Philip 
and  Queen  Mary.  He  was  seized  too  of  the  Manors  of  Bradfield  Combust,  called  Bradfield  Hall, 
of  Stanton  and  Mykellfelde  Hall,  and  of  Berdewell  Hall,  which  came  to  him  on  his  father’s  death. 
He  bought  the  Manor  of  Hepworth,  with  foldage  and  free  warren  in  the  parishes  around,  of 
William  Spring  Esqre ;  and  the  Manors  of  Brent  Illeigli  and  Fenhall,  with  twenty  messuages  in 
Lavenham,  Preston,  Kettlebarston,  Myldinge,  Monkes  Iileigh  and  Waldingfield  Parva,  which  he  bought 
of  William  Humberston  Esqre.  He  inherited  from  Sir  Thomas  Jermyn  his  father  the  Manors  of 
Old  Hall  and  Le  Hoo,  the  woods  called  Bromeley  Wood,  Le  Wood,  Oldehall  Wood,  Burye  Wood

Death  of  John  Jerrnp,  of  fiqpDot,  1607. 

By  an  Inquisition  taken  at  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  upon  the  4tb  of  July  in  the  5th  year 
of  King  James,  on  the  death  of  John  Jermyn  Esqr,  it  was  found  that  long  before  his  decease 
Sir  Thomas  Jermyn,  Knfc,  his  father,  had  been  seized  of  the  Manor  of  Depden  and  of  lands 
and  tenements  in  Depden,  Reede,  Wyckham  brook,  ITengrave,  Chevington,  and  Chetbergh  in  the 
County  of  Suffolk,  and  of  the  advowson  of  the  Church  of  Depden ;  also  of  a  tenement  called 
Yauncyes  with  garden  and  lands.  So  seized  Sir  Thomas  Jermyn,  by  a  charter  dated  27th  October, 
38th  Henry  VIII,  settled  them  in  trust  to  his  own  use  for  life,  and  after  his  death  to  the 

use  of  Anne  his  then  wife  for  her  life,  with  remainder  to  John  Jermyn,  son  of  the  said 

Thomas  and  Anne,  and  to  his  heirs  males,  and  failing  these  to  Thomas  Jermyn,  another  of  the 
sons  of  said  Thomas  and  Anne,  and  then,  he  also  dying  without  issue  male,  to  the  right  heirs 
of  the  said  Sir  Thomas  Jermyn.  Sir  Thomas  died  at  Rushbrook  in  Suffolk  so  seized,  and 
Anne  his  widow  entered.  She  afterwards  died  at  Depden  and  John  Jermyn  named  in  the  brief 
succeeded.  He  purchased  other  lands  in  Depden,  and  in  Croxton,  co.  Norfolk.  So  seized  he 
died  at  Depden  on  the  25th  of  November  last.  Thomas  Jermyn  Esqr,  his  son  and  next  heir 
is  of  the  age  of  forty  six  years  and  upwards.  The  Manor  of  Depden  is  held  of  the  Earl  of 
Exeter,  as  of  his  Manor  of  Castle  Acre ;  and  the  Messuage  in  Croxton  of  the  Masters  and 

Fellows  of  Christ’s  College,  Cambridge.

Hdbma  HoDfoatj,  imk  of  Sljomas  Jmnun,  1629. 

We  are  indebted  to  Mr.  N.  E.  T.  Bosanquet  for  the  following  note,  which  is  based 
upon  entries  in  the  parish  registers  of  St.  Mary  Aldermary,  London.  Rebecca  Rodway,  wife 
successively  of  Thomas  Jermyn  of  Rushbrook  and  Henry,  third  and  last  Yiscount  Brouncker, 
was  the  only  child  of  William  Rodway,  citizen  and  merchant  tailor  of  London,  by  Rebecca  his 
wife,  who  remarried  Sir  Thomas  Trevor,  Lord  Chief  Baron  of  the  Exchequer.  In  his  will 
(P.C.C.  8  Ruthen),  proved  1656,  the  latter  mentions  his  “daughter  Jermin.”  Lady  Brouncker 
died  24th  January  1693-4,  and  was  buried  in  the  chancel  at  Rushbrook  under  a  marble  stone 
inscribed  to  her  memory.  The  register  describes  her  as  “  The  Honoble  Rebecca  Lady  Brounker 
(ye  Lord  Jermyn’s  mother).”  Her  will,  dated  13  May  1692,  is  given  in  full  in  Mr.  Hervey’s 
“  Rushbrook  Parish  Registers,”  already  alluded  to  on  page  243.  The  reference  to  William 
Rodway’s  will,  1626,  is  P.C.C.  48  Hele.  Sir  Matin  Lumley,  his  brother-in-law,  was  overseer.

Marie  Jermyn,  in  her  will  proved  in  the  Consistory  Court  at  Norwich,  7th  January  1545, 
desires  to  be  buried  in  the  church  of  St.  Andrew  before  oure  Ladie’s  aultare.  She  gives  bequests 
to  Margaret  Jermyn,  daughter  of  her  brother  Robert  Jermyn  ;  her  brother  Fraunces  Jermv  [sic]  ; 
her  brother  Sir  Thomas  Jermyn;  her  neve  Ambrose  Jermyn  and  her  nece  Margaret  Gardiner; 
and  appoints  Mr.  Frauncys  Jermyn  her  executor. 


Mill  of  Jlntte  Jrnnon,  1665. 

Anne  Jermyn  of  Ovington  in  the  county  of  Norfolk,  widow  of  Thomas  Jermyn  late  of 
Tofts,  Esquire,  4th  Septr  1665.  To  be  buried  by  the  bodies  of  her  nearest  friends  and  relatives 
in  the  parish  church  of  the  town  of  Brooke,  in  the  said  county,  where  she  was  born.  She 
leaves  her  lands  in  Ovington  and  Saham  Tony  to  Richard  Turner  of  Ovington  and  Anne  his 
wife,  her  grandchild.  She  also  bequeaths  ten  pounds  to  Thomas  Wright  of  Downham  in  the 
county  of  Suffolk  Esquire.  Proved  in  the  Archdeaconry  of  Norwich.

Armorial  Hearings. 

The  Arms  of  Garneys  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1561  were  Argent,  a  chevron  engrailed 
Azure,  between  three  escallops  Sable.  Harl.  MS.  155.  They  were  allowed  at  the  Suffolk  Visita¬ 
tion  of  1664,  with  a  crescent  for  difference,  to  John  Garneys,  of  Mickfield,  who  derived  from 
Thomas,  the  second  surviving  son  of  John  Garneys  and  Elizabeth  Sulyard.  Harl.  MS.  1085. 
They  are  carved  upon  the  marble  slab  which  covers  his  grave  within  the  altar  rails  at  Mickfield, 
impaled  with  those  of  his  wife,  Elizabeth  Atherold — Per  pale  Sable  and  Argent,  a  lion  passant 
counterchanged.  They  occur,  too,  upon  the  monuments  and  inscriptions  to  his  descendants  in 
Kenton  Church. 

The  Crest  of  Garneys  of  Kenton  was  an  arm,  erased  at  the  elbow  and  erect  proper, 
holding  a  scymeter  Argent,  hilt  and  pomel  Or,  the  blade  marked  with  blood  in  three  places. 
Edmondson’s  Heraldry.  The  mermaid  proper,  holding  her  comb  and  mirror,  was  allowed  to  Nicholas 
and  Edward  Garneys,  of  Redisham,  also  descendants  of  John  Garneys  and  Elizabeth  Sulyard,  in 
1664.  Harl.  MS.  1085.  In  Camden’s  Suffolk  Visitation,  1612,  her  hair  and  comb  are  described 
as  golden,  and  her  mirror  and  tail  as  silver.  Harl.  MS.  1820,  fol.  1/.3. 

For  further  information  relating  to  this  house  the  reader  is  referred  to  the  Garneys 
section  in  the  first  volume  of  this  work  (pp.  189 — 194),  where  pedigrees  of  all  the  recognised 
branches  will  be  found,  and  descriptions  of  the  quarterings  brought  into  the  family  by  the 
heiresses  of  Ramsay,  Franceys,  Sulyard  and  Bacon,  of  Baconsthorpe.

1  By  his  will  (Arch.  Suff.),  22d  Aug.  1706,  John  Garneys,  of  Debenham,  gentleman,  devised  to  Grace,  his  wife,  his  capital 
messuage  called  Greenwoods,  in  Mickfield,  for  her  jointure  ;  also  other  messuages  and  lands  in  Mickfield,  Stonham  Aspall  and 
Debenham,  to  maintain  and  educate  his  children,  John,  Charles,  Mary,  Grace  and  Elizabeth  Garneys.  On  her  decease  he  leaves 
his  farm  called  Hammonds,  in  Mickfield,  to  Mary,  his  daughter ;  lands  there  called  Falsham,  and  The  Heath  to  Grace,  his 
daughter;  and  Greenwoods  to  Martha,  his  daughter,  charged  with  annuities  to  his  sons.  There  are  bequests  to  his  sister 
Clodd  and  Thomas  Clodd  of  Kenton,  gent.,  her  husband,  and  to  their  daughters  Jane  and  Elizabeth  Clodd.  Grace,  his  wife, 
to  be  sole  executrix. 

2  By  his  will  (Arch.  Suff.),  dated  February  2d,  1797,  John  Garneys  of  Westleton,  co.  Suffolk,  surgeon,  confirms 

settlements  made  at  the  marriages  of  his  daughter  Elizabeth  with  John  Woodcock,  of  Halesworth,  merchant,  and  his 

daughter  Charlotte  with  the  Rev.  Mr.  William  Kett,  of  Melton,  in  Suffolk,  clerk.  He  gives  to  Elizabeth  Garneys,  his  wife, 

the  interest  of  £400,  the  use  of  his  plate  and  furniture,  and  the  residue  of  his  personal  estate.  To  the  said  William  Kett 
and  to  his  heirs  he  devises  his  lands  in  Yoxford  called  “  Candlers.”  To  his  nephew  Thomas  Garneys  of  Kenton,  ten  guineas 
for  mourning.  And  he  makes  the  aforesaid  John  Woodcock  and  William  Kett  his  executors.

The  Arms  allowed  to  the  Kebles  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664  were : — Barry  nebulee 
of  six  Argent  and  Sable,  a  canton  Gules.  The  Crest — A  demi-eagle  displayed  Argent,  charged 
on  the  breast  with  a  bar  nebulee  (some  say  a  bar  gemel)  Gules.  ( Harl .  MS.  1085).  These  were 
the  heraldic  insignia  of  the  Kebles  of  Homerston  in  Leicestershire  in  the  sixteenth  century  (Harl. 
MS.  1180),  but  it  is  doubtful  if  there  was  any  connection  between  the  families. 

At  the  same  Visitation  Thomas  Keble  of  Old  Newton,  descended  of  a  younger  son  of 
the  Stowmarket  house,  bore — Quarterly,  1  and  4.  Keble,  as  above,  with  a  crescent  for  difference, 
2  and  3.  Gules  a  griffin  segreant  Argent,  for  Went ;  whilst  the  shield  of  Richard  Keble,  Esq., 
of  Gray’s  Inn,  and  Creeting  All  Saints,  was  Keble,  with  a  crescent  on  the  canton ;  on  an 
inescutcheon  Quarterly,  1  and  4.  Argent,  a  chevron  between  three  griffins’  heads  erased  Sable, 
for  Cotton.  2  and  3.  Azure,  a  maunch  Or,  for  Coniers  of  Coniers  Manor  in  Great  Barton. 

On  the  Keble  monument  in  Tuddenham  chancel  are  shields  with  Sicklemore,  Per  chevron 
Argent  and  Sable,  in  chief  two  sickles  erect  of  the  second,  in  base  a  cockerell  Or,  and  Keble 
impaling  Sicklemore;  also  on  a  larger  escutcheon,  Quarterly  of  six.  1,  Keble.  2,  (1)  Croftes, 
Lozengy  Sable  and  Argent.  3,  (1)  Panell,  Argent,  three  chevrons  within  a  bordure  Gules. 
4,  (1)  King,  Argent  on  a  chevron  Sable  three  escallops  of  the  field.  5,  (1)  Fetiplace,  Gules,  three 
chevrons  Argent.  6,  Went,  as  above.  A  seventh  possible  quartering  may  have  been  Sicklemore. 

The  Croftes,  Panell,  King,  and  Fetiplace  marriages  occur  upon  the  doubtful  Keble  pedigree 
in  Add.  MS.  5524.  The  arms  of  these  heiresses  are  variants  of  those  assigned  to  the  names 
in  the  Armories.  Thus,  Croftes  of  Cheshire,  Lozengee  Argent  and  Sable,  is  given  as  Lozengee 
Sable  and  Argent;  Panell  of  Norfolk,  Gules  two  chevrons  within  a  bordure  engrailed  Argent,  as 
Argent  three  chevrons  within  a  bordure  Gules ;  and  so  throughout. 

The  doubtful  pedigree  seems  to  have  been  made  for  John,  son  and  heir  of  Richard  Keble, 
Esq.,  of  Gray’s  Inn,  in  1647.  An  amplified  copy,  much  decayed,  was  discovered  a  few  year’s 
since  in  a  disused  cupboard  of  the  Ancient  House  at  Ipswich,  and  is  now  in  the  possession  of 
Mr.  John  R.  Keeble,  of  Brantham  Hall.

Armorial  hearings. 


The  Arms  of  Pretyman,  Gules,  a  lion  passant  between  three 
mullets  Or,  were  first  set  out  at  the  burial  of  Christopher  Wase,  of 
London,  for  Anne,  his  wife,  daughter  of  William  Pretyman,  of  Bacton. 
They  are  recorded  by  Camden,  who  was  present  on  the  occasion,  in 
his  book  of  Funeral  Certificates,  still  remaining  in  the  office.  In  1607 
they  were  passed  by  Camden,  Clarencieux,  and  William  Segar,  Garter, 
to  Sir  John  Pretyman,  together  with  a  Crest,  Two  lions’  gambs  erased, 
holding  a  mullet,  all  Or.  Harl.  MS.  6095,  fo.  27.  At  the  Visitation 
of  Suffolk  in  1612  they  are  appended  to  the  pedigree  of  Pretyman, 
of  Thorndon.  Harl.  MS.  1820,  fo.  6J  b.  They  were  subsequently 
allowed  to  the  Pretymans  of  Norfolk  and  Suffolk,  by  Sir  Edward 
Bysshe,  at  his  Visitations  of  those  counties  in  1664.  There  still  exists 
(1905)  at  Horningold,  in  Leicestershire,  over  the  chimney  piece  of  the 
old  manor  house,  which  came  to  the  family  by  the  marriage  of  Sir 
John  Pretyman,  Baronet,  with  the  heiress  of  Sir  George  Turpin,  the 
fine  escutcheon,  painted  upon  panel,  which  heads  the  pedigree  of  the 
Driffield  Pretymans  (see  p.  311).  The  achievement  is  that  of  John 
Pretyman,  the  Baronet’s  eldest  son,  who  died  vita  patris.  Prety¬ 
man,  quarterly  of  seven,  impales  Mennes,  quarterly  of  four.  The 


shields  are  as  follows - 


1,  Pretyman— Gules,  a  lion  passant  between  three  mullets  Or;  in  chief  a  label  of  three 

points  Argent. 

2,  Howe,  of  Stowmarket. — Argent,  a  chevron  between  three  wolves’  heads  erased,  Sable, 

langued  Gules. 

3,  Turpin,  of  Knaptoft. — Gules,  on  a  bend  Argent  three  lions’  heads  erased,  Sable,  langued 

of  the  first. 

4,  Kinnesman,  of  Lodington. — Argent,  a  fess  chequee  Or  and  Sable  between  six  cross- 

crosslets  of  the  last. 

5,  Tilley. — Argent,  a  cross  botonee  between  four  crescents  Gules. 

6,  Paynkll,  of  Boothby  Pagnel. — Gules,  a  cross  fleurie  Argent. 

7,  Gobion,  of  Knaptoft. — Quarterly  of  four,  1  and  4,  Or,  2  and  3,  Barry  of  six  Argent 

and  Gules ;  all  within  a  bordure  Sable  semee  of  fishes  Argent.

The  above  for  Pretyman  impales  Mennes  :  Quarterly  of  four  : — 

1,  Mennes.— Gules,  a  chevron  Vair  between  three  leopards’  faces  Or. 

2.1  Stuart. — Or,  a  lion  rampant  within  a  double  tressure  fleurie  counter  fleurie  Gules ;  over 

all  a  ribbon  in  bend  sinister  Sable. 

3.1  —  Argent,  a  ship  within  a  double  tressure  fleurie  counter  fleurie  Azure. 

4,  Mennes.— As  above.

Will  of  William  Sjprrtpmatt,  147 

Extract  (translated)  from  the  Court  Rolls  of  Bacton  Manor,  Thursday  before  St.  Margaret’s 
Day,  Ao.  19th  Edward  IV.  (July  1479) 

John  Furmage  (Rector  of  Bacton)  and  William  Cake,  Executors  of  the  Will  of  William 
Pratyman,  dated  13  July  1475,  surrender  in  Court — 

Seven  acres,  half  a  rood  and  14  perches  of  demesne  land  called  Blakeloud. 

One  piece  of  meadow  called  Head  halfaker,  in  a  meadow  called  Le  Kur  (in  Wyverston). 
One  acre  of  meadow  in  divers  pieces,  late  in  the  farm  of  John  Blake  of  Cotton — 
and  the  same  John  Furmage  says  this  was  done  in  fulfilment  of  the  will  of  the  said  William 
Pratyman,  according  to  the  said  alienation  ...  to  the  use  of  the  Images,  Organs,1  and 
other  ornaments  of  Baketon  Church. 


Still  of  JUire  Cake,  born  frrfoman,  1488. 

Translation.  Alicia  Cake  in  pura  viduatate  mea  de  Baketon,  the  4th  day  of  February 
1487.  My  soul  to  God  Almighty,  the  Blessed  Virgin  Mary  and  all  the  Saints.  My  body  to 
be  buried  in  the  churchyard  of  the  Blessed  Mary  of  Baketon.  To  the  high  altar  of  the 

church  there  for  tithes  omitted  xijd.  To  the  cathedral  church  of  Norwich  iiijd.  To  Jofiane 
Symmonds  my  daughter  four  pieces  of  land,  of  which  the  one  piece  was  of  Stephen  Hesset  in 

Baketon.  The  second  piece,  which  late  was  of  Roger  Mey,  lies  in  a  field  called  Marlecroft  in 

the  town  of  Cotton,  between  lands  of  John  Olyve  of  one  part,  and  lands  of  the  Bishop  of 

Norwich  of  the  other.  The  third  piece,  formerly  John  Olyves,  lies  in  the  said  field  and  town 

of  Cotton.  The  fourth  piece,  with  a  small  piece  of  pasture  in  Cotton  field  in  Marlecroft,  lies 

between  land,  late  of  William  Wyngefeld,  Esqr,  and  one  head  abuts  on  land  formerly  of  John 
Revet.  All  these  four  pieces  of  land,  with  one  piece  of  pasture  and  one  pightell,  William 
Pratyman  my  father  gave  to  me  and  John  Revet  my  husband  deceased  in  fee  simple,  as  by 
Charter  of  the  said  William  to  me  and  the  said  John  more  fully  appears.  The  said  pightel 

called  Goodlardes  lies  in  Baketon  between  a  pasture  of  John  Hervy  late  of  Cotton,  on  the 

north,  and  a  lane  leading  from  the  common  way  to  Marlecroft,  on  the  south.  I  give  and 
bequeath  to  the  said  Jofiane  Symmonds  the  said  four  pieces  of  ground,  the  pasture  and  the 

pightell  ;  out  of  the  profits  of  the  last  a  light  to  be  kept  before  the  Image  of  our  Ladye 

St.  Mary  of  Pety  in  Baketon  church,  during  her  life.  Said  daughter  Jofiane  to  bring  up  my 

son  Thomas,  and  to  find  and  keep  him  in  all  things ;  and  said  Thomas  to  obey  her. 

The  residue  I  bequeath  to  the  said  Jofiane,  and  she  to  buy  a  book  or  other  ornament 
of  use  for  Baketon  church,  and  to  pray  for  the  souls  of  John  Cake  and  John  Revet  my 
husbands,  my  parents,  and  all  benefactors.  I  make  said  Jofiane  sole  executor  of  this  will,  and 
appoint  James  Hobart,  gentleman,  and  John  Firmage,  clerk,  supervisors.  Witnesses,  my  spiritual 
father  the  Rector  of  Baketon,  Nicholas  Garnon  and  John  Reddham.  Proved  at  Baketon 
10th  March  1488.  Cur.  Ep.  Norw.  Liber,  “  Hubert,”  80b.

Iitqmsition  on  tlje  teatlj  of  William  Prtfgman,  1617. 

Suffolk.  By  an  Inquisition  taken  at  Ipswich  on  the  22d  day  of  January  in  the  15th  year 
of  King  James  it  was  found  that  William  Pretyman,  gentleman,  had  died  seised  of  a  messuage 
called  Bouncers  in  Backton,  and  of  a  close  and  other  lands  in  Cotton  and  Fynyngham,  parcell 
of  the  Manor  of  Cotton  Bresworth,  and  of  the  Manor  and  advowson  of  Cotton  Bresworth.  The 
said  William,  so  seized,  on  the  9th  of  August  in  the  first  year  of  King  James,  and  in  consideration 
of  a  marriage  previously  solemnized  between  Peter  Pretyman,  his  son  and  heir  apparent  and 
Anne  Harwell,  daughter  of  Thomas  Harwell,  gent.,  and  for  the  jointure  of  the  said  Anne,  by 
a  certain  indenture  enfoeffed  all  the  above  premises,  in  trust  for  the  use  of  the  said  William 
Pretyman  and  Peter  Pretyman  during  their  respective  lives.  If  it  happened  to  Peter  Pretyman 
to  die  in  his  father’s  life  time,  the  premisses  to  remain  to  the  use  of  the  said  Anne,  and  after  her 
death  to  pass  to  William  Pretyman  again  :  after  the  deaths  of  both  William  and  Anne,  to  pass  to 
the  right  heir  of  the  said  Peter.  Said  William  Pretyman  before  his  death  was  seized  of  another 
messuage  in  Backton  with  twenty  acres  of  land,  and  of  another  called  Dixies  in  Backton  with 
three  acres  of  land.  These  by  his  Indenture  dated  18th  May,  5th  James,  he  enfoeffed  to  Thomas 
Smyth  and  Edward  Copuldyke,  gent.,  for  the  use  of  himself  for  life,  and  after  his  decease  to 
the  use  of  Margaret,  his  wife,  for  her  life,  and  then  to  the  use  of  the  said  Peter  Pretyman 
and  his  heirs.  William  Pretyman  died  on  the  8th  of  July  in  the  15th  year  of  King  James, 
and  Peter  Pretyman  his  son  and  next  heir  was  then  of  the  age  of  forty  years  and  upwards. 
Margaret,  late  his  wife,  and  Anne,  the  wife  of  the  said  Peter  Pretyman,  are  yet  living.  The 
messuage  called  Bouncers  was  held  of  Sir  John  Pretyman,  Knt.,  as  of  his  Manor  of  Backton. 
The  Manor  and  advowson  of  Cotton  Bresworth  were  held  of  the  King  in  capite.  The  other 
messuages  were  held  as  of  the  Manor  of  Backton. 

Inq.  p.m.,  P.R.O.,  C.  364,  83.

(Mill  of  Pretgman,  1656. 

The  seauenth  day  of  August  1636,  I  Peter  Prettiman  of  Barton  Bendysh  in  the  County 
of  Norfolk,  gentleman,  doe  make  this  my  last  will.  I  giue  to  the  poore  of  Barton  Bendishe  fiue 

poundes ;  to  the  poore  of  Bacton  in  Suff.  fiue  poundes ;  to  the  poore  of  Cotton  in  Suff.  fiue 

poundes.  Ynto  my  Honorable  freind  Sr  John  Hare  and  to  his  Honorable  Ladie,  (to  each) 
twentie  poundes,  as  a  small  token  &  remembrance  of  my  love.  Ynto  my  cossen  Augustin 
Messenger  and  my  niece  his  wife  ffortie  poundes.  Vnto  Margarett  Prettyman,  daughter  of 
Charles  Prettyman  deceased,  forty  poundes.  I  stand  bound  to  leaue  vnto  Elizabeth  my  nowe 
wife  landes  or  tenementes  within  the  Counties  of  Suff.  or  Norfolk  of  the  cleei'e  yearely  value 

of  ffortie  poundes  for  life.  And  to  the  intent  (she)  shall  not  claim  any  dower  out  of  my 

Mannors  or  landes,  I  do  giue  (her)  duringe  her  life  the  messuage  wherein  John  Spaldinge  now 
dwelleth,  with  all  landes  belonginge,  scituate  in  Backton  aforesaid.  I  giue  (her)  one  other 
tenement  with  the  homestalles  and  crofte  adioyninge  in  Backton,  nowe  in  the  occupacon  of 
Lawrence  Lord,  (and)  twenty  poundes  in  money  and  all  my  plate ;  alsoe  such  goodes  as  were 
her’s  before  our  entermarriage.  The  Revercon  of  said  premisses  shall  descend  vnto  my  sonne 
George  Prettyman  and  his  heires.  And  the  inheritance  of  my  Mannor  of  Cotton  hall,  and  of 
all  other  my  Mannors,  lands  and  tenements  in  Suffolk,  shall  likewise  descend  to  him.  I  alsoe 
giue  vnto  (him)  twoe  thousand  poundes  in  money.  My  said  sonne  George  shall  confirme  my 
guifte  and  bequest  formerly  giuen  vnto  my  wife.  I  ordaine  my  sonne  Tristram  Dymond  and 
my  lovinge  brother  Richard  Prettyman  my  executors  of  this  my  last  will.  A  Codicill  made 
the  11th  of  August  1636  and  annexed  vnto  (his)  will.  My  mynde  is  that  George  Pretyman 
my  sonne  shall  haue  all  my  leases  and  stock  in  Marshland,  and  also  my  stock  in  the  Loyes 
in  Fincham  in  the  Countie  of  Norfolke. 

Probatum  nono  die  Februarij  1636.  Juramento  Tristram  Dymond  et  Richi  Pretiman 
Executorum.  P.C.C.  27  Goare.

in  Wickham  Skeith,  co.  Suff.,  and  of  lands  holden  of  the  manor  of  Cotton  Hemnall.  Said

these  lands  should  remain  to  the  sd  John  Pretyman.  He  also  surrendered  copyholds  and  shortly

of  sd  John,  entered  as  guardian  and  died  about  9  years  later,  John  being  still  in  his  minority. 
Peter  Pretyman  made  his  will  19th  July  1554.  He  gave  Katherine  his  wife  lands  in  Bacton,

Suffolk  Assizes  against  William  Pretyman  for  entering  closes  devised  by  the  said  John. 

Answer  of  William  Pretyman,  24  January  1598.  Peter  Pretyman  did  make  said  will ; 
and  John  Pretyman,  who  was  father  to  Margaret  Harrison,  and  elder  brother  to  this  Defendant 
also  made  a  will,  dated  2d  Sept.  30th  Elizabeth,  devising  lands  to  Katherine  his  wife  for  life, 
with  remainder  to  this  Defendant,  who  was  to  pay  the  said  Margaret  £300,  and  to  William 
and  John  Dunkine  £30  each.  In  July,  35th  Elizabeth,  George  and  Margaret  Harrison  accepted 
this  £300.  Katherine,  his  widowe,  still  liveth. 

Further  answer  of  William  Pretyman,  Gent.,  Junr,  16  May  1599.  Thomas  Pretyman  was 
his  grandfather,  and  dyed  before  he  was  born.  John  Pretyman,  his  other  grandson,  who  was 
eldest  son  of  Peter,  and  elder  brother  to  this  Defendant,  was  then  thirteen  or  fourteen  years  old.

Answer  of  Sir  George  Pretyman,  Knt.  : — 

This  defendant  saith  that  he  believeth  itt  is  very  well  knowne  to  this  Defendant’s  said 
Father,  that  this  defendant  was  as  deepely  engaged  in  that  undertaking  as  the  Complaynant 
was,  and  was  in  greater  danger  than  his  sayd  Father,  being  taken  prisoner  in  the  service;  and 
afterwards  inakinge  his  escape,  was  constreyned  to  fly  beyond  the  sea  for  safety  of  his  life,  and 
to  abide  there  till  near  about  the  restitution  of  his  Majesty ;  and  therefore  there  is  noe 
probability  that  his  sayd  Father  would  thinke  the  estate  protected  in  this  Defendant’s  name.

Feby.  1st  1668,  London.  Letter  of  George  Pretyman  to  Mr.  Burdenand : — 

I  am  frustrated  by  my  father  in  my  endeavours,  though  made  chiefly  for  his  advantage. 
He  tries  to  persuade  the  Commissioners  that  I  detain  the  estate,  and  prevent  the  satisfying  of 
the  King’s  debt.  I  am  resolved  to  make  no  further  efforts  to  procure  my  father’s  freedom,  but 
to  secure  my  own  estate  against  his  pretensions,  and  leave  him  to  take  his  own  course.

Thomas  Pretyman  the  Elder  of  Bacton,  the  5th  day  of  December,  1600.  To  the  poor  who 
attend  my  burial  28  each.  I  bequeath  to  my  wife  Rachel  £53.  13.  4  issuing  out  of  lands,  etc.,  in  Cotton 
to  be  paid  yearly,  also  household  effects.  To  my  son  Robert  Pretyman  £100  ;  to  my  son  John 
Pretyman  £100 ;  and  to  my  daurs :  Martha  and  Mary  £200  each.  To  my  son  in  law  Robfc  Richmond ; 
my  grandchild  Richard  Woodward ;  Thos :  Armyger  and  Thos :  Auston  my  grand  children,  and  all  my 
grand  children.  To  my  daughters  Martha  and  Mary  aforesaid,  and  daughters  Woodward,  Gooche,  Armiger. 
To  brother  William  Pretyman;  nephew  John  Wartlock ;  Robert  Clarke  my  kinsman;  my  niece  lioldero; 
and  to  my  sister  Whatlock.  Residuary  legatee  &  executor  my  eldest  son  Thomas  Pretyman ;  the  exorship 
conditionally  upon  his  properly  carrying  out  sd  Will  ;  otherwise  my  wife  Rachel  and  my  bro’  Harwell 
of  Felsham ;  Overseer  my  brother  John  Pretyman.  Signed  Thomas  Pretyman. 

Original  Will,  Norwich  Consistory,  1600,  file  118. 


Kill  of  (Seorge  freeman,  1686. 

George  Pretyman  of  Bacton,  co.  Suffolk,  gentleman,  this  14th  day  of  March  1686.  To  Peter 
Pretyman  my  sonne ;  Thomas  Pretyman  my  sonne ;  Tirell  Pretyman  my  sonne ;  .  Cudden  my  sonne 

in  law ;  John  Frere  my  sonne  in  law.  To  George  Pretyman  my  grandson,  whom  I  make  my  sole 
executor,  all  my  personal  property.  The  will  was  proved  in  the  Court  of  the  Archdeacon  of  Sudbury 
22d  August  1688.

llkaumont  of  JMtieston. 


Armorial  Searings. 

At  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664  (Harl.  MS.  1085)  the  shield  of  John  Beaumont  of 
Bildeston  was  Azure  semee  of  fleurs  de  lis,  a  lion  rampant  Or ;  on  the  lion’s  shoulder  a  mullet 
for  difference  :  Crest,  a  lion  passant  Or,  also  with  a  mullet  on  the  shoulder.  The  same  arms 
were  allowed  to  Joseph  Beaumont  of  Hadley,  differenced  by  a  martlet,  and  to  William  Beaumont 
of  Hadley,  with  a  crescent  on  the  lion’s  shoulder  charged  with  a  mullet. 

It  is  stated  in  connection  with  these  shields,  but  upon  insufficient  evidence,  that  these 
Beaumonts  came  “  out  of  Leicester.” 

On  the  slab  in  the  south  aisle  of  Bildeston  Church,  in  memory  of  John  Beaumont  and 
Susan  his  wife,  1641,  are  the  arms  of  Beaumont  as  above,  impaling  Ermine  a  cross  bow  erect 
for  Alabaster.  The  Beaumont  shield  appears  also  on  the  monuments  to  Joseph  Beaumont  and 
John  Beaumont  in  Hadleigh  Church,  to  Robert  Beaumont  and  William  Beaumont  in  St.  Mary 
Tower  Church,  Ipswich,  to  Charles  Beaumont  in  Witnesham  Church,  and  to  Benjamin  Beaumont 
in  Grundisburgh  Church,  all  in  the  county  of  Suffolk. 

Of  quite  another  family  was  John  Beaumont,  S.T.P.,  Rector  of  Hadleigh  and  Whatfield, 
1592-1599.  He  bore  Gules,  a  lion  rampant  within  an  orle  of  crescents  Argent,  being  the  arms 
of  Beaumont  of  Whitley,  co.  York,  quarterly  with  Argent,  on  a  bend  Sable  three  owls  of  the 
first,  for  Savile.  See  the  Tillotson  MS.,  fo.  392b,  now  in  the  custody  of  the  Society  of  Anti¬ 
quaries,  and  Foster’s  Pedigrees  of  Yorkshire  Families.

Roberte  Beamonte  of  Bildeston,  in  the  Countie  of  Suff,  clothyar,  calling  to  remembraunce  the
