of  issue  of  his  bodye,  to  Thomas  Beamont  my  sonne  ;  and  for  default  of  issue  of  his  bodye  to 
Henry  Beamont  my  sonne  ;  and  for  default  of  yssue  of  his  bodie  to  Julyan  Beamont  my  sonne. 
And  yf  it  happen  all  my  saide  sonnes  to  dye  whrate  issue,  then  I  will  said  tenement  and 
landes  remayne  to  my  next  heire  forever.  I  will  that  Alice  my  wief  shall  have  a  cotage  at 
the  townes  ende  with  a  close  called  Havelles  and  other  londes  and  medowes  in  Hecham  and

berston  to  Henry,  my  sonn.  To  Thomas  my  sonne  with  the  bequest  of  Robert  Lofekyn  vi1  viij8

The  xxth  daye  of  December,  1586,  I  Julion  Beamonde  of  Hadley,  in  the  county  of

God,  and  my  bodye  to  the  earth  whence  I  was  taken  ovvte,  in  hope  of  the  glorious  appearing 

of  our  Savyour  Jesus  Christ.  To  Sara  my  wiffe  and  her  heires  all  my  houses  in  Hadley,  which 

I  late  boughte  of  Mr.  Edward  Clerke.  I  give  her  three  hundreth  pounds.  To  Edward 

Beamond,  my  eldest  sonne,  twoe  hundreth  pounds  at  the  age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares.  To  John 

Beamond,  my  yonger  sonne,  two  hundreth  pounds  at  his  age  of  one  and  twenty  yeares.  To 

Sara  Beamond,  my  daughter,  one  hundreth  pounds  at  her  age  of  twenty  yeares.  To  Thomas 
Beamonde,  my  vncle,  of  Bildeston,  fower  poundes.  To  William  Boggas,  my  brother,  tenne  pounds. 
To  Mr.  Dootor  Crick,  my  brother  in  lawe,  twentye  pounds.  To  Mr.  Doctor  Chapman,  preacher 
of  the  churche  of  Deadham,  ffive  pounds.  To  Mr.  John  Holden,  preacher  of  the  Church  of 

Billesdon,  ffive  poundes.  To  vse  of  the  poore  people  of  Hadlye  tenne  poundes,  to  buye  woode  in 

the  somraer  so  that  the  poore  may  have  it  in  the  winter  for  theire  money  as  good  clieape  as  it 

was  boughte  in  the  Sohier :  and  so  to  continewe  for  ever.  To  the  Churche  of  Hadlye  the  book© 

of  Actes  and  Monumentes  of  the  churche  of  god  collected  by  Mr.  Foxe,  there  to  remaine  for 
ever.  The  rest  of  my  goodes  I  bequeath  to  Sara  my  wiffe  to  the  bringing  vpp  of  my  children  in 
the  feare  of  god,  and  to  sett  them  to  schoole  to  wrighte  and  to  reade.  I  make  [her]  my 
executor,  and  my  brother  in  lawe,  William  Wade  of  Bidleston,  to  be  my  superViso1-.  If  it  shall 
please  god  that  Sara  my  wiffe  contracte  herself  in  manage  with  any  man,  my  minde  is  that  my

ffather  in  lawe,  shall  demaunde  a  good  assurannce  in  severall  bonds  to  eche  of  them  to  the 

performance  of  this  will.  These  being  witnesses  to  this  will  :  By  me  Michaell  Beamond,  Arthure

at  full  length  in  the  Bildeston  Manor  Books,  in  the  minutes  of  a  Special  Court  Baron  held 
1st  September  1760.  John  Beaumont,  late  of  Aldham,  co.  Suffolk,  gentleman,  testator’s  eldest 
son,  had  surrendered  in  1737  lands  called  Cook’s  Croft  and  Great  Ponders,  to  his  own  use  for 
life,  then  to  John  Beaumont  of  Sproughton,  his  only  son,  and  Mary  Yesey,  this  son’s  intended 
wife,  for  their  lives,  and  then  to  the  right  heirs  of  his  said  son  for  ever.  The  son  died 
without  issue  a  few  years  later  (leaving  lands  to  William  Betts,  his  nephew,  son  of  his  late 
sister,  Anne  Betts),  and  Mary  Vesey,  now  his  widow,  remarried  John  Yere,  Esq.,  of  Norwich. 
Betts  claimed  the  copyholds  and  was  admitted.  But  Jonathan  Beaumont,  son  and  heir  of 
Jonathan  Beaumont,  late  of  Lavenham,  the  second  son  of  John  Beaumont,  the  testator  of  1725, 
and  the  right  heir  male  to  his  childless  cousin,  John  Beaumont  of  Sproughton,  demanded  his 
legitimate  reversions.  These  were  allowed.  All  parties  united  in  a  Common  Recovery  to  enable 
the  estate  to  be  sold,  and  the  conflicting  claims  to  be  equitably  settled.

1  Joseph  Beaumont,  the  eldest  son  of  John  Beaumont,  of  Hadleigh,  and  Sarah  Clarke,  was  author  of  “  Psyche,  An 
Allegorical  Epic,”  and  other  poeuis,  and  one  of  the  best  scholars  of  his  age.  He  became  Chaplain  to  Charles  II  in  1660; 
Master  of  Peterhouse,  Cambridge,  in  1663 ;  and  Professor  of  Divinity  at  that  University  in  1670.  He  continued  to  discharge 
the  duties  of  this  office  until  his  eighty-fourth  year,  and  died  23d  Nov.  1699.  See  the  abstract  of  his  will  on  page  326.

Will  of  Shorn  as  ikanmont,  1582. 

I  Tliomas  Beaumonde,  Citizen  and  Alderman  of  Norwich,  make  this  my  last  will  and 

testament,  this  8th  daye  of  November  1582.  I  desire  to  be  buried  in  Sc  Andrew’s  church  nere 
unto  my  pevve  there.  I  give  to  Anne  my  wife  my  capitall  messuage  which  I  dwell  in,  and 
my  orchard  called  Sl  Cuthbert’s  and  lands  and  tenements  in  Carrowe.  To  my  daughter  Elizabeth 
and  to  Thomas,  Richard  and  Elizabeth,  her  children  To  Marie  and  Elizabeth  Nods,  children 

of  my  daughter  Marie  Nods,  deceased.  To  Suzan  my  daughter,  now  ye  wife  of  Robert  Play- 

forde,  and  to  each  of  her  daughters,  Anne  and  Cecilie.  Unto  Margaret  Beaumont  my  daughter 
my  lease  in  bowses  in  Norwich,  in  Holme  Street,  of  the  Mayor  and  Corporation ;  Anne  my 
wife  to  be  her  guardian.  To  Thomas  Lowen  my  sonne  in  lawe  and  to  Elizabeth  his  daughter. 
To  Peter  Beamond  my  brother.  To  Thomas  Farror  my  brother.  I  bequeath  unto  Thomas 
Beamond,  sonne  of  Robert  Beamond  my  brother,  and  to  his  heires  for  ever,  my  lands  in 
Southwold  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolk.  And  of  this  will  I  ordeyne  Anne  my  wife  to  be  the 
sole  executrix. 

This  will  was  proved  in  the  Consistorial  Court  at  Norwich  on  the  22d  day  of  April 

1583  by  the  oath  of  the  Executrix. 

Cur.  Ep.  Norwic,  Liber  “  Bate,”  fo.  202.

Stubbing  of  Jlauglitoti, 


Armorial  Scarings* 

The  Arms  of  Stubbing  of  Essex,  as  depicted  on  the  “  New  Mapp  of  Middlesex,  Essex 
&  Herts,”  1720,  were  a  chevron  between  three  pickaxes,  in  “canting”  allusion,  as  it  is 
technically  termed,  to  the  stubbing  up  of  roots  and  undergrowths  in  that,  at  one  time,  wood¬ 
land  county  (see  Probert’s  Index  to  Pedigrees  and  Arms  of  Essex,  Add.  MS.  33,528,  fo.  1 63b). 
The  Arms  of  Stubbing  of  Suffolk,  engraved  upon  the  silver  of  Josiah  Stubbing,  who  was  buried 
in  Naughton  chancel  in  1686,  and  alluded  to  in  the  Will  of  his  grandson,  John  Stubbing  of 
Ray  don,  1769,  were  Gules,  a  cinquefoil  between  three  cross  crosslets  Argent;  and  his  Crest  was 
a  demi-ostrich  displayed,  holding  in  its  beak  a  key,  all  proper.  The  Book  Plate  mentioned  by 
Davy  in  his  “Suffolk  Armoury,”  is  that  of  John  Stubbing  of  Higham,  circa  1785. 

The  Stubbings  of  Bumpsted  Helion,  many  of  whom  were  buried  in  the  parish  Church,, 
were  Essex  landowners  from  the  fifteenth  century  downwards.  They  spread  into  the  adjoining 
counties  of  Cambridgeshire  and  Suffolk,  and  formed  a  well  defined  clan,  so  to  speak,  in  which  the 
Christian  name  of  Edmund  was  much  used.  In  the  earlier  part  of  the  seventeenth  century  there 
were  at  least  three  Edmund  Stubbings  among  the  beneficed  clergy  in  the  Eastern  Counties.  One 
was  Rector  of  Datchworth  in  Hertfordshire  in  1622;  another  Rector  of  Rampton,  near  Cambridge, 
in  1632;  and  a  third  Rector  of  Naughton,  in  Suffolk,  from  1594  to  1638.

The  messuages  bequeathed  by  the  testator  to  his  three  sons,  John,  Richard  and  William, 
remained  long  in  the  possession  of  his  descendants.  In  1574,  John,  the  youngest  son  of  John, 
left  Crookes  and  Harts  to  his  heirs.  Weegens  passed  from  Richard  to  his  son  William  (both  are 
named  as  residents  of  Bumpsted  Helion,  circa  1546,  in  the  Essex  Subsidy  Roll,  numbered  |-|A). 
And  this  William,  who  had  meanwhile  acquired  the  Manors  of  Bobulo  and  Bumpsted  Hall, 
settled  it,  in  1586,  upon  Henry  Stubbing,  one  of  his  younger  children.  [Chancery  Proceedings, 
Stubbyn  c  Stubbyn,  Mitford  vi,  161.]  As  late  as  1607  we  find  a  William  Stubbing  possessed 
of  Broadcroft,  Heywards,  Taillors,  Cockrells  aker  and  Sages,  the  inheritance  of  William,  the 
third  son  of  the  testator  of  1553.

called  Sages  was  a  fief  of  the  Masters  and  Fellows  of  the  Savoy ;  and  that  known  as  Mosses,

Mill  of  Militant  Stubbing,  1599. 

I  Willam  Stubbin  of  Stansfield  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolke,  this  8th  daye  of  October  in 
the  41st  yeare  of  the  raigne  of  Queen  Elizabeth,  beinge  of  good  minde  and  remembrance, 
praised  be  God  therefore,  knowing  the  estate  of  all  men  to  be  fraile  and  mortall,  and  soe  the 
time  of  death  to  be  uncertaine,  doe  ordaine,  make  and  declare  this  my  last  will.  That  is  say, 
I  comend  my  soule  to  Allmightie  God  my  Creator  and  to  Jesus  Christ  my  Redeemer,  and  my 
bodie  to  be  buried  in  the  Churchyard  of  Stansfield  aforesaid.  I  give  and  bequeath  to  Joan  my 

wife  my  moietie  and  halfe  gte  in  the  two  tenements,  the  one  whereof  is  called  Hatches  and  the 

other  Lausels,  with  the  land  and  pasture  belonging,  to  her  for  her  natural  life :  and  I  give  her 
the  use  of  all  my  household  stuffe. 

Unto  Edmund  Stubbin,  my  eldest  sonne  I  bequeath  my  abovenamed  moietie  of  Hatches 
and  Lausels,  on  my  wifes  decease,  with  the  lands  and  pastures  aforesaid.  I  give  unto  Richard 
my  sonne  tenne  poundes.  When  Edmund  my  sonne  has  the  whole  right  in  Lausells,  he  is  to 
make  an  assurance  of  part  of  it  to  my  said  sonne  Richard ;  and  if  Richard  die  without  issue 
then  it  is  to  return  to  Edmund. 

Unto  Ambrose  Stubbin  my  sonne  twenty  shillings  yearlie  for  his  life.  To  Joan  and  Agnes, 

my  daughters,  to  either  of  them  the  surae  of  fiive  poundes.  On  the  decease  of  Joane  my  saide 

wife,  the  household  goodes  to  be  equallie  pted  betwene  my  sonne  Ambrose  and  my  two  daughters. 
To  everie  poore  person  in  Stansfield  the  sume  of  iiijd  to  be  payed  on  my  buriall  daye.  My  sonne 
Edmonde  Stubbin  to  be  sole  executor.  Witnesses,  WilPm  Smith,  Willam  Grimwoode.  Proved  at 
Lavenham  22d  June  1602  by  the  executor.  Bury  Wills,  1600-5,  fo.  131.

Decimo  quinto  die  Februarij,  1634,  I  Edmond  Stubbin  of  Nawton  in  the  countie  of 
Suffolke,  clerke,  being  in  healthe  of  boddye  and  in  pfecte  mynde  and  remembrance,  thankes  be 
to  god  therfore,  yet  knoweiug  death  to  be  uncerteyne,  I  doe  make  this  my  last  will  and 
testament.  First  and  principally  I  bequeath  my  soule  into  the  handes  of  God  my  Creator  and 
mercifull  father,  and  to  Jesus  Christ  my  Saviour  and  redeemer,  and  unto  the  blessed  spiritt 
my  sanctifier  and  comforter,  in  assured  hope,  after  this  miserable  life  ended,  to  live  with  them 
in  eternytie  of  glory.  And  this  my  earthly  bodie  I  comitt  unto  the  earth,  the  comon  mother 
of  us  all,  to  be  buried  where  it  shall  please  god  in  his  providence  to  order,  in  assured  hope 
of  the  resurrection  of  it  at  that  last  and  great  daye,  to  be  made  like  unto  Christ’s  glorious 

bodie.  And  as  for  that  portion  of  goodes  it  hath  pleased  God  to  lend  me  in  this  frail  life, 

I  doe  thus  order  and  dispose  of  it : — My  loveing  wife  J ane  Stubbin  to  have  all  such  goods 
and  implements  as  she  brought  me  at  her  marriage ;  and  she  is  to  enjoy  her  thirds  out  of  all 

my  lands  &c.  To  my  sonne  Samuel  Stubbin  my  ancient  tenement  in  Stansfield  called  Lawsells, 

which  was  my  father’s  and  grandfather’s,  in  reversion  on  the  death  of  his  uncle  Richard  Stubbin, 
my  brother,  to  him  and  his  heirs  for  ever.  I  give  him  also  all  my  books  except  Aretius  on

Sarah  Coleman,  one  of  the  children  of  Joseph  Coleman,  clerk,  by  his  former  wife,  the  sum  of 
£100  at  her  age  of  twenty  one  years.  To  Joseph  and  Francis  Coleman,  two  other  of  the 
children  of  Joseph  Coleman,  clerk,  by  his  said  former  wife,  £100  apiece.  And  to  Richard 
Newman  and  Elizabeth  Newman,  son  and  daughter  of  Richard  Newman  of  Kersey  in  Suffolk, 
and  also  to  Thorney  [Thornhagh]  Gurdon,  son  of  Philippa  Guidon  of  Hadleigh,  widow,  and 
Letitia  Gurdon,  daughter  of  said  widow',  the  sum  of  £100  apiece,  to  be  paid  after  the  decease 
of  the  said  John  Stubbin.  I  give  the  Manor  of  Georges,  otherwise  called  Castells,  with  the 
scite  of  the  same  Manor,  and  all  rights,  messuages,  meadows,  pastures  and  woods  to  the  same 
belonging,  situate  in  Thorpe  Morieux,  unto  George  Clarke  of  Hadleigh,  during  the  term  of  his 
life,  and  after  his  decease  to  my  Executors,  in  trust,  to  sell  the  same.  I  direct  the  money 
arising  thereby  to  be  equally  divided  amongst  the  children  of  the  said  George  Clarke,  Sarah 
Coleman,  Joseph  and  Frances  Coleman,  Richard  and  Elizabeth  Newman,  Thorney  Gurdon  and 
Letitia  Gurdon,  share  and  share  alike.  I  appoint  my  said  husband  and  John  Wall  of  Holton 
in  Suffolk,  gentleman,  Executors.  The  residue  of  lands,  etc.,  and  all  my  personal  estate  I 
bequeath  unto  the  use  of  my  said  husband,  John  Stubbin,  his  heirs  and  executors.  In  witness 
whereof  I  set  my  seal. 

Stratford,  8th  July  1765,  John  Stubbin,  one  of  the  executors  within  named,  was  sw'orn 
faithfully  to  execute  this  will. 

Archdeaconry  of  Suffolk. 

The  testatrix,  a  descendant  of  the  knightly  family  of  Brand  of  Boxford,  was  John 
Stubbing’s  second  wife.  She  was  cousin  german  to  George  Clarke  of  Hadleigh  and  his  sisters 
Elizabeth  and  Philippa,  who  married,  respectively,  Richard  Newman  and  the  Rev.  Parker 
Gurdon.  She  names  their  children,  Elizabeth  Newman,  Thornhagh  Gurdon  and  Letitia  Gurdon. 
Elizabeth  Newman  became  the  third  wife  of  John  Stubbing,  the  testatrix’s  husband,  while 
Letitia  Gurdon  married  Vero  Kemball,  great  grandfather  to  the  present  Lady  Tollemache.  The 
Clarkes  were  children  of  the  Rev.  George  Clarke,  Rector  of  Raydon,  a  well  known  clergyman 
of  his  day,  who  married  Elizabeth  Brand,  the  aunt  of  the  writer  of  the  will.  See  the  pedigree 
of  Gurdon  of  Assington,  Suffolk  Manorial  Families,  vol.  i,  287. 


Still  of  (SUjabetlj  Stubbing,  1771. 

I,  Elizabeth  Stubbin,  of  Higham  in  the  county  of  Suffolk,  being  weak  in  body,  but  of 
sound  mind,  praised  be  God  for  the  same,  make  this  my  last  will  and  testament  this  19th  day 
of  August,  1771.  I  desire  to  be  buried  in  the  ffamily  vault  at  Holton.  I  bequeath  unto  my 
sister,  Frances  Stubbin  of  Higham,  spinster-,  the  house  and  farm,  with  all  the  garden,  orchards, 
lands,  pastures,  and  meadows  belonging,  for  the  term  of  her  life,  and  after  her  decease  to  my 
nephew,  John  Stubbin,  eldest  son  of  my  late  brother  John  Stubbin,  and  to  his  heirs.  I  give 
to  my  said  sister  Frances  for  her  natural  life,  the  messuage  now  in  the  occupation  of  John 
Chisnall,  and  afterwards  to  my  said  nephew  John  Stubbin,  charged  with  the  payment  of  seven 
hundred  pounds  in  such  share  as  follows: — To  my  nephew  Josiah,  eldest  son  of  Josiah  Stubbin

to  her  own  for  ever;  and  I  appoint  her  sole  Executrix.

Will  of  Juan  Stubbing  of  (kotU'ttljam,  1661. 

Joan  Stubbing  of  Cottenhara  in  the  County  of  Cambridge,  widdowe,  this  18th  day  of 
July,  1661.  Concerning  the  temporall  estate  which  the  Lord  hath  given  me,  I  give  to  my 
daughter  Stoughton  £150 ;  the  hundred  poundes  to  be  paid  after  my  decease,  and  the  other 
fifty  within  one  yeare  after  my  executor’s  entry  upon  his  land  in  Bobloe.  To  my  daughter 

Joannah  Stubbing  £200;  one  hundred  and  fifty  to  be  paid  her  at  her  age  of  one  and  twenty 

yeares  or  upon  the  day  of  her  marriage,  which  of  them  shall  first  come  to  passe ;  which 

severall  suines  of  money  were  given  by  their  late  ffather,  Mr  Edmond  Stubbing ;  the  other  fifty 
poundes  to  be  paid  her  by  my  executor  within  one  yeare  after  his  entry  vpon  my  land  in 

Bobloe  alias  Bobulo.  To  my  sister  Mns  Deborah  Wooley,  twenty  shillings  to  buy  her  a  ring 

withall,  as  a  remembrance  of  my  love.  1  give  to  my  sone  Edmund  Stubbings  [sic]  all  that 

part  of  the  Mannor  of  Bobloe  heretofore  in  the  possession  of  my  brother,  John  Stubbing,  with 

all  the  houses,  woods,  tythes,  rents  and  reversions  belonging,  scituate  in  Bumpsted  Hellions  in 

Essex,  and  all  other  my  lands  and  tenements,  he  to  pay  the  sumes  of  money  to  his  sisters 

as  is  specified.  I  give  him  all  my  goodes,  and  make  him  my  executor  of  this  my  last  will 

and  testament.  P.C.C.  90  Laud. 

John  Stubbing,  the  brother  named  in  the  will,  was  of  Bobulo  in  Bumpsted  Helion  in 
1638.  The  manor  was  purchased  by  their  grandfather,  William  Stubbing,  in  1546. 


JHanor  of  JBnmpstrf)  Sail. 

“  Edward  de  Vere,  Earl  of  Oxford,  obtained  a  license,  12  May  1580,  to  alienate  this 
Manor  and  lands  called  le  Gibbons  Fee  to  William  Stubbing,  Gent.,  who  held  them  of  the  King. 
He  dyed  30  Dec.  1603,  and  was  succeeded  by  his  son  Richard,  then  aged  60  years.  Edmund 
Stubbing,  Gent.,  his  brother  and  successor,  dyed  6  Sept1'  1630.  William  his  eldest  son  was  30 
years  old  ;  besides  whom  he  had  Thomas,  Henry,  and  John.  William  married  Mary  Collin  and 
dyed  5  Aug.  1638,  leaving  Edmund  his  son,  9  years.  Since  that  time  this  estate  hath  been 
possessed  by  Thomas;  and  by  another  Thomas,  who  dyed  29th  Sept1'  1744,  and  was  succeeded 
by  his  only  son  Thomas  Stubbing,  Esq.,  made  a  Justice  of  Peace  in  January  1744-5.

To  All  and  Singular  unto  whom  these  presents  shall  come,  I  Sr  Edward  Bysshe,  Knight, 
Clarenceux,  Principall  Herald  and  King  of  Armes  of  all  the  South,  East  and  West  parts  of  this 
Realme  of  England  from  the  River  of  Trent  Southward,  Send  Greeting.  Whereas  Anthony  Collett, 
Sonne  of  Anthony  Collett  late  of  Westerfield  in  the  County  of  Suff’olke  Gentleman,  deceased,  and 
Samuell  Collett,  Sonne  of  Philologus  Collett,  second  Brother  of  the  last  named  Anthony  late  of 
Westerfield,  also  deceased,  Have  desired  mee  to  Assigne  unto  them  such  Armes  and  Creast  as 
they  may  lawfully  beare ;  Know  yee  therefore  that  I  have  thought  fitt  to  Assigne  unto  them 
and  either  of  them  the  Armes  hereafter  mentioned,  viz.  : — Sable,  on  a  Chevron  ingrailed  betweene 
three  Hinds  trippant  Argent,  as  many  Annuletts  of  the  first.  And  for  a  Creast,  on  a  Helmet 
and  Wreath  of  their  Colours,  a  Hind’s  Head  coupe  Argent,  with  a  Coller  ingrailed  Sable, 
mantled  Gules,  doubled  Argent,  As  in  the  margent  more  lively  is  depicted.  Which  Armes  and 
Creast  as  before  expressed  I  the  said  Clarenceux,  by  Power  and  Authority  of  my  office  to  me 
granted  by  my  Letters  Patents  under  the  Great  Seals  of  England,  Hoe  by  these  Presents  Assigne 
Give  and  Grant  unto  the  said  Anthony  Collett  and  Samuel  Collett,  and  unto  either  of  them  and 
unto  the  Heirs  of  the  body  of  them  and  either  of  them  lawfully  begotten,  To  be  by  them  and 
every  of  them  borne  with  their  due  Differences,  according  to  the  Lawes  of  Armes  for  ever.  In 
Witness  whereof  I  have  hereunto  affixed  the  Seale  of  my  Office  and  subscribed  my  Name. 
Dated  this  fourteenth  day  of  August  in  the  sixteenth  yeare  of  the  reign  of  our  Sovraigne  Lord 
Charles  the  Second,  by  the  Grace  of  God  of  England,  Scotland,  France  and  Ireland,  King, 
Defender  of  the  Faith,  Ac.  :  And  in  the  yeare  of  our  Lord  One  Thousand  Six  Hundred  and 
Sixty  Eower. 

Edward  Bysshe,  Clarenceux,  King  of  Armes.

Will  of  Jloljn  Collett,  1599. 

The  ffourthe  day  of  Marche,  1599,  in  the  ffortith  two  veare  of  the  Raigne  of  our 
Soveraigne  Ladie  Elizabeth,  I  John  Collett  of  Westerfield  in  the  countie  of  Suff.,  gent.,  make 
and  ordaine  this  my  last  will.  I  comend  my  soule  to  Allmightie  good  and  my  bodie  to  be 
buried  in  the  church  of  Westerfeild.  I  have  greate  care  for  the  payment  of  my  debtes.  My 
executrix  shall  presently  after  my  decease  make  sale  of  all  my  corne,  cattell  and  hay,  and  pay 
[them]  with  the  money  thereof  comyng.  And  my  will  is  that  the  surplusage  shall  remayne  to 
Dameron  Collett  my  daughter.  I  further  geue  [her]  my  coppy  hould  landes  and  tenementes  in 
Little  Claston  and  Much  Claston  in  Essex,  vppon  condition  shee  shall  pay  ffortie  shillinges 
yeerly  to  Edithe  Collett  my  daughter.  In  default  of  payment  the  said  Edithe  shall  have  the 
said  landes  during  her  naturall  life.  To  John  Collett,  my  sonne,  and  his  heires  my  free  land 
lying  in  Westerfeild,  Whitton,  Thurlston  and  Witnesham,  called  Upgates.  To  Dameron  Collett, 
my  said  daughter,  and  to  her  heires,  one  peece  of  ffree  land  lying  nere  Christopher  Ashe  in 
Sainte  Margaretts  parishe  in  Ypswiche.  To  Edith  Collett,  my  daughter,  my  tytle  and  interest 
which  I  haue  in  the  house  which  I  boughte  of  Wilim  Peacocke  and  his  wife,  which  was  given 
to  them  by  John  Dameron,  my  ffather  in  lawe,  during  the  lives  of  the  longer  liver  of  them 
both.  All  the  rest  of  my  goodes  vnbequeathed  shalbe  sould,  and  the  same  to  be  equally  devided 
among  my  children.  I  do  ordaine  the  said  Dameron  Collet,  my  daughter,  my  sole  Executrix. 
I  earnestly  intreate  John  Lany,  esquier,  and  Frauncis  Lucas,  gent.,  to  be  the  overseers  of  this 
will.  And  I  geue  to  the  said  John  Lany  for  his  paynes  fforty  shillinges.  In  the  presence  of 
vs,  Frauncis  Lucas,  Thomas  Burroughe,  John  Collett.  Probatum  fuit  qqinto  die  Junii,  1600, 
Juramento  magistri  Johannis  Burroughe,  notarii  publici,  procuratoris  Damerone  Collett,  filie  et 
executncis.  P.C.C.  46  Wallop.

this  my  Last  Will  and  Testament.  I  bequeath  my  soule  to  Almighty  God,  hoping  for  his  mercy.

and  Whitton,  to  be  equally  divided  between  them  To  my  wife,  Elizabeth  Collett,  all  my 
personal  estate,  enjoyning  her  to  pay  my  debts  and  to  take  care  of  my  decent  buriall.  I  doe 
nominate  and  appoynt  [her]  and  my  sayd  sonne  Cornelius  to  be  joynt  executors. 

Proved  7tl*  May,  1678,  by  the  widow;  power  being  reserved  to  the  other  executor. 

Consistorial  Court  of  Norwich.  Original  Wills,  1678,  No.  14. 

The  seal  is  imperfect,  but  it  is  armorial.  There  is  a  chevron  engrailed  charged  with 
three  annulets,  and  in  base  a  (lion  1)  passant.  In  her  will  dated  7th  February,  1681,  and  proved 
at  Ipswich  21st  Octr  1682,  Elizabeth  Dowsing,  the  testator’s  widow,  devised  her  estate  to  her 
six  children,  Cornelius  Collett,  of  Westerfield,  gent.  ;  Elizabeth  Everitt,  of  Worlingfield,  [sic] 
widow;  Ann,  wife  of  John  Langley,  of  Ipswich;  Mary,  wife  of  Thomas  Browninge,  of  Copdock ; 
Rebeccah,  wife  of  John  Rivett,  of  Bramford;  and  Cadish,  wife  of  John  Hasell,  of  Akenham ; 
nominating  her  son  Cornelius  and  her  daughter  Elizabeth  Everitt,  executors.  She  had  remarried 
Bence  Dowsing,  of  Alderton,  co.  Suffolk,  gent.,  who  had  predeceased  her  by  a  few  months.

these  to  Cornelius  Collett,  my  nephew,  of  Woodbridge,  merchant,  and  to  my  esteemed  friend 
William  Goodwin  of  Earl  Soham,  in  trust  to  sell  the  same  and  divide  the  money  so  arising 
between  the  children  of  my  late  brother  Anthony  Collett,  viz.  : — Anthony,  Cornelius,  Robert, 
William,  Woodthorpe  and  Samuel  Collett,  Margaret  wife  of  John  Russell,  Elizabeth  Collett,  and 
Ann  wife  of  William  Jones,  share  and  share  alike.  Trustees  to  invest  £11,000,  and  let  the 
interest  accumulate  until  my  youngest  daughter  come  of  age.  To  Cornelius  Collett,  my  nephew, 
£1,000,  and  to  the  rest  of  the  children  of  my  brother  Anthony  £225  a  piece.  To  William 
Wallis,  son  of  William  Wallis  of  Birmingham,  co.  Warwick,  and  grandson  of  my  late  brother 
Anthony  Collett,  £200.  All  the  residue  of  my  estate  to  Cornelius  Collett,  my  nephew.  Wit¬ 
nesses  :  John  Davis  Plestow,  Edward  Andrews,  William  Fryett. 

Codicil  7th  Septr  1789.  Whereas  since  making  my  will  I  have  consented  to  the  marriage  of 
my  daughter  with  John  Davis  Plestow  of  Ipswich,  Clerk,  but  according  to  said  will  the  children 
of  my  daughter,  if  she  die  under  age,  would  be  entirely  unprovided  for,  I  do  hereby  devise  all 
my  real  and  personal  estate  to  such  children  in  equal  shares.  But  if  both  she  and  her  issue 
die  under  age  then  the  property  is  to  go  to  my  brother’s  children  as  above,  but  the  said  John 
Davis  Plestow  to  receive  £500.  He  also  to  be  co-executor  with  Cornelius  Collett  and  William 
Goodwin.  Probate  18  Feb.  1790.

Confirmation  of  Arms  to  '#rnro  Jltusbtt,  1576. 

To  all  and  singular,  as  well  nobles  and  gentles  as  others,  to  whom  theis  psents  shall 
come,  Robt.  Cooke,  Esqr,  ats  Clarencieaulx,  Principall  Heraulte  T  Kinge  of  Armes  of  the  south 
Est  and  West  partes  of  this  Realme  of  England,  from  the  Riuer  of  Trent  southwards,  sendithe 
greettinge  in  owre  Lord  Cod  euerlastinge :  And  wheras  auntientlie,  from  the  begininge,  the 
valiant  and  vertious  Actes  of  worthey  parsons  haue  byn  comendid  vnto  the  worlde  wth  sundrey 
monumentts,  remembrances  of  their  good  deseartes  :  Emongest  the  which  the  cheifest  T  most 
vsuall  hath  byn  the  bearinge  of  signes  in  sheildes  caulled  Armes,  wch  are  non  other  then 
demonstrations  of  prowis  T  valoire,  diuersley  distributed  accordinge  to  the  qualiteys  T  deseartes 
of  the  parsons,  that  such  signes  T  tokens  of  the  dilligent,  fayethefull  T  coragous  might  appeare 
before  the  neiglegent,  courd  T  ignorant,  T  be  a  sufficient  cause  to  moue,  stirr  T  kindle  the 
hartes  of  men  to  Imittation  of  virtue  T  nobless :  Euen  so  hath  the  same  byn  T  yet  is 
contynualy  obserued,  to  the  Intent  that  such  as  haue  done  comendable  seruice  to  their  Prince 
or  Cuntrey,  ether  in  warr  or  peace,  may  therefore  both  recieaue  due  honor  in  their  liues,  T 
also  deriue  the  same  succesiuely  to  their  posterity  after  them.  And  beinge  required  of  Henry 
Muskett,  of  Halston  in  the  County  of  Suffolke,  gent.,  to  make  serche  in  the  Registers  1 
recordes  of  my  office  for  such  Armes  T  Creast  as  he  may  lawfully  beare ;  wherupon  at  his 
request  I  haue  made  serch  accordingly  T  do  find  that  he  may  lawfully  beare  the  Armes  T 
Creast  heareafter  folio winge : — That  is  to  say  Siluer,  tow  barrs  betwene  six  leopards’  heads, 
gules :  and  to  his  Creaste  or  Cognisance,  vpon  the  heaulme,  on  a  wi’eathe  siluer  ct  gules,  out 
of  a  crowne  wtu  a  chayne  sables,  a  demy  Antelopp  gould,  mantled  gules,  dubbed  siluer,  as 
more  playnly  Appereth  depicted  in  the  margent.  The  which  Armes  'I  creste,  'I  euery  parte 
and  parcelle  therof,  I  the  sayd  Clarenciaulx  Kinge  of  Armes,  by  power  and  Authority  vnto 
my  office  anexed  I  graunted  by  letters  pattente  vnder  the  great  Seale  of  England,  haue  rattified, 
confirmed  and  allowed,  given  T  granted  vnto  T  for  the  abouesayd  Henry  Muskett,  Gent.,  and 
to  his  posteritye,  wth  their  due  diffrences  to  vse,  beare  and  shew,  in  sheild,  cotearmoure 
or  otherwise,  wthout  impediment,  lett  or  interuption  of  any  pson  or  parsons.  In  wittnesse 
wherof  I  the  sayd  Clarencieulx  Kinge  of  Armes  haue  signed  theis  psents  wth  my  hand  T 
therunto  sett  the  seale  of  my  office,  the  13th  day  of  September  in  the  yeare  of  our  Lord  God 
1576,  and  in  the  23th  yere  of  the  Raigne  of  our  Souraigne  lady  Elizab,  by  the  grace  of  God

SUFFOLK  MANORIAL  FAMILIES. 


The  Arms  originally  assigned  to  the  families  of  Muschett  and  Muskett  were  three  male 
sparrowhawks,  which  were  anciently  termed  “  muskets.”  Thus  the  shield  of  a  certain  Robert 
Muschet,  circa  1259,  is  described  as  “scutum  d’azur  et  tres  muschetz  d’or  ”  ( Matthew  Paris, 
Works,  vol.  vii,  Additamenta ) ;  and  that  of  the  Muschetts  of  Fenditton,  whose  name  is  variously 
spelt  Musket,  Muschet  and  Muchet,  in  the  Rotuli  Hundredorum,  was  Gules,  three  sparrowhawks 
Or.  This  will  be  found,  with  other  quarterings,  on  the  escutcheon  of  their  descendants,  the  Cheneys, 
in  the  Visitation  of  Cambridge,  Harl.  MS.  1534,  fo.  124  b.  In  continental  heraldry,  again,  the  arms 
of  various  families  of  Mouchet  are  variants  of  “  De  gu.  a  trois  emouchets  d’or” — “emouchet” 
being  a  sparrowhawk.  ( Riestap ,  Armorial  General ,  vol.  ii )  But  when  Henry  Muskett  of 
Harleston,  in  Suffolk,  required  Clarencieux  to  search  the  Registers  of  his  office  for  such  arms 
as  he  might  lawfully  use,  that  herald,  recalling  the  statement  that  Harleston  Manor  had  once 
belonged  to  King  Harold  ( Hollingsworth’s  Stowmarket,  p.  44),  deemed  that  its  present  possessor 
could,  very  reasonably,  bear  something  resembling  the  reputed  shield  of  that  monarch,  viz , 

Gules  crusilly,  and  two  bars  between  six  leopards’  faces  Or,  3,  2,  1,  and  so  allowed  him  the 

Argent,  two  bars  between  six  leopards’  faces  Gules,  3,  2,  1,  of  the  grant  or  confirmation. 

Thus  evolved,  the  Muskett  arms  were  set  up,  with  those  of  other  Suffolk  gentlemen,  in  the 
windows  of  Preston  Church,  by  Ryece  the  Antiquary,  in  1631  ( Suffolk  Manorial  Families,  vol.  i, 
p.  103).  They  found  a  place  in  the  dining  hall  windows  at  Butley  Abbey  towards  the  end  of 

the  seventeenth  century  (Op.  Cit.,  vol.  i,  p.  117).  They  were  still  extant  upon  the  quaint  old 

Humphrey  monument  in  Occold  Church  when  Davy  visited  that  parish,  early  in  the  nineteenth 
century.  They  appear,  too,  with  other  quarterings,  on  the  book  plate  of  Francis  Bloraefield,  the 
Norfolk  Historian,  and  upon  the  Blomeficld  monuments  in  the  Church  of  Fersfield,  of  which  he 
was  sometime  Rector.

5® ill  of  SBtlltam  jitnskett,  1594. 

William  Muskett  of  Haughley,  in  the  County  of  Suffolk,  25th  May  1594,  leaves  his  soul 
to  God  the  Father,  Son  and  Holy  Spirit.  To  the  poor  of  Haughley  ten  pounds  to  be  put  to 
interest,  so  that  the  stock  be  not  diminished  but  for  ever  remain.  Alice  his  wife  to  inhabit 
his  freehold  tenement  called  Moares,  with  its  pastures,  for  life.  To  William  Muskett  his  eldest 
son  his  mansion  house  with  its  lands,  except  five  acres  which  he  bequeaths  to  William  Muskett 
his  grandson,  son  of  the  said  William.  Also  lands  and  pastures  called  Mansuers,  Merefield, 

Moorebridge  meadows,  Stannerds  close  and  Denbridge  meadow,  and  the  messuage  called  Moares, 
on  his  wife’s  decease.  To  Richard  Muskett,  his  son,  his  tenement  called  Tothyll,  with  its  lands, 
orchards,  woods  and  underwoods.  To  Henry  Muskett,  his  son,  his  tenement  in  Barton  and  his 
meadows  there.  To  Symon  Muskett,  his  son,  all  bonds,  i&c.,  he  to  pay  all  debts  except  four 
hundred  pounds  which  was  for  the  warranty  of  Gallowfield  and  twenty  two  pounds  which  he 
and  his  cousin,  George  Thresher  of  Rattlesden,  owed  to  Mr  Jenycks  of  Woolpit.  To  John 
Muskett,  his  son,  Cookstolefield  and  Gallowfield,  together  containing  fifty  acres.  To  Thomas 

Auger,  son  of  Alice  his  wife.  To  William  Muskett,  his  eldest  son,  a  cauldron,  the  great  table 
in  the  hall,  his  corslett  and  other  arms.  The  rest  of  his  goods  to  be  divided  equally  among 

his  other  children — but  Symon  to  have  money  in  lieu  of  his  share  of  the  household  stuff. 

William  and  John  Muskett,  his  sons,  to  be  executors.  Probate,  August  1595. 

Arch.  Sudb.  Liber  “  Blomefield,”  fo.  60b. 

The  testator’s  first  wife  was  Joan,  daughter  of  Simon  Bradstreet  of  Gislingham,  one  of 
the  three  wealthy  yeomen  of  the  name  who  were  assessed  for  the  Suffolk  Subsidy  of  1543 

(35  H.  8).  It  is  all  but  proven  that  Simon  Bradstreet,  Rector  of  Hinderclav  in  Suffolk,  and 
afterwards  of  Horbling  in  Lincolnshire,  the  father  of  Simon  Bradstreet,  Governor  of  Massachusetts, 

was  of  this  family.  Simon  Muskett  of  Gray’s  Inn,  the  testator’s  son,  is  known  to  have  be¬ 
friended  one  at  least  of  the  many  Bradstreets  who  took  priests  orders  in  the  sixteenth  and 

seventeenth  centuries.

xxij  yeares  last  past,  between  the  said  George  and  Grace  Poole,  your  Oratrix’  mother,  conveyed 
a  messuage  and  lands  in  Felsham  to  the  said  George  and  Grace  and  the  heirs  of  their  bodies ; 

and  from  that  time  forward  the  said  George  Groome  tooke  the  rents  and  pi’ofitts  thereof.  He 

died  about  xxi  yeares  sythens,  having  issue  your  Oratrix  Dorothie,  and  Grace  his  widow  took 
the  rents,  dying  about  xx  yeares  since,  when  the  Felsham  messuage  descended  to  your  Oratrix 
Dorothie,  as  their  sole  daughter  and  heire  in  tayle.  She,  being  about  the  age  of  haulf  a  yeare, 
was  brought  up  by  Roger  Groome,  her  grandfather,  who  had  the  deedes  aud  evidences  con¬ 
cerning  the  messuage.  When  verye  aged  Roger  did  take  to  wyffe  one  Dorothy  Leeche,  a  younge 
maide,  and  had  a  son  by  her.  He  was  then  seised  of  messuages  and  lands  in  Yardelye,  co. 

Essex,  and  Rattlesden  and  Elmswell,  co.  Suffolk.  He  made  Dorothie  Leech  a  joynture  for  life 

of  the  Rattlesden  messuage  and  dyed  about  xij  yeares  sithens.  Dorothie,  his  widow,  who  has 
since  taken  to  husband  one  George  Cocksedge,  tooke  Letters  of  Administration  and  did  get  into 
her  hands  all  the  deeds  and  wrytinges  concerning  the  aforesaid  messuages,  and  refuseth  to 
deliver  them  to  your  Orators.  They  seek  to  defraude  yor  Orators  of  the  lands  and  tenementes 
in  Suffolk,  and  to  entytle  John  Groome,  the  infant  sonne,  to  the  same :  pretending  that  Roger 
Groome,  about  a  quarter  of  an  hower  before  his  death,  did  make  a  deed  of  feoffement,  to  the 
use  of  his  will  made  not  haulfe  an  hower  before,  and  did  give  all  his  lands  to  the  said  John 
Groome,  his  child ;  endeavouring  to  disinherit  your  Orators. 

In  the  very  interesting  depositions  which  follow,  it  is  stated  that  Grace  Poole  and  John 
Muskett  were  both  near  of  kin  to  Simon  Muskett,  Counsellor  at  law,  who  conducted  the  case 
for  the  Plaintiffs.  See  also  “  Muskett  contra  Groome,”  Chan.  Proc.,  series  ii.

Haughley,  and  Dagworth,  and  of  closes,  some  containing  from  fifteen  to  twenty  acres,  called

Bell,  of  Bury  St.  Edmund’s,  gent.,  of  the  second  part,  and  the  said  Henry  Muskett,  second  son 
of  the  said  Richard,  and  Mary  Bury,  singlewoman,  one  of  the  daughters  and  coheirs  of  Richard 
Bury,  late  of  Worlingham,  near  Beccles,  gent.,  deceased,  of  the  third  part,  that  the  said 
Richard  Muskett,  in  consideration  of  a  marriage  to  be  solemnized  between  the  said  Henry 
Muskett  and  Mary  Bury,  and  for  a  competent  jointure  for  the  said  Mary,  should  assure  the  foresaid 
messuages  and  lands  to  the  use  of  the  said  Henry  and  the  heirs  of  their  bodies.  On  the  first 
of  February  following  the  marriage  was  solemnized  at  Elsing  aforesaid,  and  the  said  Henry  and 
Mary  became  seized  of  the  aforenamed  lands.  Afterwards,  on  the  7th  of  February,  17th  James  I, 
Henry  Muskett  died  at  Bury  St.  Edmund’s.  Anne  Muskett,  his  daughter  and  sole  heir,  was  then 
of  the  age  of  two  years,  five  months  and  twenty-four  days.  Richard  Muskett,  his  father,  and  Mary, 
his  widow,  were  still  living.  Murtons  and  divers  of  the  lands  specified  were  held  of  the  King 
in  capite  for  military  service.  Inq.  post  mortem,  18tb  James  I.

The  twentieth  day  of  October,  1626,  I,  Richard  Muskett  of  Bury  St.  Edmond,  gent., 
the  vnprofitable  servant  of  God,  beinge  stricken  into  yeares,  that  is  to  say,  of  the  age  of 
eighty  yeares  &  vpwards,  weake  in  body  but  stronge  in  minde  &  in  pfect  health,  doe  declare 
this  my  last  will.  And  first  I  doe  with  a  free  hart  render  and  give  againe  into  the  hand  of  my 
Creator  my  spirritt,  which  he  of  his  fatherly  goodnesse  gave  me,  nothinge  doubtinge  but  for 
his  infinite  mercies  he  will  receive  my  soule  into  his  glory  ck  place  it  in  the  company  of  the 
heavenly  Angells  &  blessed  saints.  And  as  toucheinge  my  body,  with  a  good  will  <k  free  hart 
I  give  it  over  to  be  buried  within  the  pish  church  of  Harlston,  neere  vnto  the  Chancell  dore. 
1  give  vnto  Richard  Muskett,  my  nephewe  &  grandchild,  all  my  lands  &  tenements  &  to  his 
heires  for  ever;  provided  that  Mary,  nowe  my  loveinge  wife,  shall  holde  &  enioy  them  during 
the  minoritie  of  the  said  Richard. 

And  because  I  shall  be  much  condempned  of  the  world  for  my  vnnaturall  dealinge  with 
my  said  nephewe  and  grand  child,  Richard  Muskett,  the  sonne  of  Thomas  Muskett  (which 

Thomas  Muskett  was  my  eldest  sonne,  but  is  now  deceased),  to  give  and  assure  a  great  part 
of  my  lands  vnto  Anne  Muskett,  the  daughter  of  Henry  Muskett,  ray  youngest  sonne,  also 
deceased ;  for  the  said  Richard  Muskett,  my  grandchild,  is  also  my  next  heire  at  the  Corhon 
Lawe ;  I  do  pronounce  and  declare  to  God  and  the  world  that  my  meaninge  never  was  that 
the  said  Anne  Muskett  should  ever  have  one  foote  of  lande,  but  that  her  portion  should  be 

in  money.  I  made  no  conveyance  but  reserved  my  lands  to  my  heires  males.  But  I  must 

cotifesse  my  imbecillitie  in  worldly  affaires  was  overpowered  by  Sr  Antbony  Browne ;  and  one 
Mr.  Rockett,  a  scrivener,  being  of  counsell  with  the  friends  of  the  said  Anne  Muskett,  did, 
contrary  to  my  instructions,  make  the  conveyance  in  such  manner  that  the  lands  assured  in 
joynture  vnto  the  mother  of  the  said  Anne  [should]  descend  to  the  heirs  female  as  well  as  to- 
the  heires  male  And  so  by  their  vndirect  dealing  [they]  have  beguiled  me  of  more  land  than  is 
fittinge  for  the  portion  for  an  heire  female,  my  ratike,  estate  and  liveinge  considered. 

I  give  vnto  Mary,  my  wife,  all  my  house,  wherein  I  nowe  dwell,  in  Bury  St.  Edmond’s, 
with  my  furniture,  plate,  jewells,  &c.,  and  appoint  her  to  be  the  sole  executrix  of  this  will. 
Probate  29th  July  1628.

Simon  Muskett,  the  fourth  son  of  William  Muskett  of  Haughley  and  Joan  Bradstreet,. 
his  wife,  entered  Gray’s  Inn  in  February  1583,  and  was  in  due  time  called  to  the  bar.  He 
became  an  able  lawyer,  and  was  much  consulted  by  Suffolk  litigants.  His  signature  is  appended 
to  innumerable  documents  of  the  reigns  of  Queen  Elizabeth,  James  I,  and  Charles  I,  now  at 
the  Record  Office.  He  was  Escheator  for  Suffolk  in  1595  ;  a  Commissioner  for  the  removal  of 


374 


SUFFOLK  MANORIAL  FAMILIES. 


illegal  buildings,  the  prevention  of  overcrowding,  and  the  enforcement  of  sanitary  measures  in 
London  in  1626  ( Fcedera  Rymeri) ;  and  a  Justice  of  the  Peace  for  Middlesex  in  1634.  In  1635 
he  compounded  for  knighthood  ( Calendar ,  State  Papers,  Domestic,  p.  531).  His  Chancery  Bills 
and  Answers,  written  in  the  matchless  English  of  the  days  of  Bacon  and  Shakespeare,  are 
clear,  incisive,  and  eminently  readable.  His  Will  of  1636  was  proved  in  the  Prerogative  Court 
of  Canterbury,  P.C.C.  115  Pile. 

By  his  first  wife,  Mary,  sister  of  Sir  Robert  Newdigate,  of  Hawnes  in  Bedfordshire,  who 
died  in  1613  and  was  buried  in  St.  Andrew’s,  Holborn,  he  had  four  children,  of  whom  only 
one  daughter  survived  him.  Simon,  his  second  son,  was  baptized  at  West  Stow,  near  Bury  St. 
Edmunds,  15th  September  1594,  when  he  was  residing  at  the  Hall,  whose  picturesque  gate 
house,  still  extant,  is  described,  with  illustrations,  in  the  admirable  volume  of  West  Stow 
Registers,  edited  by  the  Rev  Sydenham  H.  A.  Hervey.  He  married  secondly,  in  1615,  Beatrix, 
widow  of  Sir  Thomas  Eden  of  Sudbury  and  lady  of  the  Manor  of  Barnes  in  Whitechapel, 
which  had  been  settled  upon  her  by  Thomas  Goodman,  Esq.,  her  first  husband.  She  also  pre¬ 
deceased  him,  in  1623,  and  was  buried  in  the  church  of  St.  Botolph’s,  Aldgate,  London.  One  of 
her  daughters,  .  .  .  Goodman,  became  the  wife  of  Walter  Halliley  of  Hackney,  who  has  given 
us  an  account  of  his  mother-in-law’s  wardrobe,  which  will  interest  alike  the  antiquary  and  the 
student  of  human  nature.  “  Dame  Beatrice  beinge  in  wante  of  cloathes  and  other  necessaries 
for  a  gentlewoman  of  her  rancke  and  ffashion,  Orators  wife  deliued  vnto  [her]  one  Taffitye 
gowne  laied  with  silver  lace,  at  the  price  of  sixe  poundes ;  one  stuffe  petticoate  at  the  price 
of  ffortye  shillinges  ;  one  hatbond  of  gold  buttons  at  the  price  of  serfven  poundes ;  one  Taffatye 
cloake  lyned  cleane  through  with  Miniver  furre  at  the  price  of  sixe  poundes ;  one  rydinge 
suite  worth  three  poundes ;  one  other  cloake  of  Taffatye  lyned  with  silke  shagge  at  the  price 
of  three  poundes ;  certen  Lynnen,  as  sheetes,  pillowbeeres,  cushion  cloathes  and  table  cloathes, 
to  the  value  of  seaven  poundes ;  and  one  longe  cushion  of  blawe  satten  imbroadered  with  sprede 
eagles  of  golde  at  the  price  of  three  poundes.”  ( Halliley  contra  Muskett,  James  I,  B.  &  A. 
H.  18,  61,  13th  Nov.  1623.) 

In  his  earlier  days  Simon  Muskett  resided  mostly  at  Gray’s  Inn  or  Bury  St.  Edmund’s, 
and  later  on  at  Clerkenwell,  then  a  fashionable  suburb.  After  his  second  marriage  he  lived  at 
his  wife’s  Manor  in  Whitechapel,  as  had  her  other  husbands  before  him.  Robert  Muskett,  his 
eldest  son,  entered  Gray’s  Inn  in  1609,  proceeding  by  and  by  to  Christ’s  College,  Cambridge. 
We  find  his  signature  to  a  Chancery  Bill,  James  I,  B.  &  A.,  S.  39,  38.  But  he  died  young, 
as  did  his  brothers  Simon  and  John.  Mary,  the  daughter,  her  father’s  only  surviving  child, 
married  Thomas  Smallwood  of  Selford  and  had  numerous  descendants,  one  of  whom  entered  a 
pedigree  in  the  Chester  Visitation  of  1664,  which  is  given  verbatim,  with  many  other  details, 
in  Earwaker’s  History  of  East  Cheshire,  vol.  ii,  336.

Mill  of  Joint  ^uskctf,  1665* 

The  18th  day  of  February,  in  the  year  of  the  reign  of  our  soverign  Lord,  Charles  the 
Second  the  18th,  and  of  our  Lord  God  1665,  I,  John  Muskett,  of  Haughley,  in  the  County  of 
Suffolk,  gent.,  taken  very  sick  whilst  I  was  in  His  Majesty’s  service  in  the  wars,  yet  of  sound 
mind  and  memory,  do  make  and  ordayne  this  my  last  will  and  testament.  First  and  principally, 
I  commend  my  soul  to  the  protection  of  Almighty  God,  hoping  through  the  death  and  passion 
of  Jesus  Christ,  my  sweet  Saviour  and  Redeemer,  to  be  made  a  partaker  of  life  everlasting. 

As  touching  that  portion  of  worldly  goods  that  God  in  his  mercy  hath  lent  me,  I  dispose  of 
it  as  followeth.  I  devise  unto  my  four  eldest  daughters,  Ester,  Margaret,  Wynefred  and  Hannah, 
my  capital  messuage  called  Bucles  house,  with  the  buildings,  lands,  meadows  and  feeding  grounds 
belonging,  lying  in  Haughley,  Harleston  and  Shelland.  Unto  my  youngest  daughters,  Rachell 

and  Ann,  my  messuage  lately  purchased  of  Thomas  Daynes,  with  the  orchards,  lands,  pastures 
and  feeding  grounds  adjoining,  lying  in  Bacton  and  Cotton,  now  in  the  tenure  of  Thomas 
Studds,  and  my  leasehold  lands  there.  My  goods,  ready  monies  and  personal  estate  I  give  unto 
my  executrix,  towards  the  payment  of  the  legacies  hereafter  named :  that  is  to  say,  thirty  pounds 
apiece  unto  my  four  eldest  daughters,  and  sixty  pounds  apiece  unto  my  youngest  daughters 

Rachell  and  Ann,  to  be  paid  them  at  their  several  ages  of  one  and  twenty  years,  or  their 

respective  days  of  marriage,  which  shall  first  happen  I  bequeath  unto  my  brother,  Barnabie 

Muskett,  of  Colchester,  ten  pounds ;  he  to  deliver  a  general  release  unto  my  wife  and  eldest 
daughters  of  his  pretended  right  unto  my  capital  messuage.  I  nominate  Wynefred,  my  loving 
wife,  sole  executrix,  and  give  her  the  overplus  of  my  principal  estate  and  [certain]  rents  for 
the  education  and  bringing  up  of  my  younger  daughters  according  their  degree  and  quality. 

I  charge  all  my  daughters  to  be  dutiful  and  obedient  to  their  mother,  especially  in  the  matter 
of  their  marriage.  I  appoynt  my  well  beloved  friend,  Mr.  Thomas  Blomfield  of  Buxhall,  to  be 

supervisor  of  this  will,  and  I  leave  him  for  his  paynes  ten  pounds  Thus,  waiting  the  pleasure 

of  Almighty  God  I  end  this  will  and  sett  thereto  my  hand  and  seale  in  the  presence  of  these 
witnesses — Thomas  Blomfield  Senr,  Robert  Devereaux,  William  Harrison  Senr,  Thomas  Harrison, 
and  others.  Probate  10th  April  1667.  Cur.  Ep.  Norwic. 

The  testator  and  Barnaby  Muskett,  his  brother,  would  seem  to  have  been  sons  of  Henry 
Muskett,  who  married  at  Haughley,  4th  February  1599,  Rebecca,  sister  of  Barnaby  Gibson  of 
that  parish,  and  niece  and  devisee  of  Barnaby  Gibson  of  Stonham,  1594,  P.C.C.  28  Scott.

The  fifth  day  of  May,  1676,  I  Richard  Muskett  of  Methwold,  in  the  County  of  Norfolke,

gold  ringe  I  weare  upon  my  finger  [<fcc.].  To  my  daughter  Hannah  Muskett  ais  Bennett  my 
other  golde  ringe  with  a  seale  of  Armes  I  weare.  To  my  sonne  Samuel  Muskett,  living  in  Bury 
St.  Edmunds,  five  shillings.  To  my  sonne  Charles  Muskett,  living  at  Mr.  Mariton’s  of  Oxburgh, 
linnen  [<fcc.].  The  residue  of  goods  I  bequeath  to  Frances,  my  wife,  and  Hannah  Muskett  ats 
Bennett,  my  daughter,  living  at  Mr.  Parlett  of  Barnham,  clarke,  whom  I  make  my  executrices. 

Cur.  Ep.  Norw.,  Original  Wills,  1678,  No.  186. 


MUSKETT  OF  HAUGHLEY. 


377 


The  testator  was  grandson  and  heir  of  Richard  Muskett  of  Harleston  Parva  in  1627, 
and  cousin  and  heir  of  Anne  Muskett  of  Bury  St.  Edmunds  in  1632.  The  baptism  of  Samuel 
Muskett,  his  eldest  son,  in  May  1640,  is  recorded  in  the  parish  registers  of  Shadingfield.  He 
sold  part  of  his  estate  to  John  Dickenson,  who  had  married  his  uncle’s  widow,  in  1641  {Fine, 
Mich.  16  Chas.),  and  the  remainder  ten  years  later  to  Edward  Wyneve  {Fine,  Fax  ter  1651),  who 
passed  them  on  to  Lady  Penelope  Hervey.  These  she  bequeathed,  in  1660,  together  with  the. 
Manor  of  Harleston,  to  Henry  Gage  Esq.,  her  third  son  {Visitation  of  Suffolk:,  edited  by  Hr.  Howard, 
vol.  ii,  177).  About  this  time  he  seems  to  have  taken  orders,  becoming  curate  of  Northwold  in 
Norfolk  in  1664.  Catherine  his  wife  was  buried  at  Weeting  in  1667  ;  Thomas,  his  son,  at 
Northwold  in  1675  ;  and  he  himself,  on  the  6th  of  October,  1678.  The  one  bequest  in  his  brief 
will,  which  recalls  his  earl}7  prosperity,  is  the  “  golde  ringe  with  a  seale  of  Armes,”  probably  an 
heirloom  inherited  from  his  grandfather.

Charles  Muskett  of  Frenze,  in  the  County  of  Norfolk,  gent.,  the  7th  day  of  September, 
1678.  Unto  Henry  Gibbs  of  Frenze,  my  son  in  law,  three  years  rent  of  the  Lang  Fenns  in 
South  Lopham.  Priscilla,  my  daughter,  his  now  wife.  Unto  Mary,  Thomas  and  Charles  Gibbs, 
my  grandchildren.  Unto  Mary  and  Elizabeth  Watts  my  grandchildren  To  Elizabeth,  the  daughter 
of  John  Blomfield,  of  Farsflield,  gent.  To  John  Muskett,  my  son,  and  his  heirs  all  my  lands  in 
Bardwell,  co.  Suffolk,  and  in  Lopham,  co.  Norfolk,  the  said  three  years  rent  excepted.  I  make  him 
my  executor.  Witnesses  : — Frances  Richards,  John  Womacke,  Thomas  Horneby  and  Robert  Fisher. 
Probate,  21st  Decr  1678  to  John  Muskett,  the  son  named  in  the  will. 

Cur.  Ep.  Norwic.,  Wills  1677,  1678,  fob  128. 


®R:ll  of  Joint  JHustatt,  168$. 

By  his  will  dated  20th  May  1688,  John  Muskett,  of  Botesdale  in  Suffolk,  mercer,  gave  his 
messuages  and  lands  in  Burgate  to  Elizabeth  his  wife  for  life,  and  then  to  Mary  his  daughter. 
To  the  said  Elizabeth  his  wife  he  devised  his  messuages  and  lands  in  Coneyweston,  subject  to 
the  payment  of  an  annuity  of  £12  to  Alice  Muskett  of  Coneyweston,  with  remainder  after  her 
decease  to  the  said  Mary  his  daughter  and  the  heirs  of  her  body,  and  failing  these  to  Henry 
Gibbs  and  Priscilla  his  wife,  testator’s  sister,  for  their  lives.  Said  lands  then  to  be  sold  for  the 
benefit  of  John  Bloinefield  of  Farsfield,  in  Norfolk,  gentleman,  testator’s  cousin.  His  messuages 
and  lands  in  Bressingham  and  South  Lopham  in  Norfolk,  and  in  Ashfield  and  Hepworth  in 
Suffolk,  he  left  to  Elizabeth  Muskett  his  daughter  and  the  heirs  of  her  body,  with  remainder  as 
before  to  Henry  and  Priscilla  Gibbs  and  to  John  Blomefield.  To  Elizabeth  his  daughter  his  silver 
tankard  and  porringer,  and  the  furniture  in  the  hall  chamber.  To  Mary  his  daughter  £500.  To 
Elizabeth  and  Mary  Watts,  his  kinswomen,  to  each  £10.  To  John  Blomefield  son  of  the  said  John 
Blomefield,  John  Breame  son  of  Robert  Breame  of  South  Lopham,  John  Breame  son  of  Charles 
Breame  of  Botesdale,  Thomas  Sargeant  son  of  Thomas  Sargeant  of  Coneyweston,  and  to  William 
Gibbs  son  of  Henry  Gibbs.  Wife  and  John  Blomefield  aforesaid  to  be  executors. 

This  will,  proved  in  the  Bishop’s  Court  at  Norwich,  is  given  verbatim  in  the  Chancery  Proceedings 
in  Muskett  contra  Muskett,  1689  {Reynardson,  1674-1692).  The  testator  did  not  live  to  sign  it.

SPartritige  of  West 


I 


These  pages  are  supplemental  to  161-170  of  this  volume,  and  are  the  result  of  further  research. 

As  stated  at  p.  161,  “Partridge  has  always  been  a  prolific  name  in  Suffolk”- — so  prolific 
that  it  is  convenient  to  study  the  West  and  East  Suffolk  branches  separately.  These  pages 
relate  to  W.  Suffolk  only — i.e.,  including  Hartismere  and  Stow  Hundreds,  as  before  1837 — and 
treat  of  Partridge  of  Acton  and  Partridge  of  Tuddenham  (near  Mildenhall). 

The  following  chronological  list  refers  to  early  bearers  of  the  name  in  Suffolk.  It  should  be 
realised  that,  in  the  original  documents,  the  first  three  letters  of  the  name  are  often  represented 
by  P,  which  may,  with  equal  correctness,  be  extended  into  either  Par  or  Per.  These  documents 
being  written  almost  always  in  Latin,  which  contains  many  more  words  beginning  with  per  than 
with  par,  it  has  become  usual  to  extend  P  into  Per  unless  Par  is  obviously  intended  (Pker,  Pva, 
etc.).  The  etymology  of  the  surname  Partridge  is,  however,  so  uncertain  that  such  forms  of  it  as 
Ptrich  may  be  extended  into  either  Partrich  or  Pertrich. 

Three  etymologies  seem  possible:  (1)  Nickname  from  bird;  (2)  place-name  ending  in  ridge, 
A.  S.  hrycg ;  (3)  Patrick. 

(1)  The  bird’s  name  is  from  F.  perdrix,  from  L.  perdix.  Hence  was,  almost  doubtless,  the 
Perdriz  family  of  Sutton  and  Eastwood,  Essex,  whose  pedigree  (Harl.  381,  fo.  115),  compiled  from 
ten  deeds,  begins  with  Will.  Perdriz,  “  vixit  temp.  H.  1  et  Steph.” ;  his  descendants  are  Perdix  in 
Liber  Rubeus,  596  and  739,  and  Pertriz,  Partriz,  Parteriz,  in  Feudal  Aids,  ii,  137. 

(2)  The  most  probable  are  :  Pettridge  hamlet,  Brenchley,  Kent,  and  Peteridge-Wood,  place  near 
Reigate.  No  examples  can,  however,  be  quoted  with  de  before  surname.  Petridge  occurs  at  Henley, 
Suffolk,  1631  ;  Pertridge  at  Stonham  Aspall,  1589;  Patridg  at  Holton  S.  Mary,  1721  (tomb). 

(3)  “  Patricius  ”  (Saint)  occurs  in  A.S.  Chron.  under  year  430.  Early  in  Henry  Ill’s  reign, 
Patricius1  was  parson  of  Burgate  ;  Patrick2  of  Blundeston  was  dead  by  1274;  Patricius3  le  Escot  of 
Framlingbam  and  Patrick3  of  Framlingham,  1273-74,  were,  apparently,  identical;  also,  perhaps,  Tho. 
Patrick3  of  Framlingham,  1278-79.  In  Suffolk  subsidy  of  1327,  Patric  :  Puntyng  is  sole  example. 

Of  either  (1)  or  (3)  was  probably  a  family  long  of  Hackford-next-Reepham,  Norf.,  first 
mentioned  as  Pertriz4  1250,  as  Pertrij 5  1285,  but  later  always  as  Pertrick  (Partrick).6 7 * 

In  mediaeval  literature,  the  bird’s  name  occurs  as  partryke 7  and  per  try  ke s — so  like  Patrick  (a 
•of  Patricius  is  long  or  short)  that  confusion  may  have  arisen  between  the  bird’s  name  and  Patrick, 
so  that  the  elements  of  partridge  became  fused  into  Patrick,  and  vice  versa,  and,  thus,  some  families 
now  named  Partridge  may  owe  it  to  a  progenitor  Patrick.  An  important  example  is  Will.  Partnc,9 
Berkshire,  1204-5.

Archdeaconry  of  Sudbury,  book  “  Brydone,”  fo.  115  b  el  seq. 

Thomas  Clarbeck  or  Clerbeck,  gentleman,  the  executor,  was  the  last  male  heir  of  an 

ancient  family  of  knightly  rank  long  seated  at  Clerbeck  Manor  in  Acton  (Copinger’s  Manors  of 
Suffolk,  vol.  i,  pp.  6,  9-12).  He  was  son  and  heir  of  Thomas  Clerbeck,  and  grandson  of  Andrew 
Clerbeck  (died  1500).  He  died  7  Dec.  1526,  and,  at  an  inquisition  held  at  Eye  on  18  Sept. 
1527,  it  was  found  that  he  held  a  messuage  called  Clerbeks,  84  acres  of  land,  12  of  wood, 
6  of  meadow,  4  of  pasture,  and  xxxis  viiijd  annual  rents,  in  Acton,  Kettlebaston,  Sudbury, 
Melford,  and  Preston,  and  that  Joan,  wife  of  William  Ttriche,  was  his  kinswoman  [aunt]  and 
next  heir  (to  wit,  daughter  of  Andrew,  father  of  Thomas,  father  of  the  said  Thomas),  and  that 
she  was  aged  fifty  years  and  more.  The  smallness  of  the  estate  may  have  been  because  Andrew 
Clerebek  was  sometime  an  outlaw,  pardoned  in  1477-78  (Copinger’s  Suffolk  Records  <&  MSS., 
vol.  i,  p.  7). 

Thomas  Clerbeck  was  probably  quite  a  young  man  when  he  died  in  1526,  and  it  is 
hardly  likely  that  Robert  Partryche,  when  he  made  him  his  executor  only  fifteen  months  before, 
thought  that  “  hym  that  god  shall  prouyde  to  be  heyre  vnto  Thomas  Clarbeck  gent  soo  he  be 
dwellin  in  Acton  and  be  of  full  age  ”  would  be  Joan,  wife  of  William  Partriche.  No  evidence 

of  relationship  between  this  William  and  Robert  Partryche  (the  testator)  has  yet  been  found, 

but  it  is  highly  probable  that  they  were  related,  and,  in  a  tabular  pedigree  which  follows,  the 
degree  of  consanguinity  is  conjectured  to  have  been  first-cousin-once-removed.  Joan  Partriche  died 
in  1530,  and  “  the  manor  passed  to  her  nephews  William  Lucy,  Henry  Mack-William,  Edmund 
Walgrave,  Roger  Martin,  Richard  Merton,  Edward  Danyell,  Thomas  Ligate,  Thomas  Smerte, 
clerk,  and  John  Cordall,”  and  “was  sold  to  Thomas  Daniel.”1  In  1619,  “the  cheefe  howse  of 
the  Daniells  is  now  buylte  ”  where  the  “  famyly  of  yB  Clerebecks  ”  was  formerly  seated.2  It  is 
now  called  Acton  Place. 

The  Clerbeck  shield — Ermine  three  bars  Gules,  each  charged  with  as  many  crosses  patee 
Or8 — was  quartered  by  the  Rookwoods  through  the  mariiage,  about  1300,  of  Alan  de  Rokewood 
of  Acton  with  Elizabeth,  daughter  and  coheir  of  Walter  de  Clerbecke.3  It  is  said  to  be  on 
the  Rookwood  tomb  (1  1520-21)  in  Stanningfield  church,4  and  in  a  window  of  Hengrave  church. 

If  Joan  Partriche  had  left  issue,  Clerbeck  Manor  would  not  have  passed  at  her  death  to 
her  nine  “  nephews.”  It  is  therefore  conjectured  that  William  Partriche  was  a  widower  when  he 
married  her. 

In  1523-24  (subsidy  yff),  three  Partriches  appear  at  Acton  :  (1)  Robert  P.  (will  above), 
assessed  at  £24,  taxed  £1.4.0;  (2)  Robert  P.,  “  servaunt,”  £1,  taxed  4d  ;  (3)  George  P.  (will  below, 
desiring  burial  at  Lavenham),  £2,  taxed  Is.  No.  (2)  was  perhaps  Rob.  P.  “my  Cosen  [nephew]” 
mentioned  in  said  George  P.’s  will.  In  1524-25  (subsidy  L§£),  Robert  P,  of  Acton  was  assessed  at  £40.

During  1558-1611  there  is  only  one  entry  of  the  name  in  Lavenham  parish-registers  : 
John  Lyllye  and  Eliz.  Patritche  were  married  14  Feb.  15|^.  Those  of  the  adjoining  parishes  of 
Cockfield,  Alpheton,  Long  Melford,  and  Preston  have  none  before  1600.  Great  Waldingfield 
has  one  entry  before  1600  :  Thomas  Partiche  [sic]  was  buried  12  Feb.  154^. 

George  Pateriche,  the  testator,  desired  burial  in  Lavenham  churchyard,  but  does  not  state 
that  his  cousin  (probably  nephew)  Robert  Partriche,  “  wth  whom  I  ame  and  haue  bine  longe 
sicke,”  lived  there.  Lavenham  is  about  7£  miles  S.W.  of  Great  Finborough,  and  it  is  not 
improbable  that  this  Robert  was  identical  with  the  Robert  Partridge  of  Finborough  who  married 
Margaret  Nunn,  died  before  25  Dec.  1558  (see  p.  164),  and  was  father  of  Robert  of  Finborough 
who  entered  his  pedigree,  and  had  his  arms  registered,  at  the  Visitation  of  1577  (see  p.  162).

This  is,  apparently,  the  last  recorded  will  of  Partridge  of  Acton.  In  1522-24  (Lay 
Subsidy,  Suff.,  yf§),  there  was  a  Wyll.  Pterych  at  Great  Welnetham,  and  a  Wyll.  Pterych  at 
Beyton.  In  1527,  the  heiress  of  Tho.  Clerbeck  of  Clerbeck  Manor  in  Acton  was  his  aunt 
Joan,  born  1476-77,  wife  of  a  Will.  Ptriche  (see  p.  394).  The  following  extracts  from  parish- 
registers  are  probable  links  between  Partridge  of  Acton  and  Partridge  of  Bradfield  S.  Clare  and 
Great  Welnetham,  but  no  proof  of  the  relationship  has  yet  been  found.  The  northern  point  of 
Acton  parish  is,  as  the  crow  flies,  4-|  miles  south  of  the  southern  point  of  Bradfield  S.  Clare 
parish,  Lavenham  and  Cockfield  lying  between,  and  5|  south  of  that  of  Great  Welnetham 
parish,  Lavenham,  Cockfield,  and  Stanningfield  lying  between.  Bradfield  S.  Clare  and  Great 
Welnetham  adjoin,  and  the  former  is  2|  miles  south-west  of  Beyton.  Great  Cornard  is  1^-  miles 
south  of  Acton. 

William  Partrich  of  Great  Welnetham,  who  died  in  1586  (see  his  will  below),  married 
Margaret  Adams,  widow.  Adams  occurs  frequently  in  Great  Welnetham  registers,  and  there  are 
six  Manwood  entries  at  Little  Welnetham  (adjoins  Great  Welnetham  and  Bradfield  S.  Clare) 
between  1573  and  1630.  The  discovery  of  Joan  Partridge’s  marriages  at  Great  Cornard  to 
Edmund  Manwood  and  Thomas  Adams,  in  1574  and  1577,  explains  the  bequests  to  “cousins” 
(nephew  and  nieces)  of  those  names  made  in  1624-25  by  Tho.  Partridge  of  Higham  and  Capel 
S.  Mary,  progenitor  of  Partridge  of  Shelley  Hall  (see  pages  168-169).  He  retrieved  the  fortune 
of  the  family,  which  was  fallen  considerably  since  the  days  .of  the  two  opulent  yeomen  Robert 
Parteryche  of  Acton  and  Sudbury  (will  dated  1489)  and  his  son  Robert  of  Acton  (will  dated 
1525);  he  did  not  marry  until  aged  36,  but  he  married  thrice,  and  had  seven  sons  and  three 
daughters ;  he  owned  lands  in  three  parishes,  and  sent  one  son  to  Emmanuel  College,  Cambridge  ; 
his  descendants  are  very  numerous,  and  some  are  still  landowners  in  that  part  of  Suffolk.

The  four  devisees  marked  *  were  probably  children  of  John  and  Bridget  Pertriche  of 
Bradfield  S.  Clare  (see  p.  396),  and,  perhaps,  testator’s  first-cousins.  Joan  was  dead  by  this  date, 
and  Thomas  was  living  far  away  at  Higham  and  was  probably  too  prosperous  to  need  such  a 
small  bequest.

(Extract,  shortened,  from  Ipswich  Great  Court  Books,  27  Ap.  12  James  I  [1614],  fo.  586.) 

“WHEREAS  there  was  latelie  a  Cart  of  Thomas  Partriche  of  Higham  [yeoman]  drawne 

with  seauen  horses  did  Rune  over  John  his  sonne  in  the  highe  weye  nere  the  friers  bridge 
whereby  he  was  sleyne  by  reason  whereof  the  carte  horses  &  furniture  were  forfeited  to  the 
towne  as  a  Deodand  have  bin  seazed  to  the  townes  use  IT  is  nowe  agreed  that  he  shall 

paye  to  the  Chamberlins  of  this  towne  to  the  townes  use  in  Redempcon  of  the  said  goods  xxs. 
in  payment  whereof  he  shall  have  his  goods  ageine.” 

Friars’  Bridge,  Ipswich,  spanned  the  Gipping  between  Boat  (now  Friars’)  Lane  in  S.  Nicholas’ 
parish  and  Portman’s  Walk  in  S.  Peter’s ;  S.  Mary’s-at-Elms  adjoins  Boat  Lane ;  their  registers 

{S.  Peter’s  burials  begin  1658)  do  not  record  John  Partriche’s  burial.  Presumably  the  accident 

happened  on  the  left  bank  near  where  Tanner’s  Lane  met  Boat  Lane  (Monson’s  map,  1848), 
for  why  should  the  (1)  waggon  have  crossed  the  (then)  little  wooden  bridge  to  the  dreary  marshes 
on  the  right  bank  1  John  was  bapt.  at  Higham  15  Mar.  159f,  so  was  aged  12  if  buried  there 
27  May  1608  (the  only  suitable  entry),  which,  though  six  years  earlier  than  the  above  agreement, 
may  tally  with  “  latelie.”  Bacon,  recording  it  ( Annalls  of  Ipswche,  455),  calls  him  “  childe.”  How 
bad  the  roads  were  to  require  seven  horses  for  one  “  Cart  ”  ! 

Dr.  Johnson  defines  Deodand  ( yiven  to  God,  that  is,  to  the  poor)  with  much  detail.  Tho. 
Partriche  may  have  had  a  “friend  at  court”:  his  nephew  John  Manwood  lived  at  Ipswich,  and 
in  1605  a  John  Manwood  was  one  of  the  “Chamberlins”  there.

(Translated  from  contracted  Latin  and  shortened.)  7  May  1477.  John  Partrych  [ptrych]  of  Fordham,. 
Norwich  diocese.  Soul  to  god  almighty,  blessed  Mary,  &c.  Body  to  be  buried  in  churchyard  of  blessed 
Mary,  Fordham.  “  j  comb  ”  of  barley  [each]  to  Fordham  church,  and  gilds  of  corpus  Christi  (of  Fordham, 
for  celebrating),  Jesus,  Holy  Trinity  of  Ixnyng  [Exning],  and  S.  Mildred.  To:  John  Cavenham  Jun.  a  gown 
of  vyolett,  Thomas  Gylby  my  Russet  coloured  gown,  John  Cavenham  sen.  my  black  gown,  Robert  Cogge 
my  green  gown.  To  Margaret  my  wife  my  movable  goods  viz.  cattle  sheep  pigs  and  fowls  and  household 
utensils.  Also  the  income  from  my  lands  in  Ixnyng  for  life,  which  lands  I  then  give  to  John  Partrych  my 
son.  And  for  said  lands  ex  parte  dei  I  require  that  John  cause  to  be  celebrated  two  trentals  of  S.  Gregory 
for  me  [and]  Margaret  and  Isabell  my  wives.  To  Margaret  my  wife  my  lands  in  the  fields  of  Fordham  & 
Saliam  [Soham  |,  held  by  copy  of  court  roll  of  Saham,  for  life.  Then  to  said  John  Partrych.  He  to  pay 
said  Margaret  xxxiij8  iiij'1.  To  John  Partrych  my  batell  exe  [axe],  med  leta  nigra  [sic],  my  red  belt  numere 
deargentate  [sic].  To  Sir  (domino)  William  Cavenham,  supervisor,  my  primer.  To  William  Brampton  A  John 
Poole,  executors,  iij8  iiijd  each.  I  attach  my  seal.  Proved  at  Fornham  14  July  1477.

Hovell  of  Badwell  Ash.  That  portion  of  the  pedigree  in  Harl.  MS.  1560  which  deals  with  the 
Hovells  of  Langham  has  never  been  quite  accounted  for.  It  was  probably  compiled  by  John  Smith 
the  elder,  Fellow  of  Eton  and  Yicar  of  Maple  Durham,  who  was  born  at  Hunston  in  Suffolk  in 
1585.  Now  Hunston  adjoins  Langham,  and  John  Smith  of  Langham  and  Julian  his  wife,  his 
father  and  mother,  are  described  as  of  Hunston  in  the  will  of  Thomas  How,  1607.  ( See  page  52.) 
They  seem  to  have  had  lands  and  houses  in  both  parishes,  and  held  for  a  time  the  manor  of 
Brent  Illeigh.  The  will  of  William  Tipshithe  of  Bradwell  (he  is  called  “  Tepshefe  ”  in  the  pedigree) 

dated  22d  Nov.  1592,  was  proved  in  the  Court  of  the  Archdeaconry  of  Sudbury.  He  names  Joan 

his  wife,  Mary,  Katherine  and  Dorothy  his  daughters,  who  were  then  unmarried,  and  John  Smith 
his  son-in-law,  whom  he  made  his  supervisor.  Like  the  other  Hovells  of  Badwell  Ash,  the  Yicar 
of  Maple  Durham  used  for  the  most  part  the  name  of  Smith ;  but  his  arms,  as  given  in  the 
records  of  King’s  College,  Cambridge,  and  on  his  son’s  ledger  stone  in  the  Chapel,  were  the 
Sable,  a  cross  Or,  allowed  to  the  Hovells  alias  Smiths  of  Ashfield  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664. 

Hovell  of  Sulgrave.  For  Yesterley  read  Yefterley,  meaning  Iffley  in  Oxfordshire. 

Hovell  of  Wyverstone.  Pedigree  A.,  last  descent.  Atleburgh,  should  be  Attlebridge,  co.  Norfolk. 

Pedigree  B.,  third  descent.  For  Wiverseon  read  Wiverston. 

Reconstructed  Pedigree,  last  descent  but  one.  For  Robert  Monceux,  17  R.  2,  1289,  read  Robert 

Monceux,  17  R.  2,  1394. 

Hovell  of  Wyverstone.  In  Cowling  alone,  as  we  have  already  said  (see  page  80)  and  the  adjacent 

village  of  Kirtling,  do  we  find  traces  of  an  unbroken  line  of  Hovells,  from  the  days  of  Edward 

the  First  to  those  of  Queen  Elizabeth.  Another  link  between  them  has  recently  been  discovered 
in  the  Probate  Registry  at  Bury,  in  the  will  of  Richard  Hovell,  1450,  which  we  subjoin  : — 

“  In  Dei  no’ie  Amen.  xij°  die  August’  A0  D’ni  1450  :  Ego  Ric’us  Hovyle  de  Cowleng  &c.  (sic). 

It’  lego  sum’o  altari  mea’  optima’  vacca’,  corp’  ad  sepultura’.  It’  lego  conc’t’  f’rm  b’e  me’  Cantab’r 

xs.  It’  frib’  de  Babwell  xs.  It’  volo  qd  Joh’  Hovell  frat’  men’  et  Margar’  ux’  sua  h’eant  ten’

Exning,  his  distant  cousin;  an  error  which  has  led  to  repeated  mistakes  on  the  part  of  succeeding 
genealogists.

Collett  of  Westerfield.  As  with  the  Hammonds  of  Ufford  ( see  vol.  i,  269),  one  at  least  of  the 
Colletts  of  Westerfield  seems  to  have  emigrated  to  Norway  towards  the  close  of  the  seventeenth 
century.  A  member  of  the  family  writes,  “  I  think  it  was  in  1877,  when  travelling  in  Norway, 
I  met  with  a  Mr  Collett  living  in  a  charming  house  called  Lundbygaard  near  Nestved,  at  the 
southern  extremity  of  the  island  of  Sielland.  He  told  me  that  his  family  came  out  from  England 
in  the  reign  of  James  II.  They  settled  first  in  Bergen,  then  removed  to  Christiania  and  eventually 
to  Denmark.  He  shewed  me  a  house,  a  very  handsome  one,  in  Sielland,  which  had  belonged  to 
the  Colletts ;  and  over  the  chimney  pieces  were  carved  our  Collett  arms.”  Mr.  Alf  Collett  of 
Christiana,  who  published  “  Families  Collett,”  was  one  of  this  family. 

Muskett  of  Haughley.  There  was  a  younger  branch  of  the  Haughley  Musketts,  whose  eighteenth 
century  gravestones  line  the  path  leading  to  the  chancel  door.  Amongst  their  descendants  were 
Thomas  Willis  Muskett,  an  officer  who  served  in  the  Peninsular  war,  and  his  brother,  George  Alfred 
Muskett,  M.P.  for  St.  Alban’s  in  the  earlier  half  of  the  nineteenth  century.  Mary  Anne,  the 
daughter  of  the  latter,  married  Henry  Woodman  of  Rickmansworth.
